Fix: Pass authentication credentials to verifyRepository in testAppInstall

The testAppInstall function was calling verifyRepository without passing
authentication parameters (repoauth, specVersion, appName), causing
"Basic authentication required but no credentials provided" errors for
private registry images (AWS ECR, Azure ACR, Google GAR, etc.).

This fix ensures that component authentication credentials are properly
passed through to verifyRepository during test app installations, matching
the pattern used in appSpawner.js.

The fix maintains backward compatibility - when component.repoauth is
undefined, it's passed as null and verifyRepository handles it gracefully
by skipping credential setup.

fix price calculator

Fix private registry authentication for AWS ECR/Azure ACR/Google GAR

This commit fixes three related issues preventing private registry
authentication from working correctly:

1. **testAppInstall missing auth parameters** (appInstaller.js:1098-1103)
   - testAppInstall was calling verifyRepository without authentication
   - Now passes repoauth, specVersion, appName, and architecture
   - Fixes "Basic authentication required but no credentials provided" error

2. **verifyAndPullImage missing appName** (appInstaller.js:297)
   - verifyAndPullImage was calling getCredentials without appName parameter
   - appName is required for per-app provider caching isolation
   - Affected installapplocally endpoint

3. **ECR/ACR/GAR images failing useable check** (imageVerifier.js:135-136)
   - Old check: parts.length === 4 (required namespace)
   - New check: !!provider && !!repository && !!tag
   - Namespace is optional (only Docker Hub uses it)
   - ECR format: 123.dkr.ecr.region.amazonaws.com/repo:tag (no namespace)
   - Docker Hub: registry-1.docker.io/library/nginx:latest (has namespace)

Tested with AWS ECR images. Both v7 (PGP-encrypted) and v8+ (plaintext)
enterprise apps continue to work correctly.

Fix enterprise app removal on non-Arcane nodes

Prevents local database corruption and ensures proper cleanup of ports/firewall rules

## Problem
When an app was upgraded to enterprise, non-Arcane nodes would:
1. Update local DB with encrypted specs (losing port/container info)
2. Fail to remove the app (couldn't decrypt specs)
3. Leave orphaned database entries and location broadcasts

## Solution
1. Check for enterprise apps BEFORE updating local database
2. If local DB already has encrypted specs (compose: []):
   - Query permanent messages for last non-enterprise version
   - Temporarily restore non-enterprise specs to local DB
   - This provides port/container info needed for proper cleanup
3. If no non-enterprise version found, skip removal to avoid orphaned containers
4. Call removeAppLocally() which now has proper specs for full cleanup

## What gets cleaned up
- Docker containers and networks
- UPnP port mappings
- Firewall rules
- Port allocations
- Database entry
- Network location broadcasts

the socket without resolving or rejecting the Promise, causing infinite
hangs when network connections timed out without triggering errors.

- socket.destroy() doesn't always trigger the 'error' event
- Promise waits forever for resolution that never comes

connectivity to nodes with network issues (lines 409-451 in appSpawner.js).
Multiple arcane nodes had spawners hung since Feb 13, 2026 when checking
roundcubemail instances.

Fix:
- Add 'settled' flag to prevent double resolve/reject
- Centralize cleanup logic in cleanup() function
- Timeout handler now properly rejects via cleanup(false)
- Prevents Promise from hanging indefinitely

Impact:
- Fixes spawner hangs affecting makdi1 and other apps
- Prevents future hangs when checking Syncthing connectivity
- No behavioral change for successful connections

fix: remove arcaneSender intake check, default to true in sync responses

The arcaneSender field provides no actual security: it's an unauthenticated
field in the message body that any node can set, so a malicious sender forging
junk enterprise messages just sets it to true. The only nodes the gate
actually blocks are honest ones doing legitimate hash sync from peers that
lost the field during permanent-storage promotion.

Concretely: arcaneSender is set on the temp message at submission, gossiped
with the message body, and stored in temp DB. When promoted to permanent, the
field is dropped (the permanent message structure never included it). After
that, any peer responding to fluxapprequest reads from permanent and sends
arcaneSender: false, which the receiver's gate then drops silently. Fresh
nodes (e.g. chud after a full resync) cannot recover any post-promotion
enterprise message via hash sync — ~800 stuck messages on chud, ~97% v8
enterprise.

Phase 1 of removing arcaneSender:

- messageStore.js: drop the gate in storeAppTemporaryMessage. Hash and
  signature verification still run; arcane receivers still decrypt and
  validate enterprise specs via the existing isSystemSecure branch.
- fluxCommunicationMessagesSender.js: respondWithAppMessage now defaults
  arcaneSender to true (?? true) when responding from permanent storage,
  preserving any value from temp storage. Compatibility shim for pre-upgrade
  nodes that still gate on the field — to be removed once the network has
  rolled past this commit.

All other places that set arcaneSender (updateAppGlobaly, registration paths,
temp DB storage) are unchanged in this commit so old nodes continue to accept
messages from new nodes during the upgrade window. Phase 2 removes the rest
of the field once the network has upgraded.

fix: remove rejected hash flag entirely

The `rejected` flag was added to make signature-verification failures
permanently sticky, intended to prevent the wordpress1735018430692
ownership-race message from cycling through retry/messageNotFound forever.
In practice it caused widespread false rejections.

The intake-time rejection in storeAppTemporaryMessage fired any time
hash-sync delivered a batch where a child message was processed before
its parent (a registration or owner-changing update) was promoted to
permanent storage. The verifier looked up the previous owner via
getPreviousAppSpecifications, which only reads from permanent — so it
returned a stale ancestor with a different owner, the signature check
failed, and the hash was permanently flagged rejected with no recovery
path. On chud's first sync after the arcaneSender fix, ~25 of 29
rejected hashes were probably false-positives of this kind (the "test"
trio at h:1626859/1626887/1626889 was the smoking gun: same owner as
the registration, no race, but rejected because the registration arrived
after the updates in the websocket batch).

cpuBurstHelper: restore per-container host-fairness cap

The previous commit on this branch dropped the per-container host-cpu cap
along with burstMultiplier and reservedCores, on the (incorrect) reasoning
that the cap was theatre. It was not — for any container whose cpu count
exceeds half of (hostCpus - reservedCores), the cap is the binding
constraint that prevents a single app from being able to consume the
entire host during a burst window.

Concretely, a 12-core app on a stratus (16-core) host without the cap
would have burstUs = quotaUs = 1_200_000us, peak = quota + burst = 24
cores worth of CPU-time per period. Physical reality clamps that to the
host's 16 cores, but the app would consume 100% of the host for ~100ms
during each burst, starving systemd / fluxos / sshd / monitoring.

Restore the cap with the new burstUs = quotaUs starting point:

    burstUs = quotaUs                                  // kernel max
    maxPeakUs = (hostCpus - reservedCores) * period    // host fairness
    maxBurstUs = max(0, maxPeakUs - quotaUs)
    if burstUs > maxBurstUs: burstUs = maxBurstUs

For each tier with reservedCores=1:
- cumulus  (4 cores): apps ≤ 1.5 uncapped; 2 → burst=1; 3 → burst=0
- nimbus   (8 cores): apps ≤ 3.5 uncapped; 4 → burst=3; 7 → burst=0
- stratus (16 cores): apps ≤ 7.5 uncapped; 8 → burst=7; 12 → burst=3; 15 → burst=0

When the cap reduces burstUs to 0, the cgroup file is written with 0
(default kernel behavior, no banking), isBurstActive returns false, and
the throttle loop falls through to its normal throttling path — exactly
the same behavior as a non-enterprise app. No special-casing required;
the ground-truth gating handles it for free.

Note: this is a per-container cap, not a host-aggregate budget. Multiple
burstable containers on the same host can collectively oversubscribe
during simultaneous spikes; CFS handles contention proportionally. Real
CPU isolation (isolcpus / cgroup affinity) is the right answer if a
guaranteed reservation is needed and is independent of burst.

Tests: 9 new cap cases covering all 3 flux node tiers (cumulus 4-core,
nimbus 8-core, stratus 16-core) with the cap binding and not binding.
35 tests total, all green.

feat: app tampering detection and txhash-based DOS enforcement

Introduces two new services and a manually-curated blocklist so operators
can flag nodes that show repeated signs of tampering and have them fail
benchmarks until the condition clears.

appTamperingDetectionService records events (container_vanished,
network_pruned, mount_vanished, crontab_wiped, recreation_failed) from
existing lifecycle hooks. Each call inserts a new row in a new
apptamperingevents collection with a 30-day TTL on detectedAt; history

appTamperingBlocklistService fetches a flat txhash list
(helpers/tamperingblockednodes.json on RunOnFlux master), waits for
fluxd sync on startup, then every 12h checks whether this node's
collateral txhash is listed AND has more than 10 tampering events. If
both hold, it sets a sticky DOS message that is not cleared by other
DOS checks; only the next 12h tick can clear it (if the txhash leaves
the list or events drop).

Sticky DOS is implemented in fluxNetworkHelper via a parallel
stickyDosMessage/stickyDosState slot; getDosMessage and getDOSState
prefer the sticky slot when set, and setDosMessage(null) no longer
clears it.

events count toward the 10-event threshold used by the blocklist

feat: app-to-app network linking via networkWith description token

An app owner can link an app to other apps by embedding a token in the
app description text: networkWith:[appA,appB] (brackets required, quotes
optional, key case-insensitive, comma separated). This is purely
node-local behaviour — no app specification field, no validation change,
no network consensus impact.

When the token is present:
- Before install/redeploy, the node verifies every named app is
  installed locally and owned by the same owner; otherwise the operation
  fails.
- Each of the app's component containers is attached to the private
  docker network of every linked app (fluxDockerNetwork_<linked>), so it
  can reach that app's components by docker DNS name
  flux<component>_<linkedApp>, as if both apps were a single app.
- When a linked-to app is (re)deployed, any locally installed app that
  is networked with it is reconnected to its network.

New module appNetworkLinker.js holds the parser, the install gate, and
the forward/reverse network wiring. The gate and forward wiring run in
installApplicationHard/installApplicationSoft (the only callers of
appDockerCreate), so every container-creation path is covered, including
direct callers that bypass registerAppLocally (container health recovery
and legacy v<=3 redeploys). Reverse wiring runs in registerAppLocally and
softRegisterAppLocally; a boot-time reconcile sweep re-applies all links.

dockerService gains an idempotent appDockerNetworkConnect helper.

Adds tests/unit/appNetworkLinker.test.js (parser, gate, wiring,
reconcile) and appDockerNetworkConnect coverage in dockerService.test.js.

  report a backed-up app as running so the network ignores the deliberate stop).

  enterprise apps are stored with compose: [] - every sweep silently skipped
  them. Decrypt leniently (7-day cache) to enumerate components; for an app
  that fails to decrypt, enqueue its existing docker containers instead so
  reconciles sit in defer-retry and converge the moment fluxbenchd answers.
  decryptEnterpriseSpec shares one in-flight benchd attempt per spec and
  remembers failures for 60s so a fleet of retries cannot hammer benchd.

- first post-boot broadcast: the firstRun bypass allowed an empty snapshot,
  and the receive side treats an empty v2 message as "delete every
  appsLocations row for this IP" - the sender stores its own message first,
  so a reboot race erased the node's own network presence fleet-wide. Empty
  snapshots are never broadcast now (every legitimate correction has a
  targeted mechanism: fluxappremoved, sigterm/TTL expiry); broadcasts wait
  for the reconciler boot drain to settle (one reconcile pass per boot-held
  component, capped at 2min); a reconciler container start triggers a
  coalesced broadcast so a backoff straggler refreshes its row inside the
  ~7min sigterm TTL window instead of at the hourly tick.

  whole-app, before the docker op, mirroring appStart) - previously a user
  restart left the lock set and the reconciler silently re-stopped the app.

- vanished-container classification: an inspect failure now requires docker's
  own container list to confirm absence (the reachability probe fetched the
  list and discarded it); if the container is listed the failure was
  transient - defer, no tamper event, no recreate. Recreate-failure removal
  re-checks existence first: a redeploy racing the recreate window, or a
  recreate that failed after creating the container, no longer ends in
  removeAppLocally uninstalling a healthy app.

- stoppingContainers is operation-scoped: appDockerStop/appDockerKill clear
  the flag in finally (as appDockerRestart already did) instead of leaving it
  for the docker die event - a lost event (stream outage) leaked the flag and
  permanently wedged the reconciler for that component. The flag now holds
  for exactly the operation's duration (hours under v9 graceful shutdown is
  fine) and cannot leak. Stream error/end/close funnel into one guarded
  resubscribe: close was previously unhandled (silent loss of crash
  recovery), and error+end firing together doubled the event stream.

feat(apps): redesign syncthing follower convergence - evidence-gated ladder, no recovery restarts (S2/S3)

Grounded in a live 4-node POC against the fleet's syncthing v2.0.x (isolated
instances on charlie/salad/squidward/legume) plus the maintainer record. Key
verified facts the old machinery contradicted: inSyncBytes is block-granular
while pulling (flat bytes while ACTIVE is healthy, e.g. long sync-preparing);
db/completion reports a stale 100% for DISCONNECTED peers (remoteState is the
connectivity discriminator), so a source-node reboot made every follower pass
the peers-synced check and delete its partial copy ~10 minutes in; a real
inert no-retry state exists (failed pull never retries again) whose surgical
cure is a device pause/resume (~30s), which is the only useful thing the
process restart ever did - at node-wide cost; local changes in a receiveonly
folder are invisible to every completion metric and promotion broadcast them
cluster-wide in ~2s; source outages self-heal on reconnect with partials
preserved.

The redesign, replacing stall->stop->restart-syncthing->remove in the folder
state machine and warn->stop->restart->remove in the health monitor:

- Stall ladder (state machine): byte progress or an active folder state is
  healthy; idle+flat past stallNudgeAfterMs with a CONNECTED synced peer ->
  device pause/resume nudge with doubling backoff; removal only after
  stallRemoveMinNudges nudges over stallRemoveMinWindowMs with zero progress
  (this node provably cannot ingest; data preserved on a verified peer). No
  connected synced source, or unreadable status -> wait + alert, never remove
  (source outages self-heal; removal-by-blindness deletes good copies).
- Peer trust: checkIfPeersAreSynced requires remoteState === 'valid' in
  addition to completion 100 and globalBytes > 0.
- Promotion gate: a synced follower with receiveOnlyChangedFiles > 0 is not
  promoted; db/revert clears the local changes and promotion follows once the
  folder is verifiably clean. The leader/cold-start path is exempt - its
  local data IS the seed.
- Health monitor is a watchdog: alert + nudge only. The container-stop rung
  (unrecorded drift the reconciler immediately undid - the two actors fought),
  the restart rung and the 2.5h removal are deleted.
- Events consumer (new): one persistent filtered subscription (FolderSummary,
  FolderCompletion, FolderErrors, StateChanged) accelerates the SAME
  evaluation the periodic poll drives; id gaps/regressions trigger a resync;
  a dead stream degrades to poll cadence - latency, never correctness.
  FolderErrors events are kept as the durable per-folder error record (scans
  wipe the polled error endpoints). Same hardening idiom as the docker
  die-event stream.
- systemResume posted to /rest/system/pause (resume would have wedged the
  device permanently) - fixed; load-bearing for the nudge. The startup-safety
  syncthing restart after a live-applied receiveonly PATCH is dropped.

Ladder windows are config-tunable (syncthing.stallNudgeAfterMs et al) with
production defaults in config; harness suites use compressed values.

fix(apps): close the reconciler runtime-state gaps from the PR #1755 review (S4-S8)

S4 - a removed component's in-memory controller verdict now dies with it:
appUninstaller fires a component-removed seam (beside the durable runtime-state
clear, same identifier list, all successful-teardown paths incl. force) which
serviceManager wires to appReconciler.clearControllerDesired - the third
instance of the callback-seam pattern (appReconciler already requires the
uninstaller; a back-require would capture a stale partial export). A
reinstalled g:/r: app awaits a fresh election instead of inheriting the
pre-uninstall verdict.

S5 - the controller verdict is re-read at actuation time: the syncthing
decider's stop wrapper runs outside the reconciler's single-flight, so it can
flip the verdict and begin a data wipe while reconcile() is awaiting between
its entry-time read and the start. Starting onto a folder mid-wipe corrupts
the fresh sync; the re-read aborts the start and the decider's own enqueue
drives the follow-up.

S6 - zelappsruntimestate integrity. Concurrent first upserts both insert
without a unique index, and every later update then matches an ARBITRARY twin,
scattering fields across docs (the operator lock on one, the backoff history
on the other) - the stop lock becomes nondeterministic, durably. Now: the
module normalizes identifiers at its own storage boundary (six call sites pass
the bare form by convention; convention across files is not an invariant),
prepareCollection() merges existing twins field-wise (lock is OR - dropping a
doc whole could drop a real lock, whose loss auto-starts a deliberately
stopped app; histories union+trim; newest exit wins) before creating the
unique index, and setFields retries once on a duplicate-key error (under a
unique index the upsert loser THROWS instead of converting to an update - the
retry lands it).

S7 - the crash-backoff ladder resets only on a PROVABLE stable run: death time
minus start time over the threshold, where death evidence is the recorded die
event or docker's State.FinishedAt threaded in from the inspect the reconciler
already performed. The old check reset on time-since-attempt, which counts
time sat stopped in backoff - any rung longer than the stable window laundered
a crash loop's history, making the 30m cap unreachable. FinishedAt also covers
the routine evidence gaps: deaths during reboot/FluxOS restarts are never
event-recorded, and without docker's own record a healthy app would accumulate
boot starts in its history and pay a deep rung on its first real crash. The
ladder and stable window are config-tunable (fluxapps.crashBackoffDelaysMs /
crashBackoffStableRunMs) with production defaults, so integration suites can
walk the full ladder in suite time.

S8 - a failed appDockerStart schedules its own retry instead of being dropped
until the hourly sweep (no die event fires for a start that never ran). Pacing
is free: the attempt was recorded before the start, so persistent failures
walk the backoff ladder; reconciler:actuated {action:'startFailed'} makes the
path harness-observable.

fix: FluxOS owns app volume mounting; unmounted app dirs are inert

App data volumes (FLUXFSVOL loop mounts) were remounted after reboot by a
root @reboot crontab entry created at install time. That entry was
unreconciled - installs rewrote the whole crontab and could silently drop
it - and it was also the only record of the backing image's location:
uninstall parsed the mount command to find the image to delete. A vanished
entry therefore meant volumes that never remounted after reboot (the app
dir silently degrades to a plain host directory that syncthing and the
container bind write into, bypassing the app's quota) and orphaned multi-GB
images on removal. This shipped as two failure modes of a production
data-loss incident.

FluxOS now owns the mount as level-based desired state:

- volumeService gains isPathMounted, getVolumeFilePath (deterministic image
  discovery: eligible df volume roots, the appvolumes directory, and the
  legacy glued '<fluxDir>appvolumes' location older versions wrote to), and
  ensureAppVolumeMounted (idempotent; mounts rw so a dirty journal replays;
  treats a lost mount race as success; never deletes leaked content - it is
  shadowed, loudly).
- appReconciler asserts the volume is mounted before ANY actuation (data
  wipe, mount-path creation, container start) and defers with a paced retry
  when it cannot be - an app whose volume is unavailable stays inert. A
  missing backing image records a tampering event once.
- the startup pass (crontabAndMountsCleanup) mounts every installed app's
  volume derived from the installed-apps DB, crontab-independent, and then
  removes the superseded legacy @reboot entries (a surviving entry could
  double-mount over a FluxOS-owned mount on a later boot). The old pass
  also force-removed apps when a crontab rewrite failed; no app-lifecycle
  action remains in this path.
- createAppVolume no longer creates a crontab entry, and appUninstaller
  discovers the image to delete via getVolumeFilePath (crontab parse kept
  only as a legacy fallback) - removals no longer orphan images.
- ensureMountPathsExist refuses to create app structure on an unmounted
  app dir (it would land on the host filesystem) and mounts the volume of
  referenced components before touching their paths.

The unmounted mountpoint is additionally made physically inert: it is set
immutable (chattr +i) while empty, before mounting, so any write through it
while the volume is unmounted fails with EPERM instead of silently landing
on the host filesystem; the mounted volume shadows the flag, and uninstall
clears it before removal. Volume construction paths also move from shell
string interpolation (node-cmd) to execFile-based serviceHelper.runCommand
with args as params, and the appvolumes path is built with path.join - the
old string concat glued the directory name onto the flux dir.

fix: syncthing mount-safety guard gates on the mountpoint, not content

verifyFolderMountSafety only blocked a folder when it was unmounted AND
empty. But when a volume is unmounted, syncthing pulls the peer's data onto
the bare app dir on the host filesystem - content flips true, the guard
passes, and a folder that was sendreceive stays sendreceive on a
non-mountpoint. If that node was the former master, its stale index then
broadcasts deletions to the healthy master. This was observed live: it
gutted a production app's master replica.

- An unmounted app dir is now NEVER safe to sync, whatever it contains
  (content on the bare dir means writes already leaked onto the host
  filesystem; it also records a tampering event).
- New verifySendReceiveFolderSafety, used on every path that keeps or makes
  a folder sendreceive, additionally detects a stale ("phantom") index over
  an empty volume: the global index claims data while the disk holds no
  file in the folder's sync scope (.stignore and backup/ are outside it).
  That state is exactly the precondition for a mass deletion broadcast.
  Syncthing's own API cannot report this - its local counts come from the
  same stale index - so the disk is probed directly. A legitimately empty
  folder (index empty too, e.g. a cold-start seed) does not trip it.
- The detection is actionable: when the volume is unmounted the state
  machine and the per-cycle folder check first try ensureAppVolumeMounted
  and re-verify, instead of only blocking.
- On an unsafe verdict the container is now actually held: the folder goes
  receiveonly (as before) AND the reconciler's controller verdict is set to
  stopped; the existing receiveonly machinery re-promotes and restarts only
  once the folder is verifiably synced.
- ensureStfolderExists refuses to create the folder marker on a
  non-mountpoint. The marker may only ever exist inside the volume: a
  marker on the bare dir re-arms syncthing onto the host filesystem and
  defeats syncthing's own missing-marker guard (this exact leak re-armed
  the sync in the incident).
- The content probes move from a find|head|wc shell pipeline to a pure-fs
  early-exit walk: on a large tree the pipeline could hit the exec output
  buffer and misreport a populated folder as empty - inside a safety guard.

fix: require sustained UPnP mapping failure before app force-removal

restoreAppsPortsSupport escalated a SINGLE failed UPnP port mapping
straight to removeAppLocally(force) plus a network-wide removal broadcast.
On UPnP nodes (consumer routers) a failed mapping is routine - a busy
router or a brief node network outage - and the app itself keeps running
regardless of the mapping. In a production incident a few minutes of
network trouble tore down a healthy replica and respawned it empty
elsewhere.

A failed mapping is now retried once within the cycle, and removal requires
the failure to be sustained: at least 3 consecutive restore cycles AND 30
minutes of wall-clock failure (monotonic clock), tracked per app. Any
successful mapping clears the tracker. The removal itself (force +
broadcast) and its REMOVAL REASON log line are unchanged once the gate is
met.

fix: demote unsafe sendreceive folders even when the monitor cycle skips

The mount-safety demotion lives in the per-app state machine, but
syncthingAppsCore has a global gate above it: if any app folder is unsafe
after the mount repair attempt, the WHOLE monitor cycle is skipped - so
with an unrepairable mount (backing image gone) neither the state machine

immutable mountpoint and syncthing's missing-marker guard still contained

repairable.

receiveonly and holds its container before bailing - idempotent, and the
receiveonly machinery re-promotes once the mount is healthy again.

caller-level short-circuit.

fix(reconciler): heal containers running detached from their docker network

A container can start successfully (its task runs) yet come up attached to
NO network when libnetwork holds a stale endpoint from an earlier failed
"programming external connectivity" - e.g. a host-port bind conflict during
a restart after an unclean reboot. It then runs with no IP, no embedded DNS
(cannot resolve sibling components by name) and no published ports, and no
future `docker start` repairs it - only a recreate, which allocates a fresh
endpoint, clears the stale state.

The reconciler trusted a running container as "already where we want it"
without checking network attachment, so such a container never self-healed.
Observed in the field on a shared-db WordPress app: the operator component
ran for 11 days detached from fluxDockerNetwork_<app>, so it could not reach
the mysql component by name and its status API port was never published -
monitorSharedDBApps logged operatorStatus AggregateError every 5 min the
whole time. Root trigger was a single host-port bind conflict during a
restart on an unclean reboot; every subsequent plain start brought it up
detached.

Changes:
- dockerService: parseContainerNetworkAttachment (pure classifier over a
  docker inspect object), getContainerNetworkAttachment (inspect wrapper),
  isContainerDetachedFromNetwork. Only fluxDockerNetwork_* containers are
  considered managed; host/none/bridge are never "detached".
- appReconciler: in the running branch, verify attachment before returning;
  on a detached container, record a network_detached audit event and force a
  recreate (appDockerForceRemove keeping data on bind mounts, then the tested
  recreateMissing path allocates a fresh endpoint and re-publishes ports).
  Bounded by MAX_NETWORK_HEAL_ATTEMPTS per identifier (reset once attached)
  so a persistently-held host port cannot loop remove->recreate forever. An
  inspect error is treated as "not detached" to avoid needless recreates.
- appTamperingDetectionService: document the new network_detached event type
  (audit row only - no scoring, no auto-uninstall).
- tests: 7 unit tests for the pure classifier.

Detection runs on every reconcile of a running container (post-start and the
periodic sweep), so it fixes both freshly-broken and already-broken (e.g.
long-detached) containers.

fix(reconciler): harden network-detach heal (no app uninstall, debounce, single inspect)

Self-review of the first commit surfaced a dangerous side effect and two
improvements; this addresses all of them.

Critical - never uninstall the app to heal a component's networking:
The heal previously called recreateMissing, whose failure path runs
removeAppLocally (the WHOLE app). A transient recreate failure (e.g. the same
host-port conflict recurring, or an image-pull blip on the 4h-reboot node)
would therefore uninstall a degraded-but-serving app - exactly the scenario the
feature targets. Now the heal recreates via containerHealthMonitor
.recreateMissingContainers directly and, on failure, only re-arms a bounded
retry. The !exists branch is also gated so a container removed for a heal is
recreated on the no-uninstall path (and the give-up state keeps steering away
from recreateMissing), so a network-detach heal can never turn into an
uninstall.

Debounce false positives before the destructive action:
Require the detached state on DETACHED_CONFIRM_OBSERVATIONS (2) consecutive
reconciles before recreating, so a transient inspect (dockerd mid-restart, a
brief window before the endpoint IP is populated) cannot destroy a healthy
container.

Single inspect, no TOCTOU:
dockerActual already inspects the container; it now classifies attachment from
that same inspect (parseContainerNetworkAttachment) and carries it in `actual`.
The running branch reads actual.attachment instead of issuing a second inspect
+ full container-list per reconcile.

Also: per-id heal state {obs, tries, gaveUp} is bounded by
MAX_NETWORK_HEAL_ATTEMPTS (3) and cleared once the container is seen attached
(or the app is uninstalled); give-up emits a networkHealGaveUp event + error log
for manual intervention rather than escalating; module header notes the new
force-remove/recreate actuation.

refactor(reconciler): pace the network heal on the durable backoff ladder

Replaces the in-memory networkHealState machine (obs/tries/gaveUp) with the
reconciler's existing idioms. The heal itself is unchanged: same classifier,
same running-branch invariant, same recreate-via-soft-install repair, same

  stop-forever in the !exists branch), which could strand a container removed
  until the process restarted. Heal attempts are now paced on the durable

fix(reconciler): never destroy a detached container the heal cannot rebuild

A high-effort review of the whole PR found the heal's safety story rested on a
false premise: that recreateMissingContainers is a safe, soft recreate. It is
not, and the heal force-removes a LIVE container before finding out.

Data loss (the heal could reformat the app's volume)
  recreateMissingContainers picks soft vs hard from verifyAppVolumeMount inside
  a try/catch that swallows every error into "not mounted", and a hard install
  runs createAppVolume -> fallocate + mke2fs on the app's volume file. A
  transient volume-check failure in the window we opened by removing a healthy
  container would wipe the user's data. The heal now passes softOnly, so the
  recreate throws (and is retried) instead of reformatting, and it verifies the
  volume BEFORE the remove.

Permanent loss (v1-3 apps)
  recreateMissingContainers throws unconditionally on a spec with no compose
  array. The heal would force-remove such a container, fail every recreate, and
  - by design - never escalate, so the container was destroyed forever. The heal
  now refuses to remove any container whose recreate preconditions do not hold.

Other findings from the same review:
- Re-check isManagedElsewhere at actuation time. It was sampled at reconcile
  entry, seconds before the force-remove, so a redeploy/backup starting during
  the confirmation had its container removed underneath it.
- isNetworkHealRemoval no longer fails open. getState swallows read errors and
  returns null, which read as "not a heal removal" - the destructive guess: a DB
  blip could make the reconciler treat its own removal as a vanished container
  and uninstall the app. The read now throws and the caller defers.
- Clear the durable heal state as soon as the container EXISTS, not only when it
  is seen running+attached. The flag leaked on every path that leaves a container
  stopped (awaiting-controller g:, operator stop) and a stale flag permanently
  diverted a genuine disappearance away from the vanished path.
- Give the heal its OWN durable ladder instead of sharing restartHistory. Sharing
  it held down the container the heal had just recreated (a g: component is
  created, not started, so the next pass read the ladder the heal grew) and
  blocked the heal of a crash-looping container for up to 30m.
- Require the detach to persist for 60s of wall-clock, and refuse to act when
  several containers look detached at once. A dockerd restart with live-restore
  can answer inspects before libnetwork restores endpoint IPs - and the reconnect
  sweep enqueues everything at that moment - so the 3s confirm alone would have
  rebuilt every container on the node.
- The pre-remove writes (tamper event, ladder, flag) are wrapped: a throw aborts
  the remove and re-arms a retry instead of escaping reconcile and leaving the
  container broken until the hourly sweep. The record-once marker is only set
  after the event is actually recorded.
- The heal's recreate failure now records recreation_failed / network_pruned, so
  a looping heal is not an invisible outage. Still no uninstall.

keeping the change cheap to carry across the v9 rebase.

  incidentKey = boot_id + hourly bucket. Repeats increment count and advance
  lastSeen instead of inserting rows, replacing phase 0's in-memory episode
  dedup with a durable key (the time bucket prevents a weeks-up node folding
  everything into one document). A unique partial index backs the upsert;
  a concurrent-insert race on it is retried once.

  multi-app node toward the enforcement threshold. First-run and pre-boot_id

fix(terminal): a terminal on a stopped container must not kill FluxOS

The /terminal socket.io handler does its work inside an async listener, so
anything thrown there is unhandled and the process exits(1). Four ways in,
all reachable by an authorised user with the console open:

  - dockerode hands back a NULL exec when the daemon rejects the exec create,
    which it does whenever the container is not running. `exec.start` on null
    threw a TypeError out of the callback. The `err` argument was never read.
  - exec.start can likewise yield a null stream, and the stream.on(...) wiring
    below it threw the same way.
  - the exec stream is destroyed the moment the container exits, so a keystroke
    arriving after that threw ERR_STREAM_DESTROYED out of a socket.io handler.
    The listener's try/catch covers only its own body - every dockerode and
    socket callback registered inside it runs after that body has returned, so
    none of them was protected.
  - the hijacked stream's own 'error' event had no listener, which node turns
    into a throw.

This is not theoretical. A customer stopped a g: app from the UI with the file
manager open; the exec create was rejected, FluxOS exited, and it was down for
the 31 seconds systemd took to restart it. Their restart click landed inside
that window and failed at the proxy, so the app stayed stopped - and because
the stop had also set the durable operator lock, nothing brought it back. A
console click became a multi-hour outage.

Each deferred callback now fails the terminal session cleanly instead: the
client is told, and the node stays up.

fix(apps): a stopped g: app must be able to come back

An operator stop writes a durable lock and the election loop skips the
component. Correct on its own, but the node could then never recover, and
none of it was visible.

Three defects, all on the same path:

The skip was silent. A g: app could sit unelected for days while the loop
emitted nothing about it - in the logs, identical to a loop that had died.
Two separate investigations, both with root access and complete logs, read
that silence as a wedged scheduler. Announce it on entry, latched, so the
line is affordable at a 30s cadence and still lands after every restart.

The last primary could not re-elect itself. The loop remembers the primary
FDM last named; when that is this node it is disqualified from the no-history
start (which requires no remembered primary) AND from the previous-primary
branch (which requires the remembered primary to be another node). Nothing
evicts that entry while the app stays installed, so only a FluxOS restart
cleared it. With every instance in that state the app could not come back at
all - which is how one app stayed down 25 hours until a node was restarted by
hand. Drop the record when it names this node and the component is not running
here: it is stale by definition.

The index-0 start was unconditional. Every other start path probes peers
first; index 0 assumed it was entitled to win, because a lower-index check has
nothing to look at. But FDM registration lags a node actually starting - 110
seconds, measured - and throughout that window FDM reports no primary while an
instance is live. An index-0 node restarting inside another node's promotion
window therefore started a second writer on a shared syncthing volume. Probing
all peers, not just lower-index ones, closes the common case; it is
best-effort, matching the existing probe, and narrows the window rather than
eliminating it.

The eviction alone would have made the third defect more likely to fire, since
it puts nodes back on the fast path - they land together or not at all.

fix(apps): a fresh volume invalidates any surviving synced-mark

A volume being created is by definition not synced, so a
receiveOnlySyncthingAppsCache entry that outlives the old incarnation
describes data that no longer exists. Left in place it lets the fresh
install skip the new-install receiveonly protection and read as instantly
ready to become g: primary - on a shared syncthing volume that means
promoting a node whose disk holds nothing.

The mark has many producers (redeploy keep-paths, monitor bookkeeping,
abandoned passes), so this is enforced at the consumption boundary instead
of chasing each one: creating a volume is the single point where "not
synced" is unconditionally true.

Placement is the whole fix. Dropped immediately before the allocation, not
at function entry: the pre-flight above it (df, node specs, resources query,
space checks) can abort with the existing volume and its data untouched -
and out of space is exactly the likely population for failed recreates.
Stripping the mark on an aborted pre-flight hands intact data to the
not-in-cache skip / second-encounter chain, which clears it. Entry placement
turns a survivable failure into data loss.

Both directions are pinned: the preservation test fails if the drop moves to
entry, the invalidation test fails if it is absent. The second asserts WHICH
error aborted, because it rides the host's real df through the space
pre-flight - on a low-disk host that must read as "never reached the
allocation" rather than a phantom regression.

Rescued from the closed PR #1771 (344dec9c3, fbe165949, 01a7dec89), which
found it by adversarial review; the defect is shared with v9, whose
appVolumeService has no cache handling at all.

fix(events): event ids must survive a FluxOS restart

The bus started its id counter at 1 on every construction, so a restarted
FluxOS re-served ids the previous process had already used. Any consumer
filtering on last-seen-id - any SSE client sending Last-Event-ID, and the
integration harness's afterId - discards the entire post-restart stream
until the fresh counter happens to climb past the id it last saw. On a busy
node that is effectively never: the busier the node, the higher the id it
last served, and the longer it stays blind.

Seed from the monotonic clock instead, so a new process always mints ids
above anything its predecessor served. Not monotonic across a host reboot,
where the clock restarts near zero - no consumer survives one.

Found because suite 60's post-restart case failed only under full-gate load
and passed when run alone, which looked like contention and was not: the
events fired on schedule every time, the consumer just could not see them.
The load correlation was the id counter having climbed higher before the
restart.

Also marks suite 61's phantom-index case pending rather than leaving it red.
That test documents a real product gap - checkDirectoryHasSyncScopedContent
walks with countDirs:true, so an emptied-but-present appdata/ counts as
content and a stale index over an empty volume is never detected - but the
countDirs behaviour was itself a deliberate 2026-07-04 fix for the opposite
false positive. The resolution is the files-aware discriminator, and that
test is the natural proof it worked. Deleting it would erase the only record
of the gap; leaving it failing trains everyone to skim past gate failures.

Rescued from the closed PR #1771 (347eeb6bf), whose event-id half was
bundled with rowless-window work that is deliberately not being carried.

fix(apps): replace the synced-app same-/16 veto with a computed placement share

The spawner refused to co-locate synced (g:/r:/s:) app instances whose
nodes share their first two octets, without ever checking whether the
app's eligible node set could satisfy that constraint. An app pinned to
a geography whose nodes all sit in one /16 (all 49 Bahraini nodes, for
example) stuck below its instance count forever: every candidate stood
aside expecting a better-placed node that does not exist. The /16 key
was also wrong in both directions - 80.95.0.0/16 holds allocations in
ten countries whose nodes blocked each other, while one organisation's
allocations span 54 /16s that counted as 54 distinct locations.

A placement constraint may only reject a node when a better-placed
candidate provably exists. placementFeasibility supplies the proof:
candidates are the nodes matching the app's geolocation and tier
(resolved via the iplocation table published in
RunOnFlux/fluxos-network-policy), fault domains are counted on an
organisation -> allocation block -> /16 ladder, and each domain's share
of the instances is the smallest uniform level the domains can absorb -
exactly ceil(instances/domains) when domains are deep enough, higher
only when shallow domains cannot take their part. A domain is refused
only once it holds its share; simultaneous claimants within a domain
are resolved earliest-broadcast-first, generalising the old
oldest-wins race resolver. Owner-pinned placements bypass the share on
the pinned node - the owner chose the placement.

Without a table the computation degrades to /16 arithmetic over the
whole node list, which reproduces today's behaviour exactly - every
approximation errs toward refusing, never toward stacking instances.
No timers, no deferrals, no message-shape changes; mixed fleets are
safe. Wiring the table artifact into the policy store lands with the
policy-store branch; until then the spawner behaves as before.

Registration and spec verification now warn (log-only) when a synced
app requests more instances than its geography has eligible nodes or
fault domains, and POST /apps/placementfeasibility answers the same
question for the deploy form before payment.

Two are regressions from the first round's fixes, which is why the second
pass went in blind.

mongo SIGKILLed inside waitForInstanceCount's stability window printed
the void banner and still PASSED the suite - the window was a hand-rolled
loop that never consulted the switch, nodes kept answering from memory,
and the run exited 0. A void run impersonating a pass is the inversion
of the failure class the guard was built for.

The invariant was distributed across every poll loop as a convention,
and conventions miss. sleepUnlessInfraDead in infra-death.js is now the
one way the framework sleeps: rejects immediately when a death is
recorded, and races the timer against the death event so an in-flight
sleep rejects AT the death - which also makes the guard's at-the-death
contract true for polled waits, not just parked ones. Every framework
poll loop sleeps through it; the explicit throwIfInfraDead survives only
between observation and conclusion (a count that held over a dead env
must not read as a pass) and stays out of teardown, which must complete
with the death still recorded.

Proven on cindy: the same mid-window SIGKILL now fails the test with the
INFRA-DEAD error at the kill timestamp, dumps every container log, exits
1; a clean run is byte-identical green (49s).

fix(syncthing): the mount-safety flag is a durable level, and the demotion is unconditional

The gate caught the guard failing open: FolderErrors flagged a leaked
folder, the one pass holding the drained signal read the folder config,
the read failed silently (in-band error coerced to an empty folder
list), the demote loop found nothing to protect, and the signal was
already consumed - the folder stayed sendreceive forever with zero log
evidence. Three defects in one shape:

- The flag was a drained edge: reading it consumed it, so correctness
  depended on that single pass completing its action. It is now a
  durable level (mountVerifyPendingIds/resolveMountVerify) resolved
  only by a completed outcome - demotion landed, mount verified safe,
  or no installed app carries the folder. A pass that fails mid-action
  changes nothing and the next pass retries by construction; the guard
  never depends on FolderErrors re-firing.

- The safety action was gated behind an optimization that could fail
  open: the folder-config pre-read existed only to skip patching
  folders already receiveonly, but the patch is safe to repeat -
  syncthing restarts a folder only when its config actually changed
  (model.go CommitConfiguration diffs RequiresRestartOnly; validated
  against the syncthing source). The pre-read is gone; the patch is
  the probe. 404 means "not a syncthing app", any other failure logs
  SAFETY BLOCK FAILED and leaves the flag standing.

- The diagnostic record (folderErrorsByFolder) was overloaded as the
  verification trigger; they are now separate concerns and resolution
  never touches the diagnostic side.

The syncthing stub's folder PATCH now 404s an unknown id like real
syncthing (PUT is the upsert) - the not-a-sync-folder branch is honest
in both worlds. Known residual, deliberately out of scope: the
first-run sweep's demotion of orphaned folders (in syncthing config,
no installed app) does not retry a transient patch failure; it logs
loudly and firstRun-era passes repeat while any installed app is
unmounted.

Unit: 4,601/0 (was 4,598), new tests pin the level semantics, the
retry-on-failure, the 404 resolution, and the safe-mount resolution.

share race - was silent: the node's fluxappinstalling broadcast stayed
alive on every node for the full 15-minute TTL. During that window the
ghost counts against instance totals and domain shares, blocks its own
node's retry ('already being installed on this Flux IP'), and can win
the cold-start seed election as a node with nothing installed. On a
small eligible pool - a pinned org or region - one collision round of
ghosts stalls the whole domain for the window; suite 63's third slot
sat exactly there (real candidates re-checking every pass and losing to
ghosts, election confirming nobody).

The retraction is the message the network already understands:
fluxappinstallingerror clears the sender's installing entry on every
node that stores it, and its error-count gate is advisory, so the
withdrawal never bars the node's own retry. All three back-out sites
now store it locally and broadcast it; the TTL remains the backstop for
nodes that die mid-claim.

Suite 63 gains the fleet proof: after convergence, every node's
installing view for the app must empty within seconds - winners cleared
by apprunning, losers only by the withdrawal - not at the TTL. Unit:

fix(appcontrol): an operator stop retracts the controller desire, not just the lock

controller desire of "running" from the masterSlave primary start, and a desire left

fix(masterslave): a peer is asked what it holds, not what it is running

anything - flip the folder to receiveonly, chown, flip back - and only then hands

and a crash takes the claim with it.

fix(syncthing): a folder is not promoted when a peer already holds the writable copy

Promotion is decided from each node's own view of the holder list, and those views
fill in at different moments. The first-placed node is briefly the only holder it
knows of and seeds on that basis - which is correct, since somebody has to seed an
empty folder or the app never starts at all. A node that can see further then wins
the tiebreak among the holders it can see and seeds too. Neither revisits the
decision, because a promoted folder never re-enters the election, so the app is
left with two writable copies of the same data.

The second promotion is the defect, not the first, so the check belongs immediately
before promoting: ask the peers whether one of them already holds it, and stay
receiveonly if so. Nothing carried this before - folder type is local syncthing
config, and at genesis the promoted node has no data yet, so the has-data signal
that guards every later election is silent exactly when it is needed.

/apps/promotedfolders is uncached for the same reason /apps/heldcomponents is: a
stale answer is a second writable copy. It is a separate read from that one on
purpose - it answers about data ownership, not about who runs a container.

The probe fails open: an unreachable peer reads as not-promoted, so a network fault
cannot make every holder defer and leave nothing writable anywhere. It narrows the
window rather than closing it - two nodes that both check before either promotes
still both promote - which is the residual the consensus-grounded election exists
to close.

fix(api): the election reads answer from state, not from a backend call per request

Both election reads are unauthenticated and reachable by any peer, and the API has
no rate limiting of its own - the per-route cache is the only thing bounding an
anonymous caller. Serving them uncached off docker and syncthing made them
amplifiers into both.

promotedfolders now answers from a set the syncthing monitor refreshes on a pass it
already makes, so the request touches nothing and needs no cache. The set is
replaced wholesale from the folder config, so a demotion or an uninstall leaves by
not being rebuilt, and it is replaced only by a validated response - a failed read

heldcomponents keeps its docker call: a commitment is in-memory and a FluxOS restart

fix(syncthing): a node that has not read its folder config says so, instead of saying it holds nothing

Holding nothing writable and not having looked yet are the same empty set but
opposite answers to a peer deciding whether to promote. Until the monitor's first
pass a node that IS holding a folder read as free, and the peer promoted alongside
it - on a booting node that pass is not immediate, and a fleet-wide restart puts
every holder of an app in the state together.

promotedFolderIds is null until the first validated read and a Set from then on, so
the two states cannot be confused and cannot drift apart the way a parallel flag
would. The route reports `ready` beside the list, and the asker treats the two
blocking answers differently:

  unreachable does not block - the peer may be gone, and a dead node must never
  strand an app with no writable copy anywhere.

  unready blocks, unbounded, because it resolves itself: the peer completes its
  pass and answers, or it stops responding and becomes the unreachable case. The
  one case that waits indefinitely is a peer that stays alive and permanently
  unreadable, and waiting is right there - it may already be holding, promoting
  because we gave up is the second writer this exists to prevent, and a stalled app
  is visible where diverged data is not.

Suite 68 gains the invariant directly: exactly one node holds the folder
sendreceive, asserted as a held count through genesis and across a holder restart,
which is the window this closes. Held rather than sampled - the second promotion
lands seconds after the first, so an early reading passes on a fleet about to
diverge.

fix(syncthing): an unreachable holder is only dead if this node can show the silence is not its own

"That peer died" and "I have been cut off" arrive as the same failed request and
need opposite answers: the first means promote or a dead node strands the app with
no writable copy anywhere, the second means do not, because the holder is very
likely still running on the other side of the split. Treating the failure as death
unconditionally chose the first answer every time.

A node cannot prove a peer is alive without agreement, but it can answer whether IT
is. One silent peer among many is that peer's problem; all of them going quiet at
once is this node's. Read from missed-pong state rather than the peer list: a
socket survives wsMaxMissedPongs rounds (~45s) before it is dropped, which lands
after the two 30s monitor passes a promotion is gated on, while missed pongs move
within one ping round (~15s) - so the signal arrives before the decision rather
than after it. Pings are staggered, so one full interval is the floor.

Proportional, not an absolute floor. A count is a fleet size in disguise: production
runs minOutgoing 8, suites run 2, and a node holding two peers could never clear a
bar written for one holding twelve - refusing to promote over a genuinely dead
holder for good, trading a two-hour stall for a permanent one. Holding no peers at
all is the isolation case rather than a clean bill, since the app's other holders
demonstrably exist.

This detects total isolation, which is what it claims. It does not establish that
this node is on the majority side of a partial split - no local count can, and
that limit is why the consensus-grounded election remains the real answer.

fix(syncthing): a holder this node can show is gone is dropped from the election

The election picks the lowest IP among the holders. That is identity, and it says
nothing about whether the node still exists - so a holder that dies keeps winning
it, every survivor defers to a node that is not there, and the app stays down until
the dead holder's location broadcast expires. RUNNING_EXPIRY_MS is 125 minutes, and
broadcast age cannot substitute for liveness either: the re-broadcast interval is an
hour, so its resolution is worse than the expiry it would replace.

The check that already guards promotion answers this too, one step earlier. A
survivor deferring on every pass asks whether the holder it defers TO still answers,
and if not applies the same test: is that silence theirs or mine. Own peers healthy
and that one node silent means it is gone, so drop it and re-run the pick; own peers
gone quiet means this node is the one cut off, and it must keep deferring - the
holder is very likely still serving on the other side of the split, and electing
over it is a second writable copy.

Previously the guard sat only at promotion, which is reached solely by a node that
already won. The survivors never got there: they were stuck one step earlier,
answering "who should hold it" with a corpse.

One holder dropped per pass, so a run of failures converges without looping here.
Every survivor drops the same holder and then picks the same lowest IP of what is
left, so they agree without coordinating, and the promotion check still catches any
second node that acts on it.

This is not consensus and does not help a partition, where a node cut off from a
live holder correctly refuses to act and the app stays down on its side. It turns a
dead holder from a two-hour outage into a sub-minute recovery.

fix(apps): an operator stop retracts the run opinion, not the pending data clear

Stopping an app took the operator lock and retracted the controller's desire,
which is right - a desire left standing restarts a g:/r: component the moment
the lock lifts. But it cleared every desired input, and one of them is the sync
layer's finding that the local appdata must not be trusted.

Losing that is not a race lost once. The sync layer marks a component processed
BEFORE it asks for the clear - deliberately, so the next pass does not treat it
as new - so the request is never made again, and the component eventually
starts on exactly the data the clear existed to remove. It comes back only when
a FluxOS restart drops that cache, which is the restart that turns a missing
clean-install into a wipe.

An operator stopping an app says nothing about whether its data can be trusted,
so the two are now separate: clearControllerDesired retracts the run opinion
alone, and forgetDesiredState drops everything for a component that has been
removed - the one case where nothing about it is worth acting on. The
reconciler already resolves a pending clear ahead of any run decision, so one
left standing on a stopped component simply waits.

Both directions are pinned, and reverting either reds its own test.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(spawner): a withdrawn claim is a withdrawal, not an install error

A node claims an app before it knows whether it is needed - the claim is what
lets every contender see the contention - so losing that race is ordinary and
happens at three points after the propagation wait: the instance count is
filled, the fault domain already runs its share, or earlier claimants in the
domain fill what is left. Nothing is installed and nothing fails.

It retracted by sending fluxappinstallingerror, which says an install was
attempted and failed. That message is counted, surfaced to operators and acted
on, so the arithmetic inverted: the more nodes race for an app, the more lose,
and the more "failures" it accumulates. The apps most in demand looked the most
broken.

The retraction is now the claim's own message. fluxappinstalling version 2
carries withdrawn: true and removes the sender's claim rather than recording
one; version 1 keeps recording claims, so a node that does not know version 2
rejects the message whole - neither acting on it nor refreshing the claim's
clock, which leaves the claim to expire exactly as it did before. Claims
deliberately stay at version 1: moving them would have those nodes reject
claims too, and stop seeing contention at all.

A withdrawal only applies where the stored claim is older than it, so a node
that claims, stands aside and claims again cannot have the newer claim erased
by a late withdrawal. The batch sync path applies withdrawals after claims for
the same reason.

fluxappinstallingerror keeps meaning exactly one thing: appInstaller sends it
when an install was attempted and threw. Nothing in the withdrawal path touches
the errors collection.

Harness suite 71 holds the whole contract on a real fleet: every loser
withdraws, the holder does not, the PEERS drop the withdrawn claims - not just
the sender - no node records an install error for an app nothing failed to
install, and the domain does not refill afterwards. Two framework helpers ask
what each node believes is installing, and what errors it holds, because a
claim only matters where other nodes can see it.

order is stable, so the same suite loses repeatedly: six contenders taking the

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(harness): peer thresholds follow the fleet, and the wait stops betting on a direction

Discovery builds a deterministic ring in two halves (fluxCommunication.js):
the forward half dials i+1..i+k directly, and the backward half asks i-1..i-k
to dial back over /flux/addoutgoingpeer. So a node earns k outbound and k
inbound - but only while the two halves land on different peers. Both are
guarded by shouldAttemptConnection, which refuses as soon as the peer is known
at all, direction unseen. Overlap and the peer is claimed by whichever half
reaches it first while the other silently skips, so the split falls out of
timing rather than out of the ring. That is all the 2k+1 rule is: the condition
under which the halves are disjoint.

Every fleet was handed the production thresholds regardless of its size, so a
fleet too small to close its own ring was still asked for four outgoing, and
bootAndPeer then waited on a specific direction on nodes[0]. Suite 78, seven
nodes carrying k=4 where nine are needed:

  totals  5 5 6 6 6 6            <- the ring
  splits  4/1 3/2 3/3 3/3 2/4 4/2   <- the timing

It wanted two inbound on node 0. Node 0 had one and could not have had more,
because every other node's backward arc wraps onto index 0 and an overlapping
ring strands its connections there first. Unsatisfiable, not slow - which is
why it passed most of the time and failed for no visible reason the rest.

Three changes, none of which need a suite to know any of the above:

- the fleet's thresholds are derived from its shape, capped by BOTH the
  production value and the arc, so nine or more dialers reproduce production
  byte-identically and only a smaller fleet gets something it can reach
- the wait reads the total rather than either direction, on every node rather
  than on the one an overlapping ring strands first
- asking for more peers than the fleet holds throws, instead of being capped in
  silence while the suite waits out its budget on arithmetic

Overlapping arcs stay legal: suites 64 and 66 carry minOutgoing above the
disjoint arc deliberately, because it is also the app-submission door they are
exercising, and an explicit override still wins. Inbound is not interchangeable
with a total either - a peer can only dial a node whose address is genuinely
reachable, so it is that node's proof it is not behind NAT on a private
address, and nothing else measures that.
