A reply is a reply. Silence alone means gone, so the holder stays in the
election and nobody promotes over it.

A peer that cannot answer this question is NOT filed as one that has not
answered yet: that state blocks with no bound, which it earns by resolving
itself, and a node predating the endpoint never will. Blocking there would hold
promotion open until somebody upgraded that node - and on a cold start every
other holder defers to the same lowest address, so one un-upgraded peer would
stop the app starting anywhere. It is recorded and stood down from instead, and
the folder gets the behaviour it had before this check existed. Peers that CAN
answer are still checked, so the cover grows as the fleet upgrades.

test(harness): a holder that predates the folder endpoint

The fleet runs one image and always will, so a version-mixed fleet - the state
every rollout passes through - could not be reached here at all. The stub now
answers /apps/promotedfolders with a status of the suite's choosing, and still
records the request while doing it, so a node's handling of a peer it cannot ask
is witnessed rather than reasoned about.

Both directions off one fleet, because the election is by address: a subject
above the stub, which must keep deferring to a holder that answered 404, and one
below it, which must still seed its cold start rather than wait for that peer to
be upgraded. Each leads with the instrument - a node that never asked would
satisfy the first assertion for all the wrong reasons.

fix(spawner): selection reads where this node is from the table the count reads

Selection took its continent and country from the node's ip-api self-report
while the candidate count and the install gate both read the published table.
The count has no alternative - it answers for thousands of nodes it cannot ask -
so the disagreement fell entirely on selection: measured across the fleet the
two differ on country for about one node in thirteen, and the table is right in
the large majority of those. A node the count credits to the table's country
then never volunteers for an app pinned there, and the app sits below its
instance count with candidates that look available.

The lookup was already being made two lines below for the region. The
self-report stays as the fallback for a node the table cannot place, which is
the same fallback the install gate takes and can only make selection stricter.

Every geolocation test had the two sources agreeing, so none of them could show
which one was read.

refactor(placement): the fault-domain ladder has two rungs, not three

The middle rung - a range's own extent, keyed when no organisation held it -
could never be reached: the extent was resolved only when the organisation was
known, and the organisation is tested first. Its unit test built a document by
hand that the store cannot produce, and checked it against a local copy of the
keying rather than the store's own, so it was green over a branch that never
ran.

Nor is it worth reaching. The artifact carries no allocation: a row ends
wherever the owner, the country or the region changes first, so a row is a
fragment of an allocation rather than one. The median ownerless range is around
512 addresses, so keying on it would split one /16 into up to 128 domains and
call nodes diverse that the /16 rung holds together - the looser direction, on
the typical case.

The two fields it read go with it. Every fleet address resolves an organisation
today, so nothing is grouped differently by this.

fix(utils): an IPv4-mapped address resolves to the address it is

::ffff:1.2.3.4 is IPv6 in form and IPv4 in substance, and it carries dots - so
the ip[:port] split claimed it and returned the empty string, which reads
downstream as an address that would not parse. Placement resolves every node
through this: the fault domain, the country and the region all hang off what it
returns.

The function had no tests at all.

fix(placement): a pinned spec is told which shortfall it actually has

An owner naming the exact machines their app may use was refused registration
when one of them was not in the confirmed node list at that moment - a node
rebooting, one that missed a check-in, one not yet installed. The owner holds
those machines and the condition resolves without touching the spec, so it is
reported rather than refused. Naming FEWER machines than instances still
refuses: no wait fixes arithmetic.

The message was wrong for both cases. It blamed geolocation and tier and told
the owner to widen the allowed locations - a field a pinned spec never set, and
one that cannot be widened to help. Each shortfall now names itself.

fix(apps): a region ban takes either source; only the table may admit

An allow written as a region name is answered from the published table alone -
letting this node's ip-api self-report satisfy it would admit nodes the count
excluded, and where the two disagree the table is the one to believe.

The same rule applied to a ban is the permissive choice, not the conservative
one: a node the table places one region over escaped a ban that named its own
region, so the ban caught fewer nodes than the owner wrote. A ban now takes
either source. The self-report can therefore only ever make this node stricter -
it can ban, it cannot admit - and a ban is written for a reason the network
cannot see, so the error worth making is excluding a node that would have been
fine.

The comment reasoned about allows only, which is how one rule came to serve two
directions it does not suit equally.

test(api): the guard's own suite binds one server, not one per request

supertest binds a fresh ephemeral server on every request(app) call, so the two
cases that make several opened several. Under a full-suite load that
occasionally answered with 'Parse Error: Expected HTTP/' - a socket that was not
the one being spoken to - which reads as a broken guard rather than the test
infrastructure it is. The server's lifetime is explicit now, and closed with the
rest of the per-test state.

fix(syncthing): a live sync connection vetoes declaring a holder dead

holderIsGone read death from the FluxOS HTTP API alone. FluxOS, syncthing and
the app container are separate processes that fail separately, so a routine
FluxOS restart looked like a dead holder to every peer at once: the holder
drops out of the election, a survivor wins, and the promotion guard downstream
reads the same API and is blind the same way. That ends in a second writable
copy beside a writer that never stopped, and SYNCTHING_MAX_CONFLICTS = 0
discards the loser's version without leaving a conflict file.

This node's own syncthing holds the connection that carries the folder to that
holder, and reports remoteState 'valid' only while it is open - evidence the
peer's API cannot give and does not need to. Strictly a veto: it can keep a
holder in the election, never remove one. Every way the answer can wrongly be
'no' (the unknown window after a reconnect, a paused folder, a device this
node never resolved) then costs nothing beyond the exclusion this PR already
makes, while a wrongly-kept holder costs bounded delay - syncthing notices a
hard-dead TCP peer within its ReceiveTimeout, minutes at worst.

test(harness): a holder that is running but unanswerable

The stub could answer the promoted-folders question with any status, and a
status - even 404 - is an answer the asking node reads as alive. A node whose
FluxOS is down does not answer at all: the connection is refused. Those are
different facts and the state machine treats them differently, so the stub can
now refuse at the transport, and suite 80 uses it to put a holder in front of
the subject that is alive but unanswerable. The test asserts on the veto's own
log line, because "did not promote" is satisfied by too many other things
here to tell the guard firing from the guard never running.

fix(syncthing): the designation is withdrawn when a gate turns the winner back

cache.designatedLeader was written at election time, before the partial-copy
guard, the peer-blocking check and the send-receive safety check - each of
which can send the winner back to receiveonly. masterSlaveApps reads the flag
to skip the primary-selection index stagger and start the g: container, so it
has to mean "is the writable holder", not "won the vote": a node that won
and stood down still advertised itself, and got a primary started against a
folder it deliberately left receive-only. Cleared on every unpromoted pass
now, and raised only after the last gate, where the promotion commits.

fix(apps): a batch withdrawal deletes the broadcast under the location's guard

storeBatchAppInstallingMessages deleted the location document only when it was
older than the withdrawal, and the signed broadcast backing it without any
guard. A withdrawal arriving after its sender had already claimed again kept
the newer location and dropped the proof behind it, leaving a claim nothing
can serve during sync. The broadcast delete now carries the location delete's
own guard object, so the two cannot drift apart. The single-message path
already covers both deletes with one early return; the batch path had no tests
of its own, which is how the two diverged.

docs(placement): a deny resolves a region name in either vocabulary

The JSDoc predated resolveRegion: an ip-api region name that the published
artifact's region-name vocabulary maps onto the table's codes produces a real
deny term now, and only a part neither vocabulary resolves bans nothing.

fix(apps): the batch path refuses a version 2 message that is not a withdrawal

Version 2 exists only to withdraw, and the single-message path refuses
anything else at that version. The batch path read the version alone and
treated the message as a withdrawal anyway - harmless while the delete is
bound to the sender's own ip, but the same one-rule-two-paths divergence
that let the withdrawal guards drift apart.

test(harness): the log wait takes the container id, not the handle

waitForLog shells out to docker logs, which wants the container's id.
The suite passed the testcontainers handle, which stringifies to
[object Object] and dies before the assertion. getId() is the same
call suite 67 makes for the same reason.

test(harness): the veto is observed through the event stream, not docker logs

The state machine's holder decisions now publish on the event bus -
syncthing:holderRetained where the live-connection veto keeps a silent
holder, syncthing:holderExcluded where the election drops one - and the
SSE client carries both, so suite 80 waits on the event the way every
suite waits on its subject rather than shelling out to docker logs. The
bus publishes only under testEventStream, so production emits nothing.

test(harness): the stub answers the deviceid question every real node answers

/syncthing/deviceid long predates /apps/promotedfolders, so even the
un-upgraded peer this stub models serves it. The stub 404ed it instead,
which starved the asking node's device cache - and the live-connection
veto reads that cache, so it was silently inert against the stub: suite
80's first execution watched the subject promote a second writable copy
six seconds after the holder's API went silent, exactly the second
writer the veto exists to prevent. The veto could not see the connection
because this node had never been allowed to learn the holder's device.

test(harness): the stub is driven by the folder id the product queries

seedSyncthingApp returns the syncthing folder id FluxOS assigns, and the
suite discarded it, keying the stub's completion state by the bare app
name instead - a folder nothing ever asks about, so the veto's query and
the peers-synced check both read the stub's defaults. Suite 40 already
consumes the returned folder for exactly this reason.

test(harness): a partition takes the syncthing connection with it

The fixture's setSynced declares the holder a connected 'valid' source
for every viewer, and the stub cannot see the partition the test then
makes - so the declaration outlives it, and the survivor's
holder-retained veto refuses the takeover forever on the strength of a
connection it no longer has. The partition step now shadows the
survivor's view: its syncthing has lost the holder, which is what a real
partition produces within syncthing's ReceiveTimeout (~450s TCP). The
harness compresses that detection lag to zero, as it does every timing.

fix(harness): the subnet lock outlives the network it guards

cleanup_on_exit released the base lock before the labeled network was
verifiably gone, and network removal is not instantaneous: endpoints
still detaching make the rm fail and keep the network listed, and a
network mid-removal can be absent from ls while its subnet is still
allocated. Either way the next run claims a base that is still occupied
and dies in its before-all on "Pool overlaps with other one on this
address space". The rm now retries until the label answers empty, and a
network that will not die keeps the lock: a dead owner's lock is
reclaimed by a later scan, which is after any teardown.
docs(harness): the lock-release comment states the invariant, not the incident

test(harness): severing a declared source is one primitive, and suite 68 uses it

setSynced testifies against the source's own device id, which outranks
every wildcard override - so a suite that partitions a declared source
away has to overwrite that same key, or the fleet's holder-retained veto
keeps trusting a connection that no longer exists and the takeover under
test never happens. severPeerSync resolves the device and marks it
disconnected; suite 68's mid-genesis leader loss now declares it, and
suite 70's inline version becomes the same call.

test(harness): mid-genesis means the seed has not seeded, held rather than raced

The designated leader seeds within seconds, so cutting it off after
deploy raced genesis and lost: the seed seeded first, and the test was
then asserting a different scenario than its name. The promotion PATCH
delay now pins genesis until the partition is verifiably in (awaitSever,
plus a fixture assertion that nothing is writable at the cut), and the
delay is released once only the survivors can act on it.

severPeerSync also fails loudly when the stub cannot resolve the device:
the silent fallback was a wildcard write that loses to the source's
device-specific testimony - a sever that severs nothing.

test(harness): cleanup steps say what failed instead of swallowing it

Cleanup must not throw - its error would replace the test's own failure
in the report - but a failed step is the first clue when the next test
inherits its debris.

test(harness): the syncthing stub logs every state write with its writer

Three runs of suite 68 disagreed about what testimony the stub held and
nothing could say who wrote it. Every sync-state, peer-completion and
reset now names its caller and its key on stdout, which the log
collector already captures.

fix(syncthing): an isolated node cannot confirm its own election

The connectivity floor was asked of a silent holder before declaring it
dead, and never of this node before it crowned itself: a partitioned
lowest-IP holder won its own election, confirmed on its stale streak,
and seeded the app on the minority side while every survivor deferred
to its IP. The floor now gates confirmation - a win while this node's
own peers are silent cannot accumulate, and isolation resets the streak
so a heal is followed by LEADER_CONFIRM_COUNT clean passes like any
other blip.

The hazard is older than the election: the stagger path probes peers
over the network and reads silence as absence, so an isolated node
could start there too. The fast election reached it deterministically,
which is how suite 68 caught it.

test(harness): the mid-genesis loss asserts both halves - survivors seed, the island does not

The scenario has two wrong outcomes and the assertion covered one: a
survivor failing to seed. The cut-off seed crowning itself on its island
is the other, and it is the half the isolation gate on election
confirmation now closes.

test(harness): an empty sync-state declaration testifies to nothing

Declaring a folder's clean slate (0/0 idle) stamped the declarer a
CONNECTED 'valid' source for every viewer - so every cold-start fixture
manufactured phantom witnesses, and the holder-retained veto believed
them: a partitioned seed stayed 'connected' in every survivor's eyes on
the strength of a fixture line that meant only "this folder is empty".
The source-testimony side effect now requires declared data, the same
rule the route already applied to unreadable declarations.

test(harness): no-peer-data is not connection testimony

setNoPeerData wrote a bare completion, and the stub's read-back default
stamps a bare completion 'valid' - so "nobody has the data" quietly
meant "every device you ask about is a connected peer at 0%", written
against the viewer's own wildcard key, which outranks device-specific
evidence. Every cold-start fixture therefore held a phantom witness no
sever could override, and the holder-retained veto believed it. The
declaration now carries remoteState 'unknown': absence of data
testifies to nothing about links.

fix(harness): a diagnostic run pays for one test, not the suite

MOCHA_GREP passes a title filter through to mocha. A fleet boot is most
of a suite's cost, and a bisection loop should not pay for the eight
tests it is not bisecting.

test(harness): genesis is judged by its commit point, not by folder flap

The pre-cut fixture read writable folders as proof the seed had seeded,
but the promotion hold pins every folder PATCH - including the demotions
that settle a newborn folder out of its writable birth state - so
folder-shaped evidence flaps for exactly as long as the hold is on. The
container is what genesis commits, and it is what the fixture checks.

test(harness): the leader is lost before genesis by ordering, not by holds

Holding the promotion could not hold genesis - the designation commits
and masterSlaveApps starts the container without waiting for the folder
write the hold was pinning. The one ordering that cannot race genesis is
cutting the seed off before the app exists: placement proceeds (the
runner reaches every node; a partition drops only node-to-node packets),
the seed is born unreachable to its peers, and nothing can have seeded
when the election first looks. No holds, no severs, no fabricated
evidence - the seed never declared anything, so the survivors judge
exactly what production would see.

fix(syncthing): the designation is raised when the promotion is applied

Deciding a promotion and applying it were one moment in the flag's eyes
and two moments in reality: the state machine raised designatedLeader at
the last gate, and masterSlaveApps could start the primary in the gap
before the monitor's folder batch reached syncthing - a container
running against a folder still receiveonly for as long as the apply
took. The state machine now records intent (designationPending), and the
monitor raises the flag after the batch lands; a failed apply throws
first, so intent survives untouched for the retry pass. A lost election
withdraws the intent with the claim.

test(harness): releasing a patch delay wakes the requests parked in it

The delay slept each held PATCH for its full duration read at arrival,
and clearing it only affected future requests - so a release could
trail its own sleepers by minutes, and every monitor cycle awaiting one
stayed frozen long after the test believed the hold was gone. Held
requests now wait on a waker as well as the timer: clearing a delay, or
resetting sync state, releases them immediately.

fix(syncthing): gone requires evidence - an unaskable device keeps its holder

The connection check answered a plain no both when this node's syncthing
said the device was not connected and when this node could not ask at
all - a device never resolved because this node's own process restarted
during the holder's outage. The two are different facts: the first is
evidence, the second is its absence, and collapsing them let the one
node with the least knowledge authorise a second writer. The check now
answers with one of PeerConnection (frozen, per VerifyResult's
precedent), and holderIsGone declares a holder gone only on DISCONNECTED
- silence plus UNKNOWN keeps the holder, costing at worst the stranding
production already has, never a second writer.

fix(masterslave): a peer that cannot be read is not a peer that is free

The probe guarding a g: primary start counted an unreachable peer as not
running the component, and started. That is the wrong way round. FluxOS
and the container fail independently, so a node whose API is down still
holds its volume and still writes to it - silence is the strongest reason
to suspect a peer IS running the component, not a clearance to start
beside it. A synced standby whose probe landed inside a holder's FluxOS
restart started a second writer next to a container that never stopped,
with SYNCTHING_MAX_CONFLICTS = 0 discarding whichever writer lost.

Silence is now acted on only with evidence, and it is the same evidence
the election already demands before dropping a holder: this node's own
syncthing showing the peer's connection to the folder gone, read on a
node that can still see the fleet. The two decisions ask one question
through one function, moved to the liveness module they share. A silence
with the connection still alive, or with no evidence either way, or read
from a node that cannot see the fleet, keeps the peer.

Four decisions changed, all the same rule: the index-0 start, the
designated leader's seed, the staggered start, and the previous primary -
which carried the defect in its own copy, and now runs through the same
probe rather than a second implementation of one rule.

Two states are kept apart where the old boolean collapsed them. A due
schedule survives a peer that could not be read, so the next pass retries
in seconds instead of serving a fresh index * 3min stagger; and the seed
claim is not spent on a non-answer, since the claim is what the decision
is made from and no decision was reached.

Nothing strands indefinitely. A peer that genuinely died loses its sync
connection on its own, which releases the start, and if it stays dead it
stops broadcasting and drops out of the location list the probe reads.
The device cache answering "which device is this peer" is in memory and
is filled by asking the peer, so it is empty for exactly the peer that
died while this node was restarting; this node's syncthing holds that
device on disk from when the peer was up, and is now read as the
fallback, keeping that case to seconds rather than the location record's
125-minute lifetime.

test(harness): the restarting-holder scenario is an acceptance test again

Written on 08-02 against the fail-open probe, this ran red in this fleet -
a six-second FluxOS restart was enough for a synced standby to start a
second writer beside the holder's still-running container - and was
skipped as needing the quorum-granted mastership lease. It does not need
one: the restarting node's syncthing connection stays open throughout,
and that connection is the evidence the start probe now demands.

The partition suite's header quoted the probe's old "fails open by
design" note. The probe no longer does, but its isolation floor detects
total isolation rather than minority status and says so, so that suite's
claim stands for a narrower reason. Its heal test stays skipped:
reconvergence needs a running holder to stand down, which this change
does not do.

test(harness): the seed is a connected source of its own folder too

The restarting-holder test declared only the standbys as synced sources,
which left the stub reporting the SEED - the node whose FluxOS the test
takes away - as disconnected. Its peers then read that as evidence the
seed had stopped and started a second writer, correctly acting on false
evidence: a syncthing that never stopped cannot be in the state the
fixture described.

Declared for every holder now, which is both the truth by that point in
the test (the standbys synced FROM the seed, so each is a connected
source) and what the other g: suites already do. The stub will not invent
a connected peer, and should not - that is what keeps it from
manufacturing witnesses - so the fixture has to state it.

test(harness): the restarting-holder fixture retracts its cold-start claim

Declaring the holders synced was not enough to describe the cluster this
test has by then built. placeGAppInOrder declares no-peer-data at genesis
under each viewer's own wildcard key, and the stub resolves
`viewer|folder|*` before `*|folder|<source device>` - so every per-source
declaration sat invisible underneath it and each holder went on reading
its peers as disconnected, which is a state a syncthing that never
stopped cannot be in.

The peers then did exactly what they should with the evidence they were
handed: they read the restarting holder as gone and started beside it.
The fixture now retracts the genesis claim as well as adding the synced
one, and the test passes 9/9 - the first time it has been green in either
direction.

Worth keeping in mind for any later g: fixture: a cold-start declaration
outranks later per-source evidence, so moving a fixture past genesis
means withdrawing it, not adding to it.

Merge pull request #1774 from RunOnFlux/feature/placement-diversity

Placement diversity: computed placement over a published IP table, network policy in its own repository, and a hardened synced-app election

fix(network): the privileged-port capability is set on legacy nodes only

Arcane grants CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE to the fluxos unit, so the interpreter
needs no file capability there. A capability on /usr/bin/node extends
privileged binding to every local user's node process, and puts the dynamic
loader into secure-execution mode for all of them, silently dropping
LD_PRELOAD and LD_LIBRARY_PATH.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

chore(network): clear pre-existing lint in fluxNetworkHelper and its tests

Destructure the peer counts and the request body, and drop a test import
that was never referenced.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

perf(verify): scale the signature pool with demand and post bounded chunks

One worker stays resident; the pool raises workers against outstanding chunks
to at most one per spare core, and releases the extras once a burst ends.
Signature verification is bursty - thousands of items while boot sync runs,
then nothing for hours - and fifteen idle isolates measure 312MB on a 16 core
node.

Batches post in chunks of 256 items. An oversized post is what pins memory:
its serialised copy is not returned to the OS once the batch is collected, and
bounding it cuts the footprint a burst retains by around 80%.

stats() reports pool occupancy for visibility into the crypto path.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

perf(registryAuth): obtain Azure ACR tokens in a throwaway worker

@azure/identity is 27MB and 269 modules, and a node only needs it when it
hosts an app pulling from a private Azure registry. Loaded into the main
isolate it stays for the life of the process, since module caches are never
released and freed pages are not returned to the OS.

The SDK now sits at the top of a worker spawned for a single token exchange
and terminated after it, which is the one way that memory is reclaimed. The
provider keeps the rest of the ACR flow, whose refresh and access token
exchanges were already plain HTTPS.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

perf(registryAuth): obtain ECR and GAR tokens in throwaway workers

@aws-sdk/client-ecr and google-auth-library join @azure/identity in workers
spawned per exchange and terminated after it. Loading the whole provider
factory now pulls no cloud SDK into the main isolate at all, against 427
modules and ~38MB before.

The ECR worker serves both calls the provider makes, returning only the
fields it reads; expiresAt survives as a Date because structured clone
preserves them. The GAR worker returns the token together with the expiry
its client exposes only after the call.

runAuthWorker takes the worker directory as an option, so its spawn,
timeout, error and teardown paths are covered directly against fixture
workers rather than only through provider stubs.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

perf(comms): size the peer deflate window to the messages it compresses

Every peer socket holds a zlib deflate context for its lifetime, so the
window and hash table are paid per peer. No-context-takeover resets the
stream after each message, so the window can only ever match inside one
message, and gossip messages are a few KB: an 8KB window with a memLevel-8
table compresses them to byte-identical output on a third of the memory.
Measured 301KB to 114KB per socket, with a 2.4-3.5% penalty confined to
large sync responses.

The listening server also serves browsers on /ws/id, /ws/sign and
/ws/payment, so it declares only its own window and leaves the peer's
alone; outbound peer sockets talk to nodes only and size both directions.
A peer on an older build negotiates back up.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

perf(pgp): run openpgp operations in a throwaway worker

openpgp holds ~19MB from require time and a node needs it for one identity
check at boot plus the secrets of v7 apps that still carry PGP-encrypted
fields - seven components across the whole network, and none for repoauth.
From v8 those fields travel inside the enterprise blob, which uses node's
own crypto. It now loads at the top of a worker spawned per operation and
terminated after it, so the main isolate carries none of it.

The throwaway-worker runner moves out of registryAuth to utils, and the
worker scripts to a single services/workers directory, now that pgp and
registry auth both use it.

Two imports of pgpService that were only kept alive by an eslint-disable
are removed; neither file called it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

perf(sync): carry a sync response through in slices, and bound the location write

A sync response holds up to 2500 events, and each one fans out into a database
operation per app it reports - a couple of thousand events became roughly forty
thousand operations, every one carrying a merge pipeline, all accumulated before
a single write. The events, their verification copies and the driver's encoding
of the whole batch were live together, which cost hundreds of megabytes that the
allocator never returned.

The response is now verified and stored a slice at a time, and location
operations are written in bounded batches within that. Upserts flush before the
pruning deletes, which only remove names absent from the same broadcast, so a
row just written is never a candidate for them.

Broadcasts also go to the verify workers as they are, rather than being copied
into a narrower shape first - the worker reads only the fields it needs.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

refactor(sync): slice every sync response through one tested helper

The apprunning handler had the slicing inline and untestable - the handlers
are not exported, and reaching them meant either widening the module surface
or simulating a socket. Extracting it gives the behaviour a real contract
with its own tests, and the installing and installing-errors handlers, which
fan out the same way, now slice too.

processInSlices covers what the handlers depend on: bounded slices, full
coverage in order, one slice at a time so each is released before the next
is built, and a handler failure propagating rather than being swallowed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

Revert "fix(network): the privileged-port capability is set on legacy nodes only"

This reverts commit 59e65c599.

FluxOS and the systemd unit ship through different channels: the code updates
by git pull, the unit only with a new ISO. Gating the setcap to legacy now
would leave Arcane nodes that have taken the code but not the new unit with
neither source of the capability. Nothing breaks while fluxos runs as root,
but the file capability sits on the shared interpreter, so anything else on
the box running node inherits it today and would silently lose it.

The unit change stands in flux_iso, where AmbientCapabilities is a no-op under
root and takes over once fluxos runs as a user. This gate lands again once
that unit is out in the field.

fix(memory): close the defects an adversarial review found in this branch

Eleven findings, four of them silent failure modes introduced here.

The verify pool claimed a worker's slot before handing it the batch, so a
failed handover retired that slot for the life of the process; enough of them
and every later verify() queued for ever with no error. It now posts first,
puts the job back if that throws, and gives each job a timeout. A chunk that
keeps killing its worker is abandoned after three attempts and its signatures
resolve unverified - a signature we could not check is one we do not trust -
and stop() settles anyone still waiting instead of stranding them.

Sync responses applied evictions inside each slice, so an eviction in an early
slice was undone by app-running events in a later one. Evictions carry no
broadcastedAt and the sender sorts on it, so they landed in the first slice
every time and the resurrection was systematic. State events are now applied
once, after every slice.

Pruning needs a node's newest broadcast across the whole response, which a
slice cannot know, so it moves out of the per-slice store into its own pass.
A failed location write now suppresses pruning entirely: stale rows recover on
the next broadcast, deleted live ones do not.

The listening socket pinned its compression window, which rejects the
handshake outright - 400, not a fallback to uncompressed - for any client
offering a smaller one, and browsers reach that server. It accepts the peer's
choice again; memLevel is compressor-local and stays.

Worker failure is now an explicit flag rather than a truthy error string: a
throw carrying no message resolved as success, which on the PGP path would
have read as a corrupt identity and overwritten the node's keypair. The runner
also tears down a worker whose handover throws, instead of leaving it holding
its dependency until the timeout, and no longer holds the event loop open.

The location batch cap was checked per broadcast rather than per operation, so
a node reporting 30 apps overran it - the original test used 20, which divides
the cap exactly and hid it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(sync): prune locations from verified broadcasts only, and evict first

Moving pruning to a response-wide pass took its input from the raw response
rather than from the verified broadcasts the previous code used. Pruning
deletes location rows, so a peer could have included an unsigned apprunning
event naming one app for a node and had every other row for that node removed
without its signature ever being checked. The newest-per-node map is now built
from verified broadcasts as they come out of each slice.

Evictions are also applied ahead of the other state events again. Accumulating
them together interleaved the two by slice, where the previous code applied
every eviction first.

test(harness): cover eviction, pruning and forged events in a sync response

No suite touched any of these. Suite 22 covers the happy path - a response
arrives, verifies through the worker pool and lands locations in mongo - but
nothing exercised an eviction inside a response, an app disappearing from a
node's newest broadcast, or an unsigned event.

briefly went wrong: pruning deletes rows, so an unverified broadcast must never
reach it. The response is seeded past a slice boundary so the eviction and the

that made the ordering defect fire.

fix(network): the network state is unknown until it is fetched

waitStarted() resolved immediately whenever the service had not been
started, so deterministicFluxList() answered "the network has no nodes"
when the truth was "I do not know yet".

fluxDiscovery sizes both of its deterministic connection loops from that
list, so an empty one makes minDeterministicOutPeers zero and the node
neither dials its deterministic peers nor asks them to dial it. It then
waits out discoveryRetryMs before trying again - a minute of a node's
first peering on a real boot, where discovery autostarts ahead of the
network state fetch. A node whose peers dial in during that window
cannot recover on the retry either: a peer holds one socket in either
direction, so every deterministic outbound target is already connected
and shouldAttemptConnection refuses all of them.

The promise now exists from module load and is resolved when the state
first populates, so a caller that arrives early waits for the answer
rather than being given the wrong one.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

perf(pgp): keep openpgp off the boot path

A node that already carries a keypair now does no PGP work at boot at
all. The keypair is written in one go and does not drift, so checking
that the public key still belongs to the private key was confirming
something already known - at the cost of a worker and a fresh load of
openpgp inside it, which is the whole cost of the operation. The check
runs when the private key is first relied on instead, and remembers
which key it verified, so a replaced key is checked rather than assumed.

Boot no longer waits for any of it either. Nothing after the identity
needs it, and a first-boot node generating a keypair has it stored long
before anything asks for the public half.

fix(pgp): wait for the identity, because writing it is not atomic

Generating an identity rewrites config/userconfig.js with a plain write
that truncates first, and configManager reloads the file when it sees it
change. A reload landing inside that window requires an empty file, which
returns {} without throwing - so the load succeeds, its fallback defaults
never apply, and the process is left with no userconfig.initial at all.
Every read of it throws until the next write settles, which took out the
login path.

A node that already carries an identity returns from generateIdentity
immediately and loads nothing, so waiting costs the fleet nothing; only a
first boot waits, and that is the boot that must not serve requests
against a half-written identity.

fix(network): readiness of the node list is asked for, not waited on

Every accessor on networkStateService answers an unknown state and a
genuinely empty one with the same value - an empty list, a zero, a null -
so each consumer invented its own reading of it. fluxDiscovery took an
empty list to mean a network with no nodes in it, sized both deterministic
loops to zero, connected to nobody and reported nothing wrong.

Readiness is now a property of the service. isReady() answers it outright,
and onReady() runs work that cannot begin without the list at the moment
the list arrives. Discovery states the precondition alongside the three it
already had, so an unknown network takes the same awaiting-and-retry path
as an unsynced daemon, and its first pass is driven by the list arriving
rather than by a retry that happens to follow it - a peer holds one socket
in either direction, so peers that dial us first take the sockets we would
otherwise have dialled them on.

The accessors no longer block. Two of their callers are loops that re-arm
only once they have finished, so an await that may never return retires
them for the life of the process instead of delaying them - and one of
those loops is the only thing that ever clears this node's DOS state.

fix(config): a read that lands mid-write does not replace the config it holds

config/userconfig.js is rewritten whole by every one of its writers, so a read can
land between the truncate and the write. require() resolves an empty or truncated
file to an object rather than throwing, so loadConfig's catch never fired: the
process was left holding a config with no `initial`, and every read of it throws
until the next write settles.

An absent `initial` is now the evidence it is — the only evidence available, since
nothing else distinguishes a half-written file from a complete one. A node that
already holds a config keeps it, because the defaults carry no zelid and no keypair,
and publishing those over a good config would have the node act under an identity
that is not its own. Only a first read, with nothing to fall back on, takes them.

fix(verify): a batch no worker would take still settles

A failed handover puts the job back on the queue and leaves the slot free, so a
dispatch pass can end with work queued and a worker idle. Every other way back
into dispatch is a worker event - message, exit, timeout - and none can arrive
while no worker is holding anything, so the job sat there until the next
verify() call happened to re-enter. One idle worker, one queued job, a caller
waiting on a promise that had nothing left to settle it.

Dispatch now re-enters itself after a failed handover. It terminates because the
attempt is counted before the handover: a chunk that cannot be posted at all is
abandoned after MAX_JOB_ATTEMPTS and its caller rejected, rather than retried
for ever.

Reachability is low - chunks are JSON-derived broadcasts and clone fine - but
this is the failure class the earlier correlation work set out to close, and it
closed every other member of it.

fix(network): the node list waits again, and the loops that cannot wait ask

Making every accessor non-blocking fixed two re-arming loops and silently
degraded twelve other callers. Only two of the fourteen were given the
replacement guard, and the ones left behind read an unknown list as an empty
network: the location refresh deletes every node-location document and cannot
rebuild for a day; the advice endpoint answers that an app can be placed
nowhere; a peer asking whether we are up is told no and increments DOS against
us. The default was inverted - the unsafe reading was free and correctness had
to be opted into.

The accessors wait again, so the twelve get the right answer without each
needing to remember. The loops that genuinely cannot wait check and re-arm
instead, which is the shape checkDeterministicNodesCollisions already used for
the daemon two lines above its list read - and monitorNodeStatus checks at the
point of use, because everything above it is app removal that needs no list.
fluxDiscovery already did this.

isReady() and onReady() stay. They are the right primitives; they were just the
only thing standing between an unknown list and a deleteMany.

The collision tests now stub isReady: they are about what the check decides once
it HAS the list, and they failed without it - which is what shows the guard is
reached.

fix(placement): the advice endpoints refuse rather than hold a request open

The node-list accessors wait for the list, which is right for the callers that
can wait - and wrong for these two, which answer a client holding a connection
open. Both now refuse with 503 before reaching an accessor.

They also used to disagree with each other. placementComputation already
refused, while placementLocations went on to build its tree over an empty list
and report that an app could be placed nowhere - the two endpoints an owner
cross-checks against each other, giving opposite answers about the same
network, from the same file.

fix(sync): a lapsed announcement does not decide what a node is running

The newest-per-node map the location prune reads is built from apprunning
broadcasts, and a broadcast past its running expiry says what a node was doing
two hours ago, not what it is doing now. It is skipped, which is how
messageStore builds the same map for its own callers.

The prune only deletes rows at or below the announcement's own timestamp, so a
lapsed one could reach nothing that was not already lapsed. That bound lives in
a database filter in another file, and is a poor place to keep the reason this
is safe.

fix(auth): a privilege check reads the config through its own manager

Five privilege decisions read userconfig off globalThis, which is populated
by ConfigManager's constructor - so they were relying on some other module
having imported the manager first. A node answers HTTP well before that is
guaranteed, and a check reached in that window found nothing and threw a
TypeError, which the caller received as a server error on an ordinary
restart.

They now read through the manager. Importing it is what guarantees the
config has been read at all, so the window closes at its source rather
than at each of the five call sites.

Null still has to be answered for, because a load that fails installs
defaults carrying no zelid rather than a config, and the two families of
caller need different answers. The three session checks deny: a comparison
against an identity we do not hold must fail rather than pass, and the
flux team paths beside them keep working because those ids come from the
static config. The two granting sites refuse the login outright instead of
resolving the caller to 'user' - that would hand the operator a session
with their own rights stripped and no indication why.

fix(placement): an empty node list refreshes nothing rather than dropping everything

refreshNodeLocations derives "departed" from absence: every held address the
node list does not carry is deleted. An empty list therefore reads as every
node having left, and deletes the whole location view in one call.

The accessor it is fed from waits for a real list now, so this should be
unreachable - but the cost of that contract ever not holding is the entire
collection, rebuilt only over the following passes and giving wrong placement
answers in the meantime. That is too much to rest on a guarantee kept in
another file, so an empty or absent list is refused here as well.

It costs one skipped cleanup pass in a case that should not arise: nothing
waits, nothing retries, and the next call with a real list does the work.

Two tests left the empty list in place as a shortcut into the drop and
view-load paths. An empty list is now a refusal, so they name a list that
still departs the held address and test what they were written to test.

fix(config): the file hash is recorded once the file has been read

reloadConfig stamped the new hash before loading, so a read that landed
mid-write recorded the half-written file as the version this node holds -
while what it actually holds is still the previous config. loadConfig
swallows its own failures, so the caller had no way to tell.

loadConfig now reports whether it read anything, and the hash is recorded
only when it did.

docs(verify): why the reap is armed from the reply path alone

Reading the call graph, scheduleReap appears once - in the worker message
handler - which looks like a burst ending any other way leaves its raised
workers resident. It does not, and the reason is a file away in the exit
handler: a worker that dies splices its own slot out of the pool, so the
only workers still resident when a burst ends are the ones that replied,
and replying is what arms the reap.

Measured rather than reasoned: a burst in which every worker crashes ends
holding one worker at every pool size tried, and a mixed burst ends with
its raised workers held by the replies that armed the reap for them.

refactor(sync): the batch store upserts, and pruning is left to its owner

storeBatchAppRunningMessages carried a prune option that its only caller
turns off, so the map it built to serve that path was assembled on every
slice and thrown away, and everything past the option check was
unreachable. Both are gone, along with the option itself.

Removing locations a node no longer reports is pruneAppRunningLocations'
job, and it does it from the newest broadcast per node rather than from
whichever announcements happened to share a batch - which is why the
option was turned off here in the first place.

fix(spawner): a location table that is not ready yet defers, it does not park

placementComputation refuses a geo-restricted question while the IP location
table is still loading - the right answer for the HTTP caller it was written
for, because advising on numbers computed over the whole network is worse than
saying nothing.

The spawner calls it too, and let that refusal fall through to its own catch,
which reads any throw there as a pre-install error and parks the app for six
hours. A table that is usually seconds from ready would cost that app six
hours of spawn attempts on this node.

It is now caught where it is raised and deferred to the next pass. The
reviewer noted the internal caller as unreachable today, which it is - it
depends on dbReady implying network-state readiness, an undocumented ordering
this branch has otherwise been removing reliance on.

Also adds fluxapps.nodeMonitorCheckIntervalMs, which nodeStatusMonitor reads
with a 120000 fallback while every sibling interval is declared.

fix(placement): the empty-list refusal says why it refused

The guard returned {refreshed: 0, dropped: 0} without a word, and the caller
only logs a pass that changed something - so refusing to act on a node list
that could not be obtained looked exactly like a pass with nothing to do.

An operator reading these logs could not tell the two apart, which is the
same absence-of-evidence problem the guard itself exists to answer.

test(harness): the domain share suite proves what it was written to prove

The suite carried both directions of the placement share in one assertion:
that a single fault domain is PERMITTED to hold all N instances - the
Bahrain regression it exists for - and that it is also CAPPED at N.

Those are not the same claim. The share permits N by arithmetic every node
computes identically. Refusing the N+1th depends on the admitting nodes
having heard each other's claims: a node counts the claimants ahead of it
in a gossiped list, and two nodes whose lists are each missing the other
both count themselves inside the remaining share and both install. The
surplus is not removed inside the window either, since
checkAndRemoveApplicationInstance is paced at 44 blocks.

Observed at roughly one run in fourteen and worse under a loaded gate,
which is the worst frequency to carry live - often enough to cost an
investigation, rare enough to teach people to skim past a red gate.

The live test now proves the regression it was written for. The ceiling is
its own test, skipped, naming deterministic placement as what makes it true
by construction and un-skips it. waitForInstanceCount takes exact:false for
the callers whose subject is that the count is reached rather than bounded;
every existing caller keeps the strict default.

fix(syncthing): a promotion is advertised when it lands, not a pass later

globalState.promotedFolderIds is built from the folder list a monitor pass
opens with, and a promotion decided in that pass reaches syncthing only at
the folder batch near the end of it. So a folder promoted in pass N was
advertised from pass N+1, about 30 seconds later.

findPeerBlockingPromotion asks a peer for exactly this set before promoting
a folder of its own - the check that exists to catch two nodes with
different views of the holder list both electing themselves. Inside that
window neither node's published set carries the folder, so neither blocks,
and the per-pass liveness memo holds the stale answer for the rest of the
pass on top of that.

The set is now reconciled where the batch applies, in both directions, so
what this node advertises becomes true at the moment it became true.

Raised on #1774 and fixed here: #1775 is stacked directly on it and merges
after it, so the window is closed before either reaches development,
without restarting #1774's gate.

docs(placement): the feasibility gate states the reason that holds

The handler justified its sign-in requirement partly on the work involved -
a pass over the whole node list with no cache able to bound it. That reason
does not hold: verifyAppRegistrationParameters and validateAppUpdate run the
same pass and stay open, so a reader finds a rule stated in one place and
quietly broken in another.

What carries the gate is compatibility. This endpoint is new, so it could ask
from the outset without breaking a caller, and its caller is about to sign a
registration anyway. The validation endpoints are long-standing and tooling
calls them before a signature exists to gate on.

Raised on #1774 and recorded here, per the same stacking as the promotion fix.

fix(apps): the single withdrawal path guards its deletes like the batch one

The batch path filters both its deletes on broadcastedAt: { $lt }. The
single-message path filtered neither, resting instead on the read a few
lines above that found the stored claim older.

That read is weaker in two ways. It proves the claim was older a moment
ago, not at the moment of deletion, so a claim arriving in between is
erased. And it consults only the location - the signed broadcast is a
separate collection written by a separate path, so a claim newer than this
withdrawal can exist there while the location the read saw is still the old
one.

Both deletes now carry the guard, which is the shape the batch path already
had. The earlier round moved the asymmetry rather than removing it: the
batch path was brought up to the single path's guard, and this is the
single path being brought up to the batch path's.

Raised on #1774 and fixed here, per the same stacking as the other two.

fix(pgp): a replaced identity is in force before the next caller reads it

A corrupt keypair is repaired by generating a new one and writing it to
config/userconfig.js. Nothing then refreshed the in-process copy - that
waited on the config watcher - so the caller that ordered the repair, and
every caller behind it, went on reading the key that had just been
replaced. Each found the same mismatch and ordered another repair: another
collateral lookup, another keygen worker, and another whole-file rewrite of
the one file that a reader landing mid-write finds carrying no identity at
all. The other writers of that file rebuild it from the same in-process
copy, so one of them landing in the window puts the corrupt pair back.

The write now refreshes the config it just wrote, so the next reader sees
the identity that is in force. Callers share one repair rather than each
running theirs over the top of the others, and the key generated is
recorded as verified - its halves were made together, so the check it saves
has one answer.

A failed write is no longer swallowed. adjustPGPidentity logged and
returned, which let createIdentity report an identity it had not stored -
the shape that makes any "we already tried" marker unsafe, because the node
that could not write is the node that must try again.

fix(apps): app volumes are mounted nosuid and nodev

An app volume holds data its owner writes, so nothing stored there should be
able to confer privilege on whatever reads it back. A setuid-root binary can
reach one by more than one route - unpacking a user-supplied archive is the
obvious one, but a copy preserves the bits too - so the guarantee belongs at
the mount rather than in any single caller.

nosuid does not prevent execution; it only stops a binary on the volume
switching to another user. An app that downloads and runs a helper from its own
appdata is unaffected, and legitimate setuid binaries live in the container
image, not in appdata. nodev likewise only stops a device node being honoured;
device access comes from docker's device mapping. Scanning live volumes across
Arcane nodes found no setuid, setgid or device files on any of them.

A bind mount inherits its source's options, so a volume handed to a container
carries these too.

Existing mounts keep their current options until they are next remounted. This
is defence in depth rather than a fix for anything currently exploitable, so no
forced remount accompanies it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(volumes): free space comes from findmnt, in bytes

node-df reported `df -kP` blocks scaled through a multiplier table with no
entry for bytes, so 'B' fell through to the KiB default, and it applied
`precision` unconditionally. The call convention used across the file API
passes a field name where precision belongs, which made `+decimal` NaN - so
getVolumeInfo returned NaN for size, used and available on every one of those
calls. The other convention returned KiB while being asked for bytes. Neither
was noticed because the only field anyone read from it was the mount path.

deviceHelper now sources the mount table from `findmnt --bytes --json`, which
needs no unit conversion at all, and both helpers throw rather than returning
an empty list so a caller cannot read "no disks" as "no space" and act on it.

Two predicates that had been copied between three call sites get names:
eligibleHostMounts is where a FLUXFSVOL may be placed, capacityVolumesInGb is
what counts towards node capacity. They differ - a loop-mounted root is a host
disk, not an app volume - so they stay separate rather than growing a flag.

capacityVolumesInGb reports DECIMAL GB. App hdd requirements and the config
reserves it is compared against are decimal, so reporting GiB would understate
every node by about 7% and start refusing apps that fit.

getVolumeInfo also selects its mount from the table by identifier rather than
rebuilding a path, so a request can only ever name a filesystem the kernel
already reports as mounted.

feat(volumes): an authorised handle replaces the per-handler guard sequence

Reaching an app's files safely takes five checks in a fixed order, and every
handler inlines its own copy. Forgetting one produces an endpoint that works
perfectly for its author and is quietly unsafe, which is not a failure any
review reliably catches.

A handler now asks a VolumeSession for a path instead of building one. The
session runs the checks and returns a VolumePath - an object, not a string -
and the executor accepts nothing else. Skipping a check no longer yields an
unsafe endpoint; it yields code that does not run.

VolumePath carries the operand as the executor container sees it, under /work.
Host paths never enter argv, so a path that somehow escaped the checks would
name a file that does not exist inside the container. That barrier holds
without depending on the checks being correct.

Authorisation lives in openVolume rather than in each handler because the check
is object-level - is this caller the owner of THIS app - and the industry fuses
object-level checks with the lookup that fetches the object, for the reason
that scattering them means one eventually gets forgotten. Broken Object Level
Authorization is first on the OWASP API Security Top 10. resolveVolumeMount
stays unauthorised beside it for backup, restore and the sweeps, which have no
user; two names rather than one function with a skipAuth flag, because a
guarantee a boolean can switch off reads as safe while providing nothing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat(volumes): file operations run in a throwaway container

The file API reaches an app's files on the HOST as root, where containment
depends on a sequence of path checks being correct in every handler. Each
operation now runs in a container with only that app's volume bound, so a path
that escapes has nowhere to land: the rootfs is read-only, there is no network,
and the container is discarded.

It also removes the host-root requirement from these operations. FluxOS must
hold the docker socket to function at all, so routing the work through docker
adds no privilege it does not already have - whereas sudo cp needs sudoers rules
that demoting FluxOS to a system user is meant to remove.

Three of docker's fourteen default capabilities are kept. cp -a cannot restore
ownership without CAP_CHOWN and does not fail when it can't: it exits 0 having
written root-owned files, and an app running as a non-root user then loses
access to its own data with nothing in the logs. FOWNER and DAC_OVERRIDE are
needed to read and re-stamp files the container does not own. MKNOD stays
dropped, so an archive cannot create device nodes, and seccomp is left at
docker's default.

The exit subscription is opened BEFORE the container starts, and on next-exit.
The default condition is "not-running", which a created container already
satisfies, and asking after start races a fast command being reaped by
AutoRemove before the request lands - either way the exit status is lost.

Concurrency is capped per app and per node, and a reached limit is refused
rather than queued: a queued request holds its connection open behind someone
else's long copy until an intermediate proxy kills it, which reads to the user
as an unexplained failure. AsyncLock grows an activeCount getter for this -
locked only answers the question for a maxConcurrent of one.

Two sweeps replace what the blanket container prune used to do by accident:
orphaned containers are selected by label, and an interrupted operation's
staging directory is reclaimed - restoring the displaced data when a crash
landed between the two renames of a publish, rather than deleting the only copy.

docs(apps): why a file operation reports no byte progress

Since coreutils 9.0, cp copies with copy_file_range(2) - one syscall, the whole
file, inside the kernel. No bytes pass through userspace, so nothing counts
them: /proc/<pid>/io stays flat, the fdinfo offset does not advance until the
end, and docker's blkio_stats is empty on cgroup v2 regardless. Measured on a
node rather than assumed. progress(1) reads those same offsets and stopped
working on cp for the same reason.

for it - a throughput cost on exactly the copies slow enough to want a bar.

fix(volumes): a publish marker names a path inside the volume, or it is refused

The boot sweep read `.flux-old-<id>.dest` and handed its contents straight to
a root `mv` as the destination. That file sits in the volume root, which the
app owner can write to - through an upload with no folder, or a copy naming it

being inside the volume or even for being relative. Any path whose parent
exists and whose leaf does not was reachable: /etc/cron.d and /etc/sudoers.d
both take a new file, and neither needs an execute bit.

The marker is written by flux-op, from inside the container, so it holds a
path in the CONTAINER's namespace - /work/<relative>, the only form an operand
ever takes. Reading it as a host path was the defect, and it was also why
restoring never worked: /work/photos does not exist on the host, so every
interrupted publish took the "destination is missing" branch and moved the
caller's displaced data to a path outside the volume, or nowhere at all. The
unit fixture asserted a host path the running system cannot produce, so the
one branch that exists to prevent data loss passed while never being exercised.

Both follow from resolving the marker where it was written: require it under
the work root, translate it to the mount, and confirm the result is still
inside after normalisation.

The names are matched exactly too. Nothing reserves these prefixes at creation
time, and the sweep deletes what it matches, so a user folder called
`.flux-op-backups` disappeared on the next restart. An unreadable marker is no
longer read as an absent one - only ENOENT means no marker was written, and
anything else keeps the data and says so. A marker whose entry never arrived is
now removed rather than accumulating in the volume root, one per interruption.

feat(volumes): a file operation reports the bytes it has published

A copy could report that it was alive and nothing else, so a dashboard showed
a spinner where the operation most needed a bar.

The reason given was that the bytes are unobservable: since coreutils 9.0 `cp`
copies with copy_file_range(2), the kernel moves the data, and no counter on
the source side sees it - /proc/<pid>/io stays flat and the fdinfo offset does
not advance until the end, which is why progress(1) stopped working on cp. All
of that is true, and none of it is the whole picture. The destination inode
grows the entire time. Measured on a node: across a 3 GB copy, stat() on the
destination tracked it smoothly while fdinfo sat at zero until the last moment.

The generic tools read fdinfo because they attach to somebody else's cp and
cannot know where it writes. This one started the process and chose the path,
so it can simply look. Nothing about the copy changes, and the in-kernel fast
path is kept - the alternative on the table was rsync, which reports its own
totals only because it moves every byte through userspace.

The walk is lstat throughout, so a symlink contributes nothing and none is
followed out of the volume, and it is bounded: a tree too large to measure
inside one tick reports no figure at all rather than one that falls further
behind the longer it runs. A bar that stalls and then jumps makes a promise a
spinner never did.

A denominator is offered only where one is real. A copy has it already, from
the measurement the capacity check makes. An extraction does not - the only
candidate is the archive's own account of its uncompressed size, which is
exactly what the size ceiling refuses to believe - and neither does a
compression, whose ratio is not knowable in advance. Those two report bytes
written and no percentage. A move reports neither: it publishes its source
where it stands, so staging is the whole operation from the first tick.

fix(volumes): a move publishes its source, and says so

same shape needs on this side.

scratch this operation created and a failure may throw it away; a source is the
caller's own data, published where it stands. They were one field called

until the next boot sweep - space the caller is paying for. stop sends SIGTERM

fix(volumes): the executor image is fetched before it is needed

answers 404 for an image the node does not hold, verified against a node's

image store rather than taken from the pull's callback, because dockerPullStream
reports the progress stream and not the outcome.

each time the fleet restarts, for an image most of them will never use.

fix(apps): an archive holds its source's contents, in both formats

Compressing handed each archiver an absolute operand and let it decide the
layout, and the two decided differently.

Info-ZIP stores the entire path minus its leading slash, so zipping /work/photos
produced an archive containing work/photos/... - one level named after a mount
directory the user has never seen, and another repeating a name they had just
chosen. Extracting it did not give back what was compressed. GNU tar, given
-C source ., put the contents at the top. Verified by execution against the
pinned image, both before and after.

failed outright for .tar.gz while the same request with .zip succeeded.

Both now run in the directory that makes the layout right and are handed a bare
operand: from inside a directory for a directory, from its parent for a file.

reproduces the source under that name - compress then extract returns what went
in, in either format, for a directory or a single file. Since zip has no
equivalent of -C, the executor takes the working directory as an option, and
takes it as a VolumePath so a path that skipped the session's checks produces
code that does not run.

what the link points at, which neither tar nor cp -a does - so a link the
extract side would refuse became ordinary content it accepts. Measured: a link
to /etc/shadow stored 260 bytes of file, and stores 11 bytes of link now.

An extension is matched case-insensitively. Plenty of software writes
BACKUP.ZIP, and refusing to extract one with a message listing the extension it
plainly has reads as a broken endpoint rather than a policy.

feat(harness): a published image is mirrored into the test registry

The executor image is pinned by digest in production, and the suites that
exercise it need that same image reachable from inside the fleet. Pulling it
from the public registry at run time is the trap: each node runs its own dockerd
on a per-run volume, so every suite starts with an empty image store, and a
ten-node env would pull it ten times per suite across a whole gate - from a
rate-limited anonymous endpoint, going red whenever that endpoint has a bad day.
Everything else external here is stubbed for exactly that reason.

mirrorImage copies raw bytes registry to registry, not docker save and load: a
manifest digest is taken over the manifest bytes, so preserving them is what
keeps the production pin resolving here, and makes the registry host the only
difference between what the fleet runs and what a node under test runs.

The published index has four entries - amd64, arm64 and an attestation manifest
for each - and an index digest covers all of them, so dropping one would change
it. registry:2 accepts all four, including the unknown/unknown platforms and
their in-toto payloads, so the faithful copy is what ships; verified end to end
by pulling the pinned digest back out of a registry configured as the harness
configures its own. Manifests are pushed depth-first because registry:2
validates that every reference resolves at PUT time.

Blobs and manifests are content-addressed, so they are cached host-side and only
the first suite of a gate touches the network at all - measured at 0.7s per
suite from cache against 11.4s cold, with the public registry blackholed to
prove the cache is really doing it.

Two gaps filled alongside it. nodeClient.request returns the whole response,
because a 202 puts its answer in Location, Operation-Id and Retry-After and a
refusal puts its answer in the status code, all invisible through helpers that
return only a parsed body; and nodeClient.del reaches the cancel endpoint.
waitForOperation polls a job to whatever it settles on, returning a failed job
rather than throwing on one, since a suite asserting that a hostile archive is
refused wants that job and its error.

Promise.all fan-out. It measures volumes the APPS write to, so everything in one
is attacker-supplied: `ln -s .. loop` made the walk measure itself until the
process died, and `ln -s / escape` measured the host. Neither needs privilege to
plant, and both callers run as the FluxOS process before any container exists -
a copy's capacity check, and the file browser, which measures every directory it
lists. So an app could take down the node hosting it, and its owner could do it
by opening their own file manager.

lstat rather than stat, iteratively rather than recursively, and bounded by
entries visited. A symlink now contributes nothing, which is also the honest
figure for what it costs to copy one: cp -a and the archivers copy the link, not
what it points at.

A tree past the bound reports no size rather than a partial one, and
getFolderSize turns that into its existing false. Callers already had to treat
false as a refusal; measure() does, and the file browser shows it as unknown.
The trade is deliberate: a genuinely enormous folder becomes uncopyable rather
than slow, which is the same direction the capacity check already fails in when
it cannot establish free space.

The walk itself moves to utils/treeSize, because the executor's progress
measurement is the same primitive and had already been written correctly -
sharing it means there is one definition of what measuring a tree means, rather
than a safe one and an unsafe one a few directories apart.

perf(volumes): a folder is scanned once, and progress costs one syscall

Two things were wrong with measuring, and neither was the bound I put on it
first.

The scan was sequential. Measured on a fleet-spec box: 20,000 files take 1169ms
one at a time and 179ms at 32 in flight, with nothing further past ~128. The
published work on parallelising du's stat loop reports the same six-fold, so it
is a property of the problem rather than of that box. Batched rather than fanned
out, because the Promise.all this replaced opened a handle per entry.

The entry budget is gone. It was a guess about hardware wearing the clothes of a
limit - 20,000 entries reads like a small number and is over a second - and
nothing needs it any more: a walk cannot fail to terminate now that no symlink
is followed. Every tool that reports a total scans the whole tree and takes as
long as that takes; rsync builds its file list, Explorer says "Calculating...".
A scan that gave up would only leave callers inventing a meaning for a missing
figure.

And the staging tree was re-walked on every tick, for the progress bar. Nothing
reports progress that way - rsync counts what it writes because it does the
writing, and we do not - and at 30,000 files it is a tenth of a core burned
continuously to draw a bar. The volume is its own filesystem, so how much it has
consumed is one syscall whatever the tree looks like. Progress is the difference
from a baseline taken before the command starts.

That figure counts everything written to the volume, not only this operation's
share, because the application keeps running throughout. It is therefore capped
at the total and never allowed to go backwards - an app deleting its own data
would otherwise reverse a progress bar. The figure a COMPLETED operation reports
is still measured from what it actually published, so the cap only ever applies
mid-flight and the bar still lands exactly on its total.

feat(volumes): an upload is written by a container, not by the node

The last operation still writing to the node's own filesystem. It could not be
fixed where it was: a write commits the moment it opens - creating or truncating
whatever the name pointed at - so checking a path and then writing to it cannot
be made safe, and node cannot express "open this only if it is inside that
directory". Linux has openat2 with RESOLVE_BENEATH and node does not expose it.
The container has nothing else mounted, so the question does not arise.

The bytes go from the request into the container's standard input and are
written into staging, published atomically like every other result. A failed
upload now leaves nothing, where before it left a truncated file at its final
name.

Three things are load-bearing:

Closing standard input is the only signal that the transfer completed, so it is
sent only when it did. The stream is piped with end:false rather than through
pipeline, because pipeline destroys its destination when the source errors and
destroying that socket is indistinguishable to the container from a clean end of
input - half a file would publish as though whole. A client that goes away has
its container stopped instead, and flux-op reclaims the staging directory.

The transfer is raced against the container's exit. A container that has stopped
reading never drains the socket and never errors: measured, the writer stalls at
about 448KB and stays there. Every refusal an upload can produce arrives that
way, so without the race each of them hangs the caller's request.

The stream's fate is subscribed to before anything is awaited. There is real
time between receiving it and having a container to feed it to, and an error
event with no listener ends the process.

The ceiling is the volume's own free space, enforced as the bytes arrive rather
than on what was left behind - so an upload that would fill the volume is
refused at the limit instead of filling it first, which matters because the
application's database is on that volume.

A request holds ONE operation slot however many files it carries, and handles
them in turn. A slot per file would refuse the second; no serialisation would
put an unbounded number of containers on the node for one request.

stall check notices minutes later.

and the only one that can be exact, because it refuses as the bytes arrive; a
parser that gives up mid-request hands the caller a broken connection instead
of a reason, which is what produced this.

fix(apps): an aborted download releases its descriptor

pipe() forwards data and ends the destination, but it does not destroy the
source when the destination dies. A client disconnecting part way destroys
the response and leaves the read stream neither ended nor destroyed, so its
'close' never fires and the handle opened above is never released.

One descriptor per aborted download, on a route any caller can abort at
will. The comment above the send claimed the handle was closed on every
path "including a client that disconnects part way", which is the case that
did not hold and the reason it read as handled.

The response's own close now destroys the stream, which closes the handle
through the path already there.

fix(peers): a peer we just heard from is alive, whatever it sent

Liveness was credited only by a pong, so the heartbeat fires first on the
connections we have the most evidence are alive. A pong is an ordinary frame
and queues behind everything else that peer sent us, and FluxOS reads that
queue on one event loop shared with the API, broadcasts and app messages — so
the busier a peer is talking to us, the later its pong is read. Three
unanswered pings later, at 15000ms x 3, we terminate it.

Measured in the peer simulator, which models this window exactly. One node
dying at 3,000 nodes: 245,936 messages read in the following minute, of which
13 were pings. 45s later every node terminated all ~82,000 of its peer
connections, rebuilt them, and did it again 60 seconds later, indefinitely —
from a single death. Crediting any inbound traffic took evictions from
~250,000 to 349 with the congestion unchanged.

isAlive now also accepts a peer heard from within the window the pong count
already allows — pingInterval x maxMissedPongs, derived rather than a new
tunable, so a genuinely silent peer is dropped on exactly the schedule it is
today and only a talking one is treated differently. lastMessageMono is null
until something actually arrives; seeding it at construction would give every
new connection a free window.

Elapsed time is measured on a monotonic clock. Wall clock is moved by NTP and
by hand, and a jump either makes an elapsed time negative or ages a peer out
by however far the clock moved. lastPingTime, lastPongTime and connectedAt
stay on the wall clock because they are reported over the API, where a caller
wants a date rather than milliseconds since this process started.

Four tests, three of which fail against the pong-only behaviour. The fourth
passes there deliberately: it asserts a peer that has sent NOTHING is still
terminated, which must not change.

Note: tests/unit/fluxPeerManager.test.js has a pre-existing no-unused-vars
error at the onclose test, present on development and untouched here.

replaced with a link was read through to whatever it named, and its

and an unbounded line in a log file that is written to disk.

and every write goes through the container. Reading was the one touch of an
