An interrupted publish leaves the displaced data, a marker, and whatever now
occupies the destination. Deciding whether that last thing is what flux-op
placed or something the app owner created while the destination stood empty
was done by following it and asking whether it resolved.

That is a question about the host's filesystem, and an absolute link written
inside a container never named a host path - so the answer was about the
wrong filesystem, and the app owner could read it: point a link anywhere,
restart, and see from their own volume whether the parked entry survived.

flux-op now records the inode and modification time of the object it is
placing, both of which a rename carries with it. A destination matching the
record IS what was published, and cleanup is certain rather than guessed. One
that does not match is the owner's own entry, where restoring would overwrite

first would refuse every marker, and changing the parser first would find no

The browser opens at the volume root deliberately - it is how an app with
several mounts shows them - and that root holds three things that are not the
owner's: syncthing's control files, the filesystem's recovery directory, and
what an interrupted file operation leaves for the boot sweep. All of them
were listed, downloadable, renameable and deletable by whoever owns the app.

Two of those matter beyond tidiness. Removing .stfolder stops syncthing
replicating the folder at all, and replacing .stignore changes what leaves
the node. The operation artefacts are read by the sweep, which decides from
them whether to restore data or delete it - so being able to write one is
being able to hand that decision its input.

The names now live in one place instead of three: the staging prefix moved
out of volumeSession, the swap prefix and marker suffix out of volumeExecutor,
and .stfolder and .stignore stop being literals where they are created. The
refusal sits in session.resolve, which every write endpoint already goes
through, and the sweep names its own artefacts with allowReserved.

Root only. These mean something to the reader that looks for them there and
nowhere else, so reserving them deeper would take names away from an owner
inside their own data - a photos/.stignore they could create and never
manage. The identifier shape stays the whole rule for the artefacts, so a
folder called .flux-op-backups is still a name a user can choose.

lost+found is reserved for the owner's own sake rather than ours: fsck puts
orphaned inodes there after an unclean shutdown, so a volume without one
recovers worse. backup is left alone - it holds their archives, the upload
path recreates it, and the backup UI reads it through its own endpoint.
.stversions is absent because no folder FluxOS creates configures versioning,
so the directory never exists.

docs(fileops): the reserved set records why backup is not in it

Every other name in that comment says why it is there or why it is absent.
backup is the one decision with no record: it sits in the same root and
FluxOS writes it, so the next reader will wonder, and the answer is that

feat(fileops): a node that cannot reach the registry takes the image from a peer

createfolder, renameobject and removeobject were mkdir, mv and rm on the
host and now run in a container, so a node that cannot fetch that image has
no file browser at all rather than four operations short of one. One
registry is not a guarantee that a node can get it, and the fleet already
holds it: every node that has run a file operation has the same image.

The pin becomes a tag and the ids it must resolve to. A tag decides nothing
on its own - it is mutable at the registry, and one inside an archive a peer
sends is whatever that peer wrote into it - so what runs is decided by the
image id, the digest of the image's own config, checked on every path
whether the image came from the registry, from a peer, or was already here.
Containers are created from the id for the same reason. Ids are per
architecture, and they rotate with the tag: the same commit rebuilt under a
new tag carries different labels and a different id.

The endpoint that hands the image over is narrow on purpose. The caller
names the id it wants and gets it only if that is the id this node is pinned
to, so there is no "send me image X" and it cannot become one; a node of
another architecture asks for an id this one does not have and is refused,
which is the answer rather than a case to handle. Only an address the
network state recognises is answered, matched on the address because a
node's api port cannot be read off an inbound connection and the fleet does
not all run on the default one. Two at a time, because thirteen megabytes to
anyone who asks is a way to spend someone else's bandwidth.

What a peer sends is checked and not kept if it is wrong: the ids the daemon
reports loading are compared with the one that was asked for, and anything
else is removed rather than left on the disk.

Measured on a node: a cold pull is 1.6 seconds for 13MB, so this is not
about latency. It is about a node that cannot reach ghcr at all.

feat(fileops): the fleet holds the image, so a peer can hand it over

Taking the image from a peer only works if peers have it, and an image that
arrives when somebody uses the file browser reaches almost nobody. Four
random peers on a fleet where a twentieth hold it miss all four times in four
runs out of five - and that is the state just after a release, which is when
a node that cannot reach the registry most needs one that can.

Every node now takes it at its own point in a six hour window, so the fleet
ends up holding it without every node fetching at once. The point is derived
from the node's address rather than drawn at random: a node that re-rolls
picks a new slot every boot, which turns a restarting fleet back into the
burst the window exists to spread. Hashed, because addresses are not evenly
distributed and their low bits least of all.

Failing to fetch is expected rather than an error - a node with no route to
the registry and no peer holding it yet tries again later, and the on-demand
path still covers a node whose slot has not come round.

The pull also stops being promisified by its callers. Two modules wrapped
dockerPullStream when they loaded, which pinned whichever function object was
there at that moment: a test replacing the property afterwards left the
executor calling the original, and its image tests passed while exercising a
pull nobody had stubbed. dockerService returns a promise now, resolved
through the module at the call, which is where the wrapping belonged.

feat(fileops): peers first, and a caller is told to come back rather than kept waiting

Three things were wrong with how the image was fetched.

A caller paid for the search. A registry timeout and four peers at two
minutes each ran inside a user's click, and nothing remembered the outcome,
so every click on a node that could not get the image paid it again. A caller
now waits ten seconds - a measured pull is 1.6 - and is then answered 503 with
a Retry-After, the same refusal the concurrency limit already gives. The fetch
carries on without them, and a cycle that has just failed answers the next
caller immediately instead of searching again.

The registry got one attempt, so a DNS blip or a single 503 lost it. It gets
two, three seconds apart.

And peers were asked last, which is backwards. Once the fleet holds the image
a peer is the faster answer and costs one central place nothing, and a peer
that does not have it refuses at once rather than timing out - so asking is
cheap even when it is futile. A node that boots without the image now asks
peers straight away and only waits for its point in the window if no peer had
it, because the registry is the only fetch that herds.

Between cycles the wait doubles from thirty seconds to an hour rather than
sitting at an hour: a node whose network returns should not be stuck for one.
Jittered, so nodes that failed together do not return together.

The wait is measured against a monotonic clock, since a wall clock correction
makes a backoff expire early or never.

refactor(fileops): which shape an operation answers in is a rule, not a habit

An operation bounded by construction answers inline - a mkdir and a rename
are one syscall whatever the tree holds - and one whose duration scales with
the data registers a job. The rule was already being followed and already
written down in part: moveobject is a job because overwriting does an
unbounded rm of what it displaced, "so instant was a claim about the common
case rather than about the operation".

removeobject is the same operation and was answering inline. rm -rf scales
with the tree, so a large one held a request open until whatever proxy is in
the way killed it - the failure the executor's own refusal-rather-than-queue
comment describes.

It is a job now, but it still answers inline when it is quick. Two dashboards
call it and neither polls, and a delete of an ordinary folder is sub-second,
so what they have always received is what they keep receiving: 200, complete.
Only a remove that outlives ten seconds becomes something to come back for,
and that is the case where holding the request was already wrong. The clause
is compatibility rather than design and says so, with the condition for
deleting it: when v2 makes the job shape the default, remove is simply a job.

The pin moves to its own file, because the harness reads it too and was
matching it out of this config's source with a regular expression - it cannot
require the config, which pulls in the gitignored userconfig.js. Changing the
shape of a pin therefore broke the runner rather than the thing under test.
It reads a value now, and gets the image ids with it.

The peer search counts peers CONTACTED rather than draws. The draw is random,
so a repeat was standing in for a peer: on a three node fleet that is a one in
sixteen chance of never asking the node that has the image, which is a flaky
suite and a real weakness.

Harness suite 81 covers where the image actually comes from - a peer when the
registry is unreachable, the registry when no peer has it, a 503 with a
Retry-After when neither can, recovery once a peer has it, and the two ways
the handover endpoint refuses. Everything else about this is unit tested with
docker and the network stubbed, so nothing until now watched an image cross a
real wire.

fix(harness): the runner reads the pin instead of matching it out of source

It took the executor image out of ZelBack/config/default.js with a regular
expression that required a digest, so a pin written any other way threw before
a suite could run - the runner breaking over how a value is written down
rather than over the thing it tests. It reads the value now, from the file the
config spreads, and gets the image ids with it.

mirrorImage takes a tag as well as a digest. A tag is resolved at the source
and everything is copied by digest from there, so the bytes that arrive are
the ones the tag named at that moment rather than whatever it names when a
blob is fetched later, and the manifest is pushed under the tag as well
because that is what the nodes ask for.

docs(fileops): the inline remove records what has to be true before it goes

It answers inline when it is quick so two dashboards that do not poll keep
the answer they have always had. That is scaffolding, and scaffolding with no
removal condition becomes permanent - the next reader cannot tell whether it
is a principle to preserve or a thing to delete.

The condition is now stated where the rule is, and it is checkable without
asking anyone: the callers are named, what they would have to do is named,
and what gets deleted when they have done it is named - the deadline, the
option that exists for nothing else, and the inline answer itself.

feat(fileops): a refusal names what the caller is waiting behind

One operation per app means the owner of an app with a four hour copy
running is refused when they make a folder. That is right, and the refusal
told them nothing: which operation, how far along, or whether it can be
stopped - all of which the node knows.

It now carries the running job's id, kind and status url, so a client can
link to it, watch it or cancel it rather than retrying until it happens to
work. The fields are additive on the envelope the refusal already returns.

Retry-After stops being a flat five seconds pretending to know. A copy that
has moved a known fraction of a known total in a known time can say when it
will be done, and does; anything else keeps the default, which is this
branch's own rule about progress applied to a header - a denominator is only
offered where one is real. Capped at five minutes, because an estimate of
hours belongs in the job a caller can watch rather than in an instruction to
sleep.

fix(apps): an app network outliving its app is reclaimed at boot

An app network is created per app and removed by the uninstaller, and by
nothing else. An uninstall interrupted between the container going and the
network going - a reboot, a crash, a removal that failed both its retries -
leaves one behind for ever, because nothing looks again.

That is not cosmetic. Each network carries an explicitly assigned
172.23.<octet>.0/24, and getFreeFluxAppNetworkOctet walks 1..255 for one
nothing is using: a leaked network holds its octet permanently, and when the
last of them is gone the answer is null and no app can be installed on that
node again. Rare, never self-healing, and terminal when it arrives.

At boot, before anything installs, the networks are compared against what the
database says is installed and the ones nothing owns are removed. The expected
NAMES are built from the app records rather than app names being parsed back
out of network names - a name can only be recovered from
fluxDockerNetwork_<name> by assuming what a name may contain, and being wrong
there removes a live app's network.

Two things are left alone whatever the caller said: a network with anything
attached, because something is using it, and one that cannot be inspected,
because a daemon that will not answer is not evidence of an orphan. Same rule
as dockerNetworkState, which reports unknown rather than absent for exactly
that reason.

Raised as the third non-blocking note on #1778.

test(apps): the network reclaim's boot half is a module with tests

The sweep itself was covered and the half that decides what it sweeps was
not: it sat in serviceManager, which has no test suite, so nothing exercised
building the expected names from app records or the guard that keeps an
unreadable app list from reading as "no app owns anything".

It is a module beside fileOperationRecovery now, which is the same shape -
one thing reclaimed at boot, testable on its own - and covered for each way
the app list can fail to answer.

fix(fileops): a caller still sending is not a container getting nowhere

The stall check reads what the volume has consumed, which is the honest
signal for a command writing into staging and no signal at all for an
upload. What a client sends lands in filesystem blocks, so one trickling a
small file over a slow link moves nothing measurable for the whole window
and has its container stopped while it is plainly still sending.

Bytes arriving from the caller now count as the operation getting somewhere.
They are the direct evidence and they are exact, where a block appears only
once enough of them have.

Counted where the pipe is attached rather than before it: a data listener
starts the stream flowing, and one added before the destination exists loses
whatever arrives in between.

The test lives with the other upload tests because that is where a container
can have its stdin attached - written first in the block next door, where
run() failed before the ticker ever started and the assertion passed having
exercised nothing. It asserts the ticker polled before asserting what it did
not do.

test(harness): an upload slower than the stall window is carried, not stopped

Nothing exercised the stall check at all - not a trickle, not a genuine
stall - so the unit tests were the only thing standing behind a check that
stops a container mid-upload when it gets it wrong.

The suite now sends a small file over twenty seconds against a six second
window. The volume never moves during it, because too few bytes arrive to
fill a filesystem block, which is exactly the shape that used to read as a
container getting nowhere.

The client grows a trickling upload for it. The body is built by hand rather
than by FormData, because what is under test is bytes arriving over time and
FormData hands over a body that is already complete.

docs(config): why the image pin lives in the release, and where it is proven

Two things a reviewer of this repository cannot see, both now written where
the pin is.

Rotating the image needs a FluxOS release. That is deliberate: what the image
does is coupled to the code that drives it - the marker it writes is parsed
here, so changing one changes both - and publishing the pin where the fleet
reads policy would let a merge choose the program every node runs as root
over an app's volume, with no staged rollout. What that would buy is small,
because the container has no network, a read-only rootfs, every capability
dropped but three, and one volume mounted.

And the behaviour nothing here can exercise - the byte ceiling, the link
refusal, discarding staging, the marker written before anything moves, the
signal handling - is covered in the image's own repository, in containers
configured exactly as this configures them, on both architectures. Someone
reading only this repository should not conclude those are untested.

Raised as the last non-blocking note on #1778.

fix(fileops): a job the registry refuses to read is not a job that succeeded

completed() read the registry with no owner, so every job registered by an
authenticated caller came back null and the answer fell through to a
hardcoded SUCCEEDED - a removeobject that failed was reported to the
dashboard as having worked. The owner is threaded through, a missing job
says the result could not be read, and a failed one answers with the same
message/name/code triple the legacy handler sent, which is what the
dashboards read.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(fileops): a FIFO in an app's own volume is not something to wait on

openNoFollow opened O_RDONLY | O_NOFOLLOW with no O_NONBLOCK, and opening a
FIFO for reading waits for a writer. An app can mkfifo the name the boot
sweep looks for in its own volume root; serviceManager awaits that recovery,
and a hang is not an error, so everything after it - the network reclaim,
syncthing, the pgp identity, the watchdog - never ran, across reboots.

Fixed in the shared helper so both callers are covered: O_NONBLOCK plus a
regular-file check taken from the descriptor. sendFile already checked
isFile(), but after the open, so it hung before reaching it.

The helper returns the stat it already took rather than leaving callers to
take their own a microtask later - which is what set Content-Length from a
second reading and let a concurrent append widen the file in between.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(fileops): dockerode's own reader frames the load stream, not a regex

loadImage hand-rolled stream framing while pullImage, in the same file, used
docker.modem.followProgress twice. The hand-rolled version reset its buffer
on every chunk, so a "Loaded image ID:" line split across two writes named
nothing; it returned before the removal loop on the success path, so extras
were kept; and it never reported tagged images at all, which let a peer
leave images on our disk under names of its choosing with nothing left that
could name them again.

The framing is deleted rather than repaired. loadImage returns {ids, tags},
both paths discard what is not the expected id, and a tag is resolved to its
id before removal - an archive may legitimately deliver the wanted image
with a tag, and removing that tag would delete the image just fetched.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(fileops): the peer serve notices a caller leaving, and the sweep asks when an object was born

Two fixes in one file, plus what makes them observable to the harness.

serveImageToPeer took a slot, awaited the export, and only then subscribed
to res.on('close'). close fires once, so a caller that hung up during the
export was never noticed, the await never settled and the finally never ran.
Two of those exhaust PEER_IMAGE_SERVE_LIMIT and the node serves no peer
until FluxOS restarts - and peers are the primary source, so a leaked
counter pushes the whole fleet onto the registry the design exists to avoid.
Subscribed before the export, and the archive is discarded if the caller has
already gone. The source-IP strip is no longer greedy to the last colon,
which turned an IPv6 address into a single digit.

The sweep compared the identity flux-op recorded against what now occupies
the destination, using inode and mtime. mtime cannot answer that question: a
reused inode means a new object with a new mtime, and an app writing into a
directory it was just given produces one too, so both present identically
and the sweep refused in both cases - leaving a full second copy of the
owner's data on a fixed-size volume, hidden from them by the reserved-name
work in this same branch, re-evaluated every boot forever.

Creation time survives rename(2), does not move when the object is written
to, and no syscall sets it. Because libuv reports ctime as birthtime when
the kernel has nothing better - identical at creation, drifting on first
write - the record says which clock it used and FluxOS compares the field it
names. A two-field record, which is what image v1.0.0 writes and what may be
sitting on volumes now, reads as mtime and keeps working unchanged.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(fileops): a reserved name is decided from where the path lands, not how it was spelled

The volume root holds names that are not the owner's - syncthing's control
files, ext4's recovery directory, and what an interrupted operation leaves
for the boot sweep. resolve() refused them, but only when the caller's path
had no separator in it, so `.stignore` was caught and `here/.stignore` was
not.

That looks safe until the app makes `here` itself: `ln -s . appdata/here`
runs inside its own container, and `here/.stignore` then names the root's
own file. The string test never fires because the path has a separator, and
the containment check passes because the path really does resolve inside the
mount. Both are true, and neither is the question being asked.

Decided now from the resolved real parent against the resolved real mount.
The mount is resolved too rather than compared as given, because it can
itself be reached through a symlink. The name test runs first, so the two
realpath calls happen only for a name that is reserved at all and the
ordinary path is unchanged.

This replaces the lexical test rather than joining it: where the parent is
the root the two agree, and verifyRealPath returns a path it cannot resolve
unchanged, so a name under a directory that does not exist yet compares as
itself and stays the owner's.

Five tests on a real disk, because a stubbed filesystem has no symlinks to
lead anywhere: the bypass, the same trick nested one level deeper, a
root-level name where the mount genuinely exists, and controls that
appdata/.stignore and .flux-op-backups are still the owner's to write.

test(apps): the UPNP tests close the gate that the random port opens

Two tests in availabilityChecker turned UPNP on and then left
isPortUPNPBanned real. The port under test is drawn at random from the whole
range when nextTestingPort is unset, and the test config bans '81-442' and
2189 - so on 363 draws in 65534 the checker refused the port and returned
before it reached mapUpnpPort, leaving lastUPNPMapFailed false and failing
the assertion.

0.554% per test per run, which is frequent enough to be seen and rare enough
to be dismissed as flake. Both were: the failure looks identical to a load
or ordering problem and passes on any re-run.

Stubbed false in both, in the order the checker asks the questions. Proved
by forcing the draw to 197 and to 2189 - one for each branch of
isPortUPNPBanned - which failed both tests before and passes both after. The

fix(fileops): a caller still sending has to be sending at a rate, not a byte

667df8d60 fixed a real bug - a client trickling a small file fills no whole
filesystem block for minutes, so the volume reads as idle and the upload was
being stopped at ten minutes for it. What it wrote down was "has a byte
arrived", and one byte per window answers that forever. The only remaining
bound was server.requestTimeout at two hours, and with maxConcurrentPerNode
at 4 that is every file operation slot on the node held for two hours, for
every app on it, by four connections sending almost nothing.

The window now asks how much arrived DURING it and compares that against a
floor. Same ticker, same window; nothing new is timed. The clock and the
byte mark move together, because a window that reset one without the other
would measure itself against the previous window's total.

Only where a caller is attached. A copy or a move sends no bytes at all, so
a floor applied to every operation would stop each of them on its first
window.

64 kbit/s, set where a caller below it could not finish anyway: it carries
~58MB in the two hours the request has, so this mostly writes down a bound
that already existed. It clears the worst usable mobile link by a wide
margin and sits thousands of times above the trickle it exists to stop.

A refusal now says what happened - how many bytes in how long, against the
rate a transfer has to keep - because "made no progress" is untrue and
unactionable for a caller who was, slowly, sending.

The test for this direction did not exist, which is why the hole shipped:
every test here asserted only that a slow sender SURVIVES. Suite 74's
trickle carried 39 bytes over 20 seconds, a rate no floor worth having sits
below, so it now carries ten times that - still far short of one filesystem
block across the window, which is the condition it exists to create.

test(harness): a sender under the floor is stopped, and told why

Suite 74 had the same asymmetry that let the hole ship: every test about
rate asserted that a slow sender SURVIVES. The unit test for the other
direction runs against a fake socket and a stubbed statfs; this is the only
place a real container, a real attach and real wall-clock timing decide it,
and the only place the answer has to reach a client that is still sending.

Half a byte a second against a floor of four, on the same volume as the
trickle that clears the same floor five times over - so the rate is the only
thing separating them.

The refusal now names the rate in the unit it is configured in. Dividing by

which is the only place anyone would be reading it.

fix(fileops): a destination that contains the source is refused where the caller can read it

pair() refused a destination inside the source and not the reverse, and
overwrite skips the exists check that would otherwise have stopped it - so
replacing photos with photos/2024 reached the executor. The image cannot
carry that out: displacing the destination takes the source away inside it,
the publish stops between its two renames, and the caller's whole folder is
parked under a name the reserved names hide from them until the next boot
sweep. Completing it instead would delete everything else in photos, which
they never named.

The image refuses it now too, and should - it is the thing doing the
renaming and it must not hold that invariant on trust from a caller. This is
here so the answer is a sentence the client can show rather than an exit code
from a container.

One predicate used in both directions rather than a second copied condition,
so the two cannot drift. Compared through path.relative, because a string
prefix reads photos-2024 as living inside photos - which the second test
holds it to.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

refactor(fileops): the extraction guard is named for what it refuses

The image's flag refused links and let a FIFO through, because a FIFO is not a
link - it is not data at all. It now refuses anything that is not ordinary data,
and is named for that, so this side follows.

A FIFO reaching the volume matters for the same reason a link does: the result
is published where the download endpoints read from the host and syncthing
replicates to other nodes. Its arrival route is the one this flag exists for -
tar carries and recreates them, and extracting an archive is the only operation
that sets it.

The image and this pin move together by construction, so the two names cannot
disagree on a running node.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(fileops): a capacity check measures what a tree occupies, not what it says

measureTree summed each file's own reported length, and three callers wanted
two different things from it without ever having to say which - which is the
defect rather than the arithmetic.

The capacity check is the one that was wrong. volume.measure feeds
requireSpace, which compares its figure against the volume's free space - a
count of blocks - and a file occupies whole blocks however few bytes it holds.
A directory of ten thousand one-byte files reports ten kilobytes for itself and
costs forty megabytes, so a copy passed a check it could not meet and ran out
of space partway, leaving the partial tree requireSpace exists to prevent.

The final progress figure was wrong for a second reason: the running figure is
the volume's own used-bytes through statfs, so a closing reading in apparent
bytes made the bar jump downwards at the last tick - in the one reading added
to stop it stopping short of its total.

The dashboard listing keeps reporting what the files say, because that is what
a listing means by the size of a folder, and it now says so rather than leaving
the next caller to guess.

`size === false` is gone with the getFolderSize call it belonged to. measureTree
and the lstat above both throw, so the fail-closed behaviour is unchanged and
there is no unmeasurable answer left to test for.

The fixtures could not have caught any of this: none of them supplied `blocks`,
which every real lstat does. They do now, which is why the published figure in
the executor test moves from 9000 to 12288 - three 4096-byte blocks, and the
honest answer.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

chore(config): the executor image is pinned to the release that was tested

v1.1.0 is the first flux-volume-tools release whose published bytes are the
bytes its tests ran against: each architecture is built once, pushed by digest
with no tag, pulled back out of the registry and exercised through it, and the
manifest list is assembled from the digests that passed.

Both image ids were derived from the registry and then confirmed against what
docker reports for the pulled image, so the two halves of the pin come from
independent instruments rather than from the run that produced them.

fix(fileops): a node keeps the image it fetched, and reaches the source that has it

The first run of the volume suites found two ways a node ends up without
the executor image, and so without a file browser at all.

A peers-only round recorded a failure. The prefetch asks peers and nothing
else - the registry fetch is the one that herds, so it waits for this node's
slot - and a round that only asked peers has learned nothing about the
registry. Recording it as a failure let it answer for one, and every caller
was refused for a minute over a source that had never been tried, with the
prefetch's own registry attempt still hours out. On a cold fleet, where no
peer holds it either, that is every operation on the node: the case the peer
path exists for is the case it broke.

An image taken from a peer had no name. A peer serves the archive addressed
by id and the daemon writes names only for a reference that carries one, so
what arrives is nameless - and a nameless image is a dangling one, which the
prune before every app install takes. The node lost the image it had just
fetched at the next install and asked a peer again, forever, on exactly the
nodes that took the peer path because they cannot reach the registry. The
comment claiming performDockerCleanup could not reach it was reasoning from
the registry path, where the tag survives.

Named by the receiver rather than carried in the archive, because the name
has to be this node's word for what it verified. Serving by tag was the
alternative and it cannot propagate: a node that received an archive by id
holds no tag to export, so it works one hop and no further.

test(harness): the boot sweep and the image source are asked the right question

Neither suite had ever been executed. Both were asking for something the
product does not produce, and one of them was green about it.

Suite 72 writes its markers as a single line. The sweep has required an
identity line since the sweep learned to ask when an object was born, and it
refuses a marker without one BEFORE it decides anything about the path. So
the test that needs a marker followed could not pass, and three that need one
refused passed at the wrong check - green against a build with the
containment removed, which is the property they exist to hold. The unit tests
were updated when the identity landed; this file was not. Built through one
helper now, so a one-line marker cannot be written again by hand.

Suite 81 asks whether the image arrived by inspecting a TAG. An image taken
from a peer arrives under no name, so the suite reported "the image never
arrived" on the one path it exists to prove, and its removal helper then
could not take an untagged copy - every later test began holding the image it
was supposed to be missing. Asked and removed by id now, which is the
predicate the node itself decides on.

Its peer count asserted exactly one. The peer is drawn at random from the
network state, this node included, so on a fleet of three the node holding
the image is the first draw about a third of the time. Bounded by the fleet
instead: what the count can honestly say is that the search stopped once a
peer supplied it, rather than running on past the answer.

fix(fileops): the image is pinned under both names docker files it by

Docker files an image under different content digests depending on how it
stores images, and a published image is not one blob but an index naming one
image per architecture:

  classic store       this architecture's own config digest
  containerd store    the digest of the index covering every architecture

Only the config digest was pinned. The containerd store is the default from
Docker 29, which on 2026-08-14 was 5,587 of the fleet's 6,066 nodes - so nine
nodes in ten pulled the image successfully and then refused it, and went on
refusing it, because no retry makes two different numbers agree. That takes
the whole file browser down, createfolder, renameobject and removeobject
included, and it is what failed every volume suite on cindy.

Both are now recorded and either is accepted, which weakens nothing: they are
content digests over the same bytes, the index covering the per-architecture
manifests and those covering their configs and layers, so neither can be
forged without breaking the other. The identifier that answered is the one the
container is created from, because it is the only one the local daemon can
resolve.

The comment at expectedImageIds records what to delete once pre-29 docker is
off the network: the config digest goes and the index digest stands alone,
with no architecture in it. `fluxos-docker-versions` is the survey that says
when.

Suite 81 asked the same question the wrong way and is fixed with it, and the
release workflow now prints both halves so the next pin cannot be half filled
in by hand.

test(harness): the extraction refusal is matched on what the guard now says

The guard was widened and renamed from --no-links to --ordinary-only in this
release, because it refuses anything that is not a regular file or a directory
- tar recreates FIFOs, and a flag named for links told the next reader
something untrue. Its message moved with it.

The assertion still matched /link/i, so it held the image to wording the
release deliberately changed while the refusal itself was correct: the
extraction was refused, exit 4, and nothing was placed. Matched on "ordinary"
now, which is still specific enough to tell this refusal from a corrupt
archive or one too big for the volume - the distinction the assertion exists
to make.

test(harness): the acquisition event is read the way every other suite reads one

waitForEvent resolves the whole entry - {id, event, data} - and the payload is
inside it. This read the fields off the entry, so source, peer and asked were
all undefined and the suite reported a peer transfer that had worked perfectly
as one the node failed to recognise.

Never caught because the suite had never run: the assertion it broke is the
one that distinguishes an archive read correctly from an archive misread, and
it could only ever have failed.

fix(fileops): the image is named under the identifier the archive delivered

Naming used whichever identifier is pinned first, which is this architecture's
config digest. A containerd-backed daemon files the image under the index
digest and knows nothing about the config one, so the call answered

  (HTTP code 404) no such image

and the image stayed nameless - the exact state the naming exists to prevent,
and one the prune before every app install then acts on. The failure was
already non-fatal and logged, so the transfer succeeded and the node went on
to lose the image at the next install, on the 92% of the fleet that files
images this way.

Named by the id the archive actually delivered instead, which is the only one
the local daemon can act on.

Found by suite 81, which noticed no image had appeared under any name; the
unit test added here reproduces it without a fleet.

fix(fileops): a peer's archive is bounded and looked at before the daemon sees it

Four defects, one ordering: the download went straight into docker load and
was only judged afterwards.

Unbounded in TIME. PEER_IMAGE_TIMEOUT_MS is documented as how long a peer has
to hand over the archive and does not do that: axios settles a stream request
when the response HEADERS arrive, so the timer is spent before the body
starts. A peer that answered and then went quiet left docker load waiting on a
body that never ended - the shared acquisition promise never settled, so no
retry was scheduled, the registry was never reached, and every file operation
on the node was refused until FluxOS restarted. No attacker required; a NAT
dropping the connection mid-archive does it. Bounded now by arrival rather
than by total time, so a slow link still finishes.

Unbounded in SIZE. Nothing was known about the bytes until they had all
arrived, and they arrived into the docker store - so a peer could write until
the disk the tenants' applications are on was full.

Names. docker load APPLIES the names an archive declares, taking them off
whatever this node had under them, so a peer packing in one of this node's own
app image names renamed it - and removing the stolen name afterwards does not
give it back, it leaves the real image nameless and the next prune deletes it.
This node's own serve path exports by id and declares nothing, so an archive
that declares anything is doing something we never do: refused, not repaired.

Debris. A transfer that died midway left whatever docker had already written,
with nothing that would ever look at it again.

Taken to a file rather than to memory: the ceiling has to be generous enough
never to refuse an honest archive, and holding that much heap on a node whose
memory is the constraint trades one denial of service for another.

The stall test's red proof is a HANG, which is the production symptom exactly.

fix(fileops): serving the image does not walk the fleet list once per caller

Deciding whether a caller was a node meant copying the whole network state -
around 13,000 entries - and splitting a string per entry, and it ran BEFORE
the caller had been shown to be anyone. Measured at ~2.4ms of the event loop
per request, so roughly 400 a second saturate the one core FluxOS has and
stall everything on it: app installs, operation polling, peer messaging. The
route is unauthenticated and the image id it wants is public config, so that
was reachable by anyone on the internet rather than by a node.

A set of addresses is built once per window instead, however many callers
arrive - the same answer at a constant cost, and held only while the endpoint
is being used. The one other unauthenticated route in the tree that walks the
fleet list is wrapped in cache('30 seconds') for the same reason.

The ceiling check moves above it too: a node with no capacity to serve should
not pay to find out who is asking.

The address extraction is deliberately unchanged. It mishandles IPv6, but so
does the fetch side, and the two halves have to move together.

Unit tests no longer write the peer archive to a real disk. That file is
incidental to what they check, and a full disk or a permission would have
failed them for a reason that is not the code; where a real archive IS the
thing under test, dockerService.archiveNames tests it against real tars.

fix(fileops): serving the image is bounded by what the caller actually takes

A slot came back only when the caller DISCONNECTED. A caller that neither
disconnects nor reads does neither - the export blocks on backpressure and the
slot is held for as long as the socket is open - so two connections took every
slot on a node until FluxOS restarted, and nothing said so: the node's own
operations kept working, so it looked healthy while serving no peer at all.
Cheap to do to the whole fleet at once, which pushes every node onto the
registry, the load peer serving exists to avoid. And reachable by more than
node operators, since an application's container egresses under its host's
address.

Bounded now by bytes leaving the export, which is exactly what a caller taking
nothing stops, so a slow but honest caller still completes. The ingress side
already reasons this way; there was no equivalent here, and not even the
two-hour backstop that covers ingress.

The ceiling is now taken in the same tick it is tested. Testing it, awaiting,
then taking it let every request arriving together read the same count and all
pass - it bounded nothing at the one moment it was for.

HEAD is refused. Express answers it from the GET route and node discards a
HEAD body without applying backpressure, so a HEAD bought a full export off
the disk for one packet and no bandwidth.

The ceiling itself goes from 2 to 4. Its own comment said it was there so a
node could not be asked to spend its bandwidth by whoever asks most often, and
a concurrency count never bounded that - one caller asking serially spends
without limit. What it can honestly bound is simultaneous exports, and against
that, at fourteen megabytes a stream, 2 and 4 are the same. 4 leaves more of
the fleet able to answer during a pin rotation, when the few nodes holding the
new image are the bottleneck for everyone else.

A refusal and a stall are both logged, because neither was visible before.

The ceiling test derives the limit by filling it rather than naming it, so it
stays true when the number moves.

fix(fileops): a round is shared only when it looks where the caller needs it to

acquireImage handed the in-flight round to every later caller regardless of
what that caller had been allowed. A file operation arriving while the
prefetch's peers-only round was running therefore inherited a refusal from
sources it had never asked - and because that round was also thenRetry:false,
nothing was scheduled afterwards either. The caller was told no while the one
source that would have answered went untried, and the window is not short:
four peers that blackhole take minutes. A caller allowed the registry now
waits for the round in flight and then goes on to the sources it was allowed.

`asked` meant two things on the same event: peers contacted on one branch,
registry attempts on the other. Anything summing it added different
denominators, and the peers this node asked first were invisible whenever the
registry won - which is most of the time. It means peers asked on every branch
now, with the registry reporting its own attempts beside it.

Retry-After reported only the backoff, which is zero while the first round is
still running and after any round that does not schedule a retry - so it
clamped to its five-second floor while the node went on refusing for the full
minute of the silence window, and a client that honours the header retried
about twelve times for nothing. It now reports the longer of the two things
that actually make the node refuse.

fetchImageFromPeer reports how many peers it asked instead of throwing that
number away inside a message, which is what makes the count available on the
registry branch at all.

fix(apps): the image fetch starts before the boot sweep that needs it

recoverInterruptedFileOperations was awaited first and startImagePrefetch
called after it. The sweep puts a displaced destination back by running a
container, so a node that boots without the image cannot do it: the failure is
per-entry, logged at warn, and nothing looks again until the next restart.
That leaves the owner's data parked under a reserved name their file browser
hides and their delete refuses, for as long as the node stays up - and the
condition that stopped it generally clears within minutes.

Safe to move only now that a caller allowed the registry no longer inherits
the prefetch's peers-only refusal; before that, starting the fetch first would
have made the sweep MORE likely to join a round that never reaches the
registry.

No unit coverage: serviceManager has no test module and proxyquiring it for an
ordering assertion would be a larger fixture than the change. Verified by
reading, and the two calls are adjacent.

fix(fileops): a node does not draw itself when looking for a peer

Every other caller of getRandomSocketAddress passes its own address so the
draw can skip it. This passed null, which never matches, so a node could spend
one of only four peer attempts asking itself for an image it had just
established it does not hold. Negligible across the fleet, one draw in three
on a fleet of three - which is what the harness runs.

Not fatal if the address cannot be determined: a draw that might waste an
attempt is better than no peer search at all.

The IPv6 half of this finding is NOT a defect and is deliberately not
"fixed". The fetch side splitting a socket address on ':' looks wrong beside
the serve side's careful IPv6 handling, but the network state cannot hold an
IPv6 node: parseSocketAddress refuses more than one colon and ipPattern is
IPv4-only. Checked against the live fleet - 0 of 6,063 nodes carry one. Making
the fetch side parse IPv6 would add handling for a case the addressing does
not support and diverge from parseSocketAddress; the serve side's care is
defensive, not a claim that such a peer exists.

test(harness): a peer that does not play fair, and a way to wait for the fleet view

Every peer in every other suite is a real FluxOS node behaving correctly, so
nothing exercised what a node ACCEPTS from one that is lying to it - and the
archive is the one thing a node takes from another node and then runs. Suite
82 covers the unbounded archive, the archive that declares this node's own app
image name, the peer that answers and goes silent, and a caller arriving while
one is stalling.

The rogue peer is this process rather than a stub image: the docker bridge
gateway IS the host, so a node reaching the gateway address reaches the
runner, and misbehaviour becomes a few lines of JavaScript instead of an image
to build and keep in step. It is registered as a fourth node from the same
fixture the real ones come from, which also makes the runner an accepted
caller of the image endpoint - so the serve side is exercised here too: HEAD,
and callers that hold slots by never reading.

Its tar is written out rather than taken from a library. The runner depends on
none, and a hostile archive is the wrong thing to build with a helper that
only knows how to make correct ones. Checked against node-tar and GNU tar
before it was relied on.

waitForNetworkState/waitForNetworkStateSize are general, not for this suite.
A node's view of the fleet is a cache refreshed on a timer, and every endpoint
that reports a list asks the daemon instead - so a suite that changed the node
list had no way to know when the node had read it, and sleeping long enough is
what turns into a flaky suite. networkStateService now publishes each refresh
on the test-only bus, which is what makes that waitable.

test(harness): the hostile-peer suite honours the answer the node gives it

Five of its eight failed on its first run, all with the same refusal: "the
file operation image is not on this node yet and is being fetched; try again
shortly". That is the product working. A node whose acquisition has just
failed refuses every caller for a silence window rather than repeating the
whole search per click, and the suite fired one request into that window and
took the refusal for a result.

It comes back now, bounded, and asserts on the last answer if the node never
does - so "eventually" is still an assertion. Which also exercises the
come-back contract rather than only the happy path.

The test that causes it moves last. It cuts this node off from every source
and restarts FluxOS, so anything after it was asking a node freshly taught it
cannot get the image - a different question from the one each meant to ask.
Ordering rather than retrying is the real fix; the retry is there because any
test could leave the node in that window.

And the suite's own teardown hung: server.close() waits for every connection
to end, and several of these tests deliberately leave one open. The responses
are tracked and taken down between tests and at the end.

fix(fileops): both halves of the image transfer read an address the same way

The serve side takes care over an IPv4-mapped address and an IPv6 literal. The
fetch side split on the first colon, which reads ::ffff:1.2.3.4 as an EMPTY
host and 2001:db8::1 as host "2001" port "db8" - so one half of one feature
disagreed with the other about what an address even is.

Reasoned away earlier on the grounds that the network state is IPv4-only by
construction, which is true - parseSocketAddress refuses more than one colon,
and 0 of 6,063 live nodes carry an IPv6 address. That argument was wrong
twice. The mapped form is not hypothetical: the serve side strips it
BECAUSE it occurs. And leaving the two halves inconsistent is a trap for
whoever adds IPv6, who will read the careful half and assume the other matches.

Through bareIp/extractPort now - the same parser the rest of the tree uses -
and a literal is bracketed so it can sit in a URL at all. The fleet membership
set is built with bareIp too, so an address is recognised in the same terms it
is dialled.

fix(fileops): the sweep decides nothing it cannot decide soundly

The sweep compared an inode number and a creation time to tell a completed
publish from an entry the app owner made at the destination, and deleted the
parked copy when they matched. Neither field is unique: filesystems reuse inode
numbers at once, and inode timestamps come from a coarse clock. Measured on
ext4 over 200 trials, the inode is reused every time and the creation time
collides 108 times - so the sweep was deciding whether to delete somebody's
only copy of their data on evidence a coincidence satisfies. The unit test
saying otherwise has been red on Linux CI since it was written; it passed on
macOS only because APFS timestamps are finer.

The comparison is gone rather than repaired. A publish is one atomic exchange
now (flux-op v1.2.0), so nothing is parked under a swap name and no marker is
written - there is no completed-or-not question left to answer. What remains is
what an image before v1.2.0 may have left on a volume, and for those the rule
is the one that cannot lose data: place the entry when its destination is
empty, and when the destination already holds something, keep both and say so.
Space on a fixed volume, which can be reclaimed by hand, against a deletion
that cannot be undone.

resolveMarkerRecord no longer requires an identity either. Nothing compares it,
so demanding it would only refuse markers that are otherwise perfectly
readable - including every one the first release of the image wrote, which
carried the path alone.

chore(config): the executor image is pinned to the release that exchanges

v1.2.0 publishes a flux-op whose publish is one atomic exchange, so there is no
interrupted state for the boot sweep to recover from and no marker for it to
read. The sweep changes with it.

Both ids derived from the registry and then confirmed against what docker
reports for the pulled image, on both architectures, so the two halves of the
pin come from independent instruments rather than from the run that produced
them. The published image was content-checked as well: it carries the exchange
and the string .flux-old- is gone from it entirely.

refactor(apps): deviceHelper drops the resolver nothing calls

mountForTarget has had no callers since the executor started resolving mounts
through the session. The reviewer flagged it in both of their rounds and it was
listed as outstanding twice more after that without being acted on.

Its sibling, mountFor, is what the code uses.

refactor(fileops): the marker scheme goes, because nothing writes one

A publish is one atomic exchange as of flux-op v1.2.0, so nothing is ever
parked under a swap name and no marker is ever written. The code that read
them was kept for one commit on the grounds that a volume somewhere might
still hold one - but this feature has never been released, so the only volumes
that could are a harness fleet that is destroyed after every run and a dev
node. Carrying a reader for that is carrying the attack surface both of the
review's findings lived in, to protect nothing.

Gone: resolveMarkerRecord and the bounded marker read, the swap and marker
branches of the sweep, SWAP_PREFIX, MARKER_SUFFIX, isSwapName and
isSwapMarkerName. isReservedName still covers what it always did that matters -
syncthing's own files, and the staging directory, which is still created.

The sweep now does one thing: delete staging entries. It cannot restore
anything because there is nothing to restore, so `restored` goes from its
return shape and from the recovery tally rather than being reported as a
permanent zero.

Suite 72's boot-recovery block loses the tests that plant markers, which would
otherwise assert that a sweep ignores something nothing creates. What it keeps
is what recovery is now: staging is reclaimed, and everything else on the
volume - including a name that merely resembles an artefact - is left alone.

docs(fileops): the sweep is described by what it does, not what it used to

Both headers still set out the three kinds of entry an interrupted publish
could leave and the rules for telling them apart. There is one kind now, and no
rule to apply to it beyond deleting it - a comment describing a scheme the code
no longer has is worse than none, because the next reader trusts it.

fix(networkstate): a node it has not heard of yet is not a node that is absent

search(), includes() and getRandomSocketAddress() awaited waitIndexesReady,
which is the indexing lock. That lock is free before the first fetch has ever
run, so the wait returned at once and the lookup read an empty index - and
every node in the fleet came back absent.

A peer acting on that answer rejects a legitimate node. Observed in an
integration gate: a node answered "pubkey not in node list" to four sync
requests 58ms before it logged building its first index. The requester is
never asked again, so it fell back to the block timer and never completed
state sync.

The list has three conditions, not two. Never fetched, where the node cannot
answer and has to wait; fetched and empty, where "absent" is the truth and it
answers immediately; fetched and populated, where it answers from the index.
Waiting on the first population instead would have hung the empty case for
the life of the process, so what is tracked is the first fetch coming back.

Waiters are released when the manager stops, where no fetch is coming.

test(harness): the hostile peer stops generating when the node hangs up

The unbounded-archive test counted bytes the fake peer pushed, not bytes the
node took. While the node is reading, pipe() throttles the generator to what
it accepts; the moment the node cuts the connection at its ceiling, writes to
the dead socket are discarded rather than pushing back, so the generator ran
free until the 'close' event was dispatched.

How much it produced in that window tracked how busy the box was. Run alone it
landed under the 512MiB bound; in a full parallel gate it reached 529MiB and
failed a node that had done exactly the right thing - one cutoff, at
134,217,728 bytes on the nose.

The generator now stops at the hangup rather than at the close event, so the
count is of bytes that were actually taken.

test(harness): the peer-threshold test can reach its own assertion

test(harness): a caller that has not sent anything is holding no slot

The serve-ceiling test opened a holder per round with connectAndIgnore, which
returns as soon as connect() is called - before the socket is up and well
before the request is on the wire. statusOf resolves on response headers, so
each round was fast, and the loop could run all twelve before a single holder
had arrived. Nothing held a slot, so nothing was refused, and the assertion
failed on a node that was behaving correctly.

The node's own log settles it: nine refusals, "already serving 4", every one of
them in a 0.7s burst AFTER the loop had given up - the twelve requests landing
together once the loop stopped racing them.

connectAndIgnore now resolves when its request has been written, and the loop
awaits it, so each round adds a holder before the next probe asks about the
ceiling. The failure message names how many callers were holding, so a real
regression here says something.

fix(fileops): rename does not overwrite what it lands on

Publishing over the destination exchanges the two entries and then removes what
was displaced, so renaming onto a name that already exists deleted it - from a
GET with no confirmation step in front of it.

There is no flag to turn it back on. The removal is unbounded, which is why
moveAppsObject answers 202 and runs as a job; this endpoint answers inline, so
permitting an overwrite here would put an unbounded delete inside a held
request. A caller that means to replace something uses moveAppsObject, which is
the general form and handles this case too.

fix(docker): bound the manifest a peer's archive is read from

archiveNames read manifest.json into a string with no ceiling. The archive
around it is a file, bounded at PEER_IMAGE_MAX_BYTES precisely so a peer cannot
put 128MB in heap - and then this read it back out into heap, on the one path
whose job is handling what a lying peer sends.

64KB. The archive holds one image, docker refuses to build deeper than 125
layers, and each is listed as a path of about 80 bytes: ~10KB of Layers plus a
config path and tags, against a real one measuring 1.2KB. Past the ceiling the
bytes are drained and dropped, and the archive is refused as not describing one
image - which sends the caller to another peer or the registry, like any other
malformed archive.

fix(fileops): a filename is not an option to the archiver

compress handed the operand to tar and zip bare. The component rule rejects
only the separators and the control characters, so a name beginning with a dash
is one an owner may legitimately have - and both archivers read it as a flag
and refuse the request with a usage error that says nothing about the file.

"you may not specify more than one '-Acdtrux'", `zip -r -q -y out -dashfile.txt`
with "short option 'a' not supported". Both accept it after `--`, and store the
name unchanged - which a `./` prefix would not.

warns about: the unit tests assert the argv FluxOS builds, and suite 75
round-trips such a file through compress and extract on a real volume.

fix(fileops): copy and compress carry a ceiling, not just an estimate

fix(ioutils): a folder size is a number

getFolderSize could answer `false`, and the file browser put that straight into
a listing's `size` - a boolean where every sibling entry has a number, and NaN
for anything that did arithmetic on it.

The value was also nearly unreachable, and the contract it came with was wrong
in both directions. It promised `false` when a folder "could not be read at
all" and told callers to treat it as a refusal rather than as zero; measureTree
catches an unreadable entry and an unopenable directory, so that case already
answered ZERO, and the only thing left that could throw was nothing in
particular.

So it returns bytes. The docblock says what the number means instead: it
approximates upwards of nothing, which is what a size in a listing is for and
what du does with the same problem. Deciding whether something FITS needs a
bound on what actually lands, which is where that now lives.

refactor(fileops): one way to arm the acquisition timer

left referenced by nothing survives stopImagePrefetch, so it would fire on a
node that asked not to fetch.

fix(fileops): the peer archive ceiling is a RAM ceiling, so size it like one

The archive goes to os.tmpdir(), and that is tmpfs on ArcaneOS and on any node
whose systemd puts /tmp there - measured on both an Arcane node and the test
box. tmpfs pages are reclaimable only to swap, so 128MiB was what a peer could
make a node hold in memory. A CUMULUS has 8GB for itself and every application
on it.

The pinned image saves to 5.9 MiB, so the ceiling is now 32MiB - over five
times an honest archive. It can be that tight because the image is pinned in
this repository and cannot grow past it without a release that can raise it,
and because a refused archive falls through to the registry rather than failing
the operation.

test(harness): extraction carries a link, and refuses what is not data

Suite 72 asserted that an archive holding a symlink is refused. It is not, and
has not been since --ordinary-only became --data-only: a link among an app's own
files is data its owner put there, what bounds a hostile archive is the container
the extraction runs in, and what answers a link left in the result is the reader -
every walk here lstats and the downloads open with O_NOFOLLOW.

So the test now asserts what actually holds. The archive extracts, the link lands
as a link rather than as the host file it names, and the ordinary file beside it
comes through too. The fixture assertion is unchanged and still load-bearing:
built without -h, because with it tar dereferences and the archive holds a regular
file, which is how the first version of this test passed while proving nothing.

Where the line is drawn instead now has its own test. A FIFO is not data - whatever
opens one without O_NONBLOCK waits for a writer that never comes, so one published
onto a volume is a reader that hangs - and tar both carries and recreates them, so
an archive is all it takes. It is refused, nothing is published, and the refusal
names the entry.

Matched on the entry rather than on the reason. The wording belongs to the image;
matching it is what held the old test to a sentence the image had already changed.

test(harness): a taken destination fails the job, not the call

Suite 72's neighbour asserted that copying onto a name that is already taken is
refused synchronously - a non-202 from the POST. It is not. The check and the move
are one operation inside the container, precisely so that nothing can occupy the
name in between, so the call is accepted like any other and the refusal arrives as
the job's outcome.

Which is what the test is named for: the poll answers 200 whatever the job did, and
completion is read from the body. A client reading it from the status would call
this a success. The test now proves that, by starting a copy that will fail and
reading Failed and the reason out of a 200.

It was also the reason three later tests in this suite failed. The 202 it did not
expect was a job it therefore never polled, and that job held the per-app slot, so
every copy after it was answered 503 by a lock doing its job.

fix(apps): a call that makes or unmakes a container is refused until boot settles

Boot reconciliation decides which applications this node is keeping, and it runs
behind daemon readiness, node confirmation and DB sync - so it lands well after
the API starts answering. On the run that turned this up, the API served an
install 68 seconds into a boot chain whose last gate had not opened.

An app created in that window has no location record, because a record is written
from the running broadcast an app only makes once it has run. Reconciliation then
reads the absence as "this app was reassigned elsewhere" and removes it. The app
was installed, launched, and deleted inside two seconds.

The internal actors already hold off: the reconciler queues into bootPending
rather than actuating, and crash recovery waits for the same gate. Nothing at the
front door did, so ten endpoints that create or destroy a container answered
throughout - appstart, appstop, apprestart, apppause, appunpause, appremove,
installapplocally, testappinstall, redeploy and redeploycomponent.

They now answer 503 with a Retry-After until the gate opens. A point-in-time read
of the gate rather than a wait on it: the boot chain can run to its five-minute
daemon timeout, and a caller told when to come back is served better by that than
by a connection held open for it. globalState offers a promise for waiting, and
this deliberately does not use it.

Read-only endpoints are untouched. So is appexec, which runs inside a container
the node has already decided to keep.

test(harness): the boot gate is held shut, and the refusal read from behind it

Suite 38 now proves the refusal rather than the absence of the bug. Without a test
that reaches the window, deleting the guard leaves every suite green, because the
installer below waits for the gate and never knocks on a closed one.

The window is held open rather than raced. manageAppsOnBoot waits on daemonReady,
which opens only once the node's daemon RPC answers, so failing that node's RPC in
the stub parks the boot chain with the API already serving. Arriving first instead
would assert whichever of two clocks won, and the suite would report on the timing
rather than on the contract.

Three assertions, because a status alone does not say the call was refused: 503,
a Retry-After for a caller that would otherwise poll flat out, and the container
the call would have started still sitting exited. Then the RPC is restored and the
same call is no longer refused - asserted as "not 503" rather than on a status,
because what appstart answers for an app boot reconciliation has already restarted
belongs to appstart, not to this guard.

The boot:settled wait is scoped with an afterId read while the gate is provably
shut. waitForEvent answers from its buffer, and the buffer still holds the event
from this node's previous boot in the test above.

installOnNodes waits for boot:settled before installing. It installed as soon as
the API answered, which is how the node came to delete an app it had launched two
seconds earlier.

test(harness): a stub peer answers the port check a node asks a peer to make

Before installing, a node opens its ports and asks a RANDOM peer to confirm they
answer from outside, retrying a bounded number of times and aborting the install
if nobody confirms. The stub answered 404, so it was a peer that could never
confirm - every node that drew one burned an attempt, and a fleet carrying
several failed installs that had nothing wrong with them. Two nodes in a
fourteen-slot fleet drew stubs on every attempt and aborted.

It now connects. Answering blind would have been shorter and would have masked
the exact failure the check exists to find: the asker opens those ports for this
check alone. The refusal names the port, because the asker reads that number back
out to decide which one to retest, and the ports are probed together rather than
in turn - the asker gives the whole exchange one timeout, and a serial walk
spends it before it can answer.

The handler is async now, so the whole of it is wrapped: a request that fails
while being read rejects rather than throws, and an unhandled rejection ends the
process. A stub that dies mid-suite is worse than one that answers badly.

No suite asserts a port-availability failure, so nothing was relying on the 404.

test(harness): suite 39 builds its contest rather than waiting for one

The suite converges an app on three of ten nodes and asserts that more than three
wanted it, because converging on three says nothing unless there was a contest:
with only three claimants the same green result arrives with the backoff deleted.

That assertion tripped on 2026-08-16 at exactly three claimants. It was right to.
The fourth node to look could already see three claims and never claimed at all -
the standdown working, and the better it works the less there is left to resolve.
Measured at six to nine claimants when the assertion was written; a fleet of ten
on one box no longer reliably produces one.

So the rivals are arranged. Four stub peers claim after the real nodes have
committed, backdated so every real claimant is ranked into surplus at its next
read, then give the slots up so the fleet fills them. A rival that speaks FIRST
suppresses a claim instead of contesting it - a node will not claim against a
claim it can already see - which is the ordering suite 78 established for one
rival. The run this was built against produced thirteen claimants and five real
withdrawals, against three by chance before it.

The floor gate gets a fleet of its own, without stubs. Its premise is that every
node installs and a stub cannot: it holds no FluxOS, so it never claims and never
runs anything, and leaving the rivals in would make the target unreachable by
construction. They also cannot stand in as peers for the nodes that do install -
a stub answers fluxapprequest and nothing else, so a node that draws one as its
app-state sync peer waits out the sync and never learns there is anything to
place. That left one node idle before the split.

The claim count is now a fixture check and is labelled as one; the stubs supply
it. What carries the suite is that a REAL node was outranked and gave way, and
that it gave way rather than failed - a node standing aside attempted nothing,
and reporting it as an install error would make the apps with the most contenders
look the most broken.

fix(apps): a node whose shared filesystem cannot be identified reports no size

Every mount is classified by comparing its device against the filesystem the
node shares, and that comparison re-stated the apps folder once per mount,
inside the loop's own error handling. A single failure there - a missing
folder, a permission, a misconfigured FLUX_APPS_FOLDER - therefore arrived as
one caught error per mount, each sizing its mount at zero. The call then
returned bind 0, volume 0 and status success, and cached it: every app on the
node showing almost no disk in use, indefinitely, with a log warning as the
only trace, because the interface only blanks its values on an error.

The shared filesystem is one fact about the call rather than a step in the
loop. It is resolved once, where the classifying happens, and a failure to
resolve it fails the call. Sizing the mounts some other way would answer a
different question under the same field name - a walk measures apparent size
where a dedicated volume is charged its whole filesystem - so the honest
outcome is no reading rather than a plausible one that is quietly too low.

A container with no mounts has nothing to classify and never asks, which also
keeps a docker failure the error the caller sees.

fix(apps): the cpu watermark dates the window, not the work that followed it

are awaited before the watermark is stamped. A sample arriving during those
awaits is not in the snapshot, so it takes no part in that decision - and a
watermark dated afterwards puts it behind the next window's floor as well, so
nothing ever counts it. The array used to be held live, which is why this only
became reachable when the window began being copied.

The watermark now carries the time the window was taken, so the boundary sits
where the decision actually stopped looking and a sample landing mid-flight is
still ahead of the next one.

Both paths stamp it, and both do so twice - the burst-active skip and the
decision itself - so all four now read from the same instant.

fix(apps): a peer is told which components this node holds stopped on purpose

Retiring apppause takes away the only way an owner could hold their g: master
in place while they worked on it. A paused container stays in `docker ps`, so
FDM's health check passed, the election saw a running primary, and the role
never moved. `appstop` is what is left, and what stopped a peer electing over
the gap was controllerDesired - in-memory, written only at the moment a node
WINS an election and never re-asserted while it goes on being the primary. A
FluxOS restart empties it, so whether the owner kept their master turned on
whether their node's FluxOS had happened to restart since it was elected.

The fact needed is already stored, durably, on the right node: `appstop` writes
operatorStopped into zelappsruntimestate, and the reconciler and the election
both honour it. It simply never left the node. heldComponents now reports it, so
the answer a peer reads is about OWNERSHIP rather than about what is up.

Not filtered to g:. The list answers "is this component mine", which is true of a
stopped component whatever its storage mode, and the only caller asks about g:
components alone - so filtering would cost a spec lookup to leave out entries
nobody looks up.

operatorStoppedIdentifiers throws where getState swallows. getState's callers ask
about one component and act locally, so a read failure reads as "no lock" and the
next pass asks again. This answer leaves the node, and an empty list tells a peer
the component is free - which it acts on by starting a second writer on the
shared volume.

That failure has to be visible to the caller too, and it was not. FluxOS reports
errors inside a 200, so a peer that HAS the endpoint and could not serve it is
shape-identical to one too old to have it - and the old-peer path falls back to
the container list, which cannot see the lock at all. Adding a database read to
the answer without this would have opened a new hole: Mongo down and docker up,
and an owner-stopped primary reads as free. An in-band error is now UNKNOWN,
which also covers a restarted node's window before it reconnects to its database.

heldComponents' docblock also claimed it was uncached; the route has carried a
one-second cache since the peer-probe work.

Suite 52 gains the case end to end: stop the master, restart FluxOS to empty
controllerDesired, clear FDM so the election opens at once, then assert the
restarted node still reports the component held and the standby records a
refusal. Asserted on the standby's decision, not on elapsed time - a node waiting
out a stagger looks identical to one correctly holding off.

fix(apps): a due start at the front of the queue asks the peers behind it

The staggered start serialises candidates by election order, so a node whose
booked turn comes due checks the nodes AHEAD of it before starting. At index 0
there are none, and the walk asked NOBODY - which the caller read as clear. Same
for index -1, this node absent from the location list.

That is the blind start the index-0 branch already takes scope 'all' to avoid,
reached from the staggered paths instead, and it is not unreachable there. It
needs three things at once, which is why it is rare rather than impossible: a
remembered primary, so the index-0 branch that probes every peer is skipped; a
booked turn, so the previous-primary branch, which requires none, is skipped;
and index 0 by the time the turn is due. The turn is booked at index >= 2 and
index is re-derived from the location list every pass, so the instances ahead
ageing out is all it takes - an ordinary sequence during a multi-node outage.

What makes it harmful is FDM's registration lag: for ~110s after a node starts,
FDM still reports no primary. A less senior node can be live and invisible
throughout, and starting beside it puts two writers on the same syncthing
volume. Escalate rather than answer: a start is never issued without some peer
having been asked. An empty 'all' is a real answer and falls through unchanged,
and a node that does have someone ahead of it still asks only that node - the
stagger's whole point.

The per-place wait moves to config, replacing four `index * 3 * 60 * 1000`
literals with a named helper read at call time. It is why no harness suite
exercises a staggered start: at three minutes a place, reaching one costs
minutes of wall clock, so the class goes uncovered at rig level. A suite that
wants one compresses it in its own configOverrides, NOT in the shared harness
config - that would re-time every existing g: election suite for the benefit of
the one that needs it.

The unit config carries 30000 rather than the production 180000, deliberately.
The code falls back to three minutes when the key is missing, so a config value
equal to the fallback cannot tell "read from config" from "key misspelled and
silently defaulted" - which is exactly how statsSampleIntervalMs came to read
undefined. The test asserts to the millisecond against the configured value and
refuses to run if the two are ever equal.
