fix(apps): the narrowed stats keep the figure a memory reading is useless without

Docker's memory `usage` counts page cache - file data the kernel holds only
because something read it, and releases the moment anything else wants the
space. `docker stats` subtracts it, and so does every consumer that reports a
container's memory. The narrowing kept `usage` and `limit` and dropped
`memory_stats.stats`, which is where that figure lives, so the subtraction now
takes away nothing and the number reported climbs with disk reads and never
comes back down. Nothing errors; a customer's RAM bar simply reads high.

It was missed because the round-1 check for consumers of the dropped fields was
run against fluxos-frontend, which reads `usage` and `limit` raw. The two game
dashboards - palworld and minecraft, byte-identical here - do
`usage - (stats.inactive_file ?? stats.cache)`, and they are the ones on a
customer's screen.

Read from whichever key the host's cgroup version exposes and reported under the
v2 name, so a consumer's own fallback chain settles on the first key. Null where
neither is present, which leaves that consumer exactly where it is today.

Cost, measured over ten components at a week of samples each: the full docker
reading was 469MB, the thirteen extracted values are 32MB, and this makes it
36MB. One number gives back 0.9% of what dropping the other twenty-seven saved,
and it comes out of the reading already in hand - no extra call, no extra
syscall. The docblock now carries those figures and the rule they imply: a value
belongs in the extract if a consumer cannot do its job without it, not if it is
cheap to carry.

The sampler's interval body had no unit coverage at all - its only assertion was
that startAppMonitoring is a function - so the docker -> stored direction was
pinned by nothing, and what extractSample chose to keep was visible only through
the endpoints downstream. There are now four tests over a single tick, including
one that pins the whole kept set so a later addition has to be argued for. The
unit config gains fluxapps.statsSampleIntervalMs, without which arming the
interval throws on the first line that reads it.

fix(apps): a disk reading that is short says so, and keeps the number du gave it

A mount that could not be measured contributed zero, and the total was then
cached for a minute and served as `status: 'success'`. Palworld's dashboard
reads `disk_stats.used` and never looks at the status, so a customer saw a disk
figure short by a whole mount, held for the cache window, indistinguishable from
a real one.

Refusing to answer - the rule already applied to the apps-folder stat one level
up - is the wrong fix here, and du is why. Measured on Linux: `du -sb` over a
directory with one unreadable child PRINTS THE RUNNING TOTAL and exits 1. The
realistic trigger is not permissions, since this runs as root; it is a temp file
vanishing mid-walk on a busy app. cmdAsync was util.promisify(child_process.exec),
which rejects on a non-zero exit and discards stdout, so the figure du had already
computed was thrown away - and failing the whole call on that would have replaced
an occasional under-count with a once-a-minute total loss of the disk reading, on
exactly the apps that write the most.

So: take du's number whenever there is one, and treat only a run that produced no
usable total as an unmeasured mount. Those are recorded, the reading goes out as
`status: 'partial'` naming them, and it is NOT cached - a short answer gets
recomputed next tick rather than standing for a minute. A complete reading is
unchanged: 'success', and cached.

walkedUsage moves to serviceHelper.runCommand, which passes argv with no shell
and is what preserves stdout on a failed exit. Two things at once: the mount
source is a path from docker, and `sudo du -sb ${source}` made any metacharacter
in it part of the command - the rule this codebase already adopted in 209424554.
node-cmd leaves the file with it.

docs(api): where an answer goes, and why a 410 in the body is not a wire status

The PR body read as though the retired routes answered HTTP 410. They answer HTTP
200 carrying `{ status: 'error', data: { code: 410, name: 'Deprecated' } }`, so a
caller checking response.ok sees success. The table put that beside
/apps/appmonitorstream's 404 as if the two were the same kind of thing, and they
are not: the stream route is deleted, so its 404 is a real transport-level answer
with no handler behind it.

The code is right, and this says why rather than changing it. FluxOS answers a
request that REACHED a handler in the body at 200, and reserves wire statuses for
refusals that happen BEFORE one runs - the middlewares, a payload too large, a
resource that does not exist to be addressed. Roughly 315 handlers answer in band
against 27 that set a status, and the 27 are all of the second kind;
operationsController writes `res.status(200).json(createErrorMessage(...))`
explicitly rather than let the two blur. dataOrThrow already documents the reason:
the in-band shape exists so a transport failure cannot impersonate a service
answer, and an error carried at a non-200 status puts them back on one channel.

These four handlers run, verify ownership, and report that an operation is no
longer supported. That is an answer, not a transport refusal.

None of which was written down anywhere, which is how counting the call sites
without reading what they were produced the wrong conclusion on the first pass -
that new code was drifting toward wire statuses. It is not drifting; it applies
the rule. So the rule is now stated in messageHelper, where both shapes are
defined, rather than only in a PR body that stops existing at merge.

feat(telemetry): facts as events, cadence as a counter

The g: election was the one major loop in FluxOS a test could not observe. 93
publish sites exist across ZelBack and advancedWorkflows had none, so the only
way for a suite to wait for it was to guess at the clock - which is how suite
52 came to sleep 45 seconds derived from the PRODUCTION cadence while the
harness runs the loop ten times faster.

The rule this establishes, written at the top of fluxEventBus.js:

  An event marks something that HAPPENED. Every publisher in this codebase is
  of that kind, and because things happening are rare, a 1024-entry ring is
  generous. A heartbeat - "the loop ran again and did nothing" - is not a fact
  about the system, it is a fact about the clock, and putting one in the ring
  spends a SHARED budget every other consumer draws from. The chatty publisher
  does not pay that cost; whichever other event a test needed pays it.

  So "the loop ran N times, and took branch X each time" is a TALLY. Count it
  and let the reader ask for the number, rather than broadcasting twenty
  messages a minute so it can count them.

Accordingly:

- ONE event, masterSlave:started, at the single funnel every start branch goes
  through. A node committing to become primary is a fact.
- Counters for the rest: cycles, and per-component operatorStopped, heldOnPeer,
  primaryObserved, started. The operatorStopped counter deliberately sits
  OUTSIDE the once-guard its log line uses - the log reports the state change,
  the counter reports every pass that honoured it, which is what a test
  asserting "the election kept skipping it" needs.
- Read over /flux/testcounters, which 404s in production exactly like
  /flux/eventstream. Both are dead when testEventStream is false, which is the
  production default, so publish() and count() return on their first line.

The bus also stops failing silently. Its ring holds 1024 entries and since()
returned whatever survived with no indication anything was missing, so a
consumer resuming into a wrapped ring could not tell "nothing happened since
you last looked" from "plenty happened and I threw it away" - and a later wait
for one of the lost events ran out its whole budget and reported as a product
bug. oldestRetainedId() exposes the gap, sseHandler announces it as a
stream:gap sentinel, and node-client fails every parked wait AT the drop,
naming it. That is verbatim the treatment waitForEvent already gives a dead
container; a dropped event is the other way a wait becomes unanswerable and it
was the one not checked.

Nine unit tests, all mutation-checked: counters that do not increment, counters
served as raw Maps, paths flattened to one key, oldestRetainedId pinned to 0,
the gap never announced, and the gap announced unconditionally all go red.

fix(apps): an unauthenticated request can no longer hang the socket

deprecatedPauseResponse lost the try its base handler had, and ran
appname.split('_') on req.query.appname before any authentication. Express's
default extended query parser turns ?appname=a&appname=b into an ARRAY and
?appname[x]=1 into an object, neither of which has .split. The rejection was
dropped and res was never written - the socket stayed open with nothing left to
answer it, since fluxServer sets a two-hour requestTimeout and node stops
applying it once the request has been received. Reachable by anyone, on
/apps/apppause and /apps/appunpause, repeatedly.

It was the only site of its kind: a check over every .split('_') in the three
service files found exactly one without an enclosing try. Review round 1 raised
this shape and closed it as "not reachable, verifyPrivilege has its own catch",
which checked the line below rather than the line above.

The order is now validate, authenticate, act. The split cannot come after the
privilege check, because the app name is what the privilege is scoped to - so
a non-string name is refused BY NAME before anything touches it, and the try is
back as a backstop. Rejecting explicitly rather than leaning on the catch
matters: without it the split still throws and the catch still answers, but
with a raw "appname.split is not a function", telling the caller their request
failed for a reason internal to us rather than for the name they sent.

Also in this pass:

- The CPU throttler's watermark write had no null check while its own sibling
  burst-skip write, twenty lines above, did. The window is snapshotted before
  two awaits and stopAppMonitoring can land in the gap - an uninstall, a
  reconciler recreate, the sampler noticing the container has gone - so the
  write lands on undefined, throws to the function-level catch, and abandons
  the pass. Every app ordered after it goes un-inspected and unthrottled for
  fifteen minutes. There are four such writes, not two: the v3 path and the
  compose path each have a guarded one and an unguarded one.

- setInterval does not default a missing delay. It coerces to NaN and treats
  anything below 1 as ONE MILLISECOND, so a config without statsSampleIntervalMs
  runs the sampler about a thousand times a second, asking docker for stats on
  every monitored component. This key has gone missing before - the test
  config's own comment names the incident - and the ?? this PR added went to
  masterSlaveStaggerMs, the key that was never at risk.

- /apps/startmonitoring and /apps/stopmonitoring were not behind alwaysRespond.
  Their bodies are byte-identical every call, so express ETags them and a
  revalidating caller gets an empty 304 from the second call on - unable to read
  the deprecation notice that is now the only thing those routes exist to serve.
  Precisely what alwaysRespond was added to prevent.

- Both orchestrator catch handlers labelled their log by reading a property off
  the value that had just failed. A throw raised inside a catch is not caught by
  that catch: a null entry threw on app.version, the catch threw again on
  app.name, and the loop was abandoned with every remaining app unmonitored and
  nothing logged at all. Labels are now built by a helper that cannot throw.

- resolveAppSpecs accepted any truthy value, so a string would have been walked
  character by character - the hole its own comment documents one level down for
  the compose list. Nothing reaches it today (serviceManager is the only caller
  and always passes null); this is the guard arriving before the caller.

watermark guard removed, the ?? removed, alwaysRespond removed, the outer catch
re-reading app.name, and the Array.isArray removed all go red.

test(election): pin the rollout window a released peer cannot report through

/apps/heldcomponents landed on development; master does not have it and is 356
commits behind. A released node CAN hold the durable operator-stop lock and
DOES honour it - it simply has no route with which to say so, and answers 404.

A 404 is a peer answering the old way, so the probe falls through to the
container list. An owner-stopped master has no container, so it is not in that
list, and the asking node reads the component as free and starts it: a second
writer on the shared volume while its owner edits files on the first.

There is nothing better to ask. A peer cannot answer a question its code does
not contain, and reading the 404 as "holds nothing" would be the same start
reached from the other direction. The hole closes only when the last node
upgrades, and the harness cannot reproduce it - createTestEnv's legacyNodes
toggles ArcaneOS vs legacy, the platform, not the FluxOS version.

So this asserts what HAPPENS rather than what we want, deliberately, so the
next person to touch that fall-through has to decide about it instead of
discovering it. The existing test covers the 404 path only for a peer that IS
running the component, where the container list happens to give the right
answer; anyone reading the suite would conclude the path was covered.

Mutation-checked: making a 404 rule the peer out instead of falling through
goes red and names the exposure.

fix(reconciler): a paused container is a state to normalise, not a healthy one

Docker reports a PAUSED container as Running: true - the processes are frozen
but the record says they are up. dockerActual read that flag and reported the
container healthy, so the reconciler took no action, the sampler skipped it
(State !== 'running') and its charts flatlined with no explanation, and FDM went
on routing traffic to something that would never answer. Nothing in ZelBack
reads State.Paused at all, so the state was invisible to the whole system.

It also put this function at odds with appStartupManager. That enumerates boot
candidates from the LISTING's State, where paused is not 'running', so every
boot it collected the container, decided it needed starting, and enqueued it -
and the reconciler inspected a different field, concluded it was already
running, and did nothing. Boot handed it over; this declined. Every boot,
forever. The two now agree.

Paused is not startable: docker refuses with "cannot start a paused container,
try unpause instead", and appDockerUnpause was retired with the rest of pause,
so no primitive remains that releases one directly. Rather than teach the
reconciler a paused-specific recovery, it now NORMALISES: docker stop works on
a paused container and leaves it exited, which is a state every existing branch
already understands. The following pass starts it on the normal path - backoff
pacing, mount-path recreation, the controller re-read, and the CFS burst
reapplication appDockerStart owns. appDockerRestart would clear the pause in one
call but skips that burst step, which is why the stop is the right lever.

Placed ahead of the DATA WIPE, not merely ahead of the run decision. A paused
container is live - frozen processes, but the volume is still mounted and held -
and the wipe path stops a running container first because "an rm -rf under a
live container corrupts it". With running false for paused and the normalisation
below it, the wipe would have skipped that stop and deleted data out from under
a container still holding it. Mutation testing surfaced that; there is now a
test for it.

Handled before the desired-state branch too, so it is correct in both
directions: a paused container that should run gets started, and one the
operator has stopped ends up genuinely stopped rather than left frozen because
"stop" found nothing to do.

Nothing can create a paused container from here on. This is for the ones that
already are, and for those a node that has not upgraded yet can still make
during the rollout. A daemon or host restart clears them (they return exited,
verified in an isolated dockerd), but a FluxOS restart does not - and that is
the one an upgrade performs.

Five tests. Mutation-checked: dropping the paused fact, disabling the
normalisation, and starting instead of stopping all go red. The re-enqueue line
is covered by consequence rather than directly - MANAGED_RETRY_MS is 5s, longer
than a unit test waits - via a two-pass test that the container converges.

fix(restore): acquire before destroying, and never redeploy the peers

A restore deleted appdata before it had anything to put back, and then told
every other instance to hard redeploy - which removes their app directory and
their backing volume. The intent was "make the peers match me, they will resync
over syncthing"; the implementation destroyed the peers' only copies first, so
an instance holding nothing turned every copy in the network into nothing. That
is what an archive of one config file, taken from an instance that had never
synced, did to a customer's 35 GB world.

Nothing is destroyed now until a complete replacement is known to exist. The
archive is fetched and then read end to end - one decompression pass that writes
nothing - which establishes that it is whole and readable while the data it
would replace is still there, and yields the size the free-space check needs.
Only then does appdata make way for it. There is no judgement about how much
smaller the archive is than what is on disk: rolling back to an early checkpoint
is what a restore is for, and refusing it would block the ordinary case to guard
against a wrong one.

The peers are no longer told to redeploy, hard or soft. They hold the only other
copies, and resuming the paused folder is what carries the restored data to
them. Where an r:/s: component is concerned every instance is running and
writing, so those peers are restarted - which recreates no volume and clears any
operator stop; a g: component's other instances are already stopped and adopt
the restored data when the role next moves, and an unsynced component's data
never left this node. That distinction now comes from the primary mount's flags,
the same predicate syncthing is configured from, rather than a substring search
that reported sync on apps that have none.

Syncthing folders are paused for the duration instead of deleted, per component,
so the freeze finally happens for composed apps - stopSyncthingApp was addressing
them by app name, which matches no folder. An unpack that fails leaves a
directory that is neither copy, so that component's folder is demoted to
receiveonly and its container held: the peers heal it, and the elected role moves
away on its own because a demoted folder is not electable. Its cache entry has to
record NOT settled or the folder state machine skips the healing path and starts
the container on exactly that partial data.

type and the component names are validated. Both came from the request body
straight into a path that tar interpolates into a shell as root, so an app owner
could run arbitrary commands on every node hosting their app.

The downloaded archive is removed once the app is back up, not the moment the
unpack returns - it is the only thing a later failure can be retried from. An
uploaded or local archive is never removed at all: that is the owner's copy, and
restoring from it must not consume it.

Also: restore of a version <= 3 app reached .compose and threw, so it has never
worked; getVolumeInfo answers null rather than false, which makes the existing
`=== null` guard in backupRestoreService live for the first time; and tar and
gzip failures no longer throw a second error out of the catch that was meant to
report them.

destroyed, not that anything arrived.

its own runtime installer, which shells out to helpers/installSyncthing.sh - a

fetch a binary from the internet, and the version under test has to be one we
chose. That FluxOS's installer then finds syncthing already on PATH and does

labour, not a workaround. Nothing here writes syncthing's config: it generates

apiport+2 through the API exactly as it does on a node. The endpoint switch
lives in NODE_CONFIG, which the config package merges over the mounted

covers the tarball. The key is vendored rather than fetched so it is pinned in

signed this file - and is indifferent to other signatures riding along.

their own folder configs - a folder had to be neither kept nor re-added
underneath them. Neither flow deletes a folder any more: both pause it and
resume it, and for a restore the resume IS how the new data reaches the peers.

to respond may be live and unheld - and appdata sits INSIDE the replicated
scope, because the folder path is the mount root. Clearing it under a live
sendreceive folder turns the clear into deletions this node broadcasts to every
healthy peer. That is the quiet half of the 2026-08-04 loss, needing no redeploy
at all, and a g: restore runs on the elected primary precisely because that is
where the folder IS sendreceive.

fix(syncthing): stop restarting the daemon on a latch we can never have set

Validated against the syncthing source at v2.0.15, the version the fleet runs,
and re-checked at v2.1.3-rc.2 - lib/config/wrapper.go and lib/api/confighandler.go
are byte-identical between them.

`requiresRestart` is a one-way latch. There is exactly one write to it
(wrapper.go:342-345, Store(true)) and no reset anywhere, so once true it stays
true for the life of the process. It is set only when a config subscriber's
CommitConfiguration returns false, and across all ten subscribers in the codebase
there is exactly one such return: model.go:3122-3128, for Options fields tagged
`restart:"true"`. There are two of those fields, auditEnabled and auditFile.

FluxOS never sets either. It PATCHes options - the four discovery and listen
settings - and PATCH does not touch them; and every folder operation it performs
routes to model.restartFolder, an in-process folder stop/start that leaves the
latch alone. No folder field is process-restart-only; the only one exempt even
from the folder restart is `label`.

So the endpoint was never answering "did the change I just made need a restart".
It answers "has anything, since this process started, ever needed one" - and
FluxOS could only ever read a `true` that something else set, hours earlier.

On a normal node the check therefore returns false and nothing happens, which is
why this has gone unnoticed. What it is, is loaded: the moment anything sets the
latch - an admin PUT, or the syncthing GUI - it never clears, and the monitor
restarts the daemon on every pass. The stopSyncthingApp loop never resets
folderId, so from the first match onward it restarts once per folder. Syncthing's
own supervisor gives up after four restarts inside sixty seconds
(cmd/syncthing/monitor.go:105-111, "Too many restarts; not retrying further") and
exits, leaving the daemon down until something else starts it.

Both call sites go. Nothing replaces them and nothing logs: the condition is one
we have just established we cannot cause and will not act on, and the latch never
clears, so a log line would repeat every pass forever. What is lost is the
ability to apply an auditEnabled/auditFile change without a manual restart, which
FluxOS does not make. Syncthing's own web GUI never reads this endpoint either.

Also adds suite 93, the backup sync gate end to end. That gate is what would have
stopped the 373-byte archive existing at all, and it had unit tests and no
harness coverage - suite 44 drives a backup but tests the lease. 93 covers the
incident's own shape (an instance that has never synced), a partial copy, the
forced override, and that a refusal stops nothing: the gate runs before the app
is touched, so refusing must not cost a healthy app an outage.

fix(backup/restore): tell a daemon that cannot answer from a container that will not stop

Found by suite 44 on the first full gate to see the container-stop guard.

The guard proves a container is down before archiving or replacing its data. It
proved it by inspecting the container and treating any unrecognised failure as
"still running". A dockerd restart makes every docker call fail, so a backup
running across one was refused - and refusing releases the lease it was holding,
which hands the app straight back to the reconciler in the middle of the
operation. That is the actuation suite 44 exists to catch, and it caught it.

The two cases are not the same. "I asked, and the container is up" is a reason to
refuse: something is wrong and an archive taken now would be torn. "Docker did
not answer" establishes nothing at all - and it clears on its own in seconds.

appReconciler already had this exactly right and said so in a comment: an inspect
failure is ambiguous, the errors are version-dependent, so rather than
pattern-match them it probes the daemon with a list call and uses the ANSWER.
That is what dockerActual does, and it separates the daemon being unreachable,
the daemon being up but that one inspect failing, and the container being gone.
The guard here pattern-matched for a 404 - the thing that comment warns against -
and folded the rest into "running".

dockerActual is now exported and used here, so there is one answer to "what is
this container actually doing" rather than two. Where it cannot answer, the stop
waits and asks again rather than reading the silence: the wait is not standing in
for the fact, it is how the fact becomes obtainable, and it holds the lease while
it does. Bounded, so a daemon that stays down still refuses - with a message that
says the daemon did not answer, rather than claiming a container refused to stop
when that was never established.

A test that only covered the 404 is replaced by four, one per state the daemon can
be in. dockerListContainers is now stubbed: it is a network boundary, and left
real those tests passed or failed on whether the machine running them happened to
have docker.

fix(backup): reading an archive is bounded by silence, not by how big it is

Inspecting an archive and measuring a directory both took the default fifteen
minute child-process cap. Their duration is set by how much data they were
given, so that cap can only ever kill the largest apps - the ones this path
exists for - and it does so after the app has been stopped and the archive
downloaded. The refusal then tells the operator their backup is unreadable when
it is merely large.

Both now stream. runStreamingCommand consumes output as it arrives and takes an
idleTimeout, so a command is stopped once it has produced nothing at all for
that long: a 35GB archive listing for an hour runs to completion, a read that
has stalled does not. Every line is the evidence, which is why the directory
walk drops -s - du reports each directory as it passes and only its last line
is the total, so summarising would leave nothing to observe.

Nothing is held whole any more, so the buffer ceiling that shaped the old
pipeline is gone with it, and with the aggregation done here rather than in awk
there is no shell left: root was the only reason these are child processes, and
root wants sudo, not an interpreter. A path is now an argument that cannot be
read as syntax rather than one carefully kept away from it.

operator dressed as a corrupt archive.

fix(restore): an elected container is started only where FDM confirmed the primary

The restore ended with appDockerStart(appname), and a bare app name fans out to
every component in the compose array - elected ones included. The backup path
forty lines earlier filters them out with a comment naming the hazard: starting
one here puts a second writer on the shared volume. The restore had the same
hazard and no guard, and the folders return to sendreceive a few lines before
that start, so the container came up writing into live replicated storage.

Three ways in. The stop is the same fan-out, so restoring component A stops
component B - and a g: component that was never a target of this restore was
stopped and then started here. The FDM check only refuses on a positive answer,
and getMasterIpFromFdm never returns fdmOk: false, so an unreachable FDM read as
permission. And force skips the check entirely.

The fix is not the backup's blanket filter. A g: restore is MEANT to run on the
primary - the guard's own comment says restoring anywhere else is quietly undone
by the writer - so refusing to start elected components outright would tax every
legitimate restore with an election cycle of downtime. The FDM answer is instead
kept rather than discarded after the refusal check: confirmed primary starts
everything as before, and only an unconfirmed one leaves elected components to
the election. That leaves the restore acting on what FDM actually said: a
confirmed primary is permission to start a writer, and neither of the other two
answers - no primary yet, or no answer at all - is.

Four unit tests, and both drills discriminate: the original fan-out fails the
three leave-alone cases while the confirmed-primary one still passes, and the
blanket filter fails only the confirmed-primary case. An existing test -
"removes the copy it downloaded only once the app is back up" - fails under the
blanket filter too, so the tree already disagreed with that version.

Suite 86 gains the fleet case, on the suite that already owns "refuses on an
instance that is not the one holding the live copy": a forced restore on the
standby must leave the elected container down, asserted over a window rather
than sampled once, with the standby's stopped state checked first so a stopped
container afterwards means something. The harness client learns `force`, which
is API-only by design and so has no other way to be exercised.

The crash ladder paced every stop, whatever caused it. recordRestart pushed a bare
timestamp and restartWaitMs indexed the ladder off the count, so an operator
restarting their own app walked the same rungs as a container that could not stay
up. Six deliberate restarts inside twenty-one minutes put a customer's game server
on the fifteen-minute rung; from the outside that is indistinguishable from the app
refusing to come back, and it is what the ticket was actually about.

The exit code was already on the document - recordExit persists lastExitCode right
beside lastDiedAt - and nothing read it. It is now the input to the decision, but
only in the direction it is sound. Non-zero, or OOMKilled, proves a fault. Zero
proves nothing: an image whose entrypoint is a wrapper script ending in `exit 0`
reports a clean stop for a segfault, and no init we wrap around the container can
recover a status the image already discarded, because the loss happens a level
below anything we can inject. Palworld's official image does exactly this, so its
SIGSEGVs and its operators' shutdowns arrive as the same number.

So the ladder needs a backstop that does not consult the code at all. Five automatic
restarts inside sixty seconds is itself evidence of a fault, and it disposes into
the same ladder rather than into a state a human has to clear - the tight loop that
actually costs the host is a container exiting in milliseconds, which trips this in
about a second. A container that merely restarts often is not a host problem and is
deliberately left alone.

exitCode null is a container that has never run, which is an initial start rather
than a death, and must not be read as a fault. Both new constants are config-driven

A reconcile pass reads isOperatorStopped, then acts on that answer once docker
has replied. An operator stop landing in that gap is not seen: the pass starts a
container the operator has just stopped, and the next pass reads the lock and
stops it again. The customer sees their app resurrect for a moment after they

cycles, the pass defers, and the stop lands while it is resuming:

  appReconciler - docker unreachable for <app>, deferring reconcile
  GET /apps/appstop/<app> 200

  appReconciler - <app> desired stopped, stopping

that the check and the action are not atomic against a concurrent writer, and
the writer does not go through the queue that would serialise them: appStop
writes the store directly while the reconciler actuates off its own per-key
single-flight.

applyIntent puts the write in that same slot. It waits out a pass already
deciding for the identifier, holds the key while the write lands so enqueue
coalesces rather than starting one against a half-written intent, and enqueues
on release so the next pass reads what was just written. The two are now
mutually exclusive by construction.

inFlight becomes a Map of the holder's promise rather than a Set, because a
caller has to be able to WAIT for a pass, not merely observe that one is
running.

That narrows the window and leaves the defect, and a green suite would then
report a race that is still there.

The wait is bounded by one pass of ONE component - a docker probe and at most
one action - so an operator's command never queues behind unrelated work.

Each of the three guarantees fails its own test when removed: skipping the wait,
not holding the key, and not enqueueing afterwards.

fix(reconciler): a pass that throws is retried, not left to the hourly sweep

Every failure this file anticipates ends in one of two decisions: pace a retry,
or deliberately do not because no retry can fix it. A pass that THROWS made
neither - it was logged and forgotten, and with the operator's stop now
actuated here rather than inline, /apps/appstop could answer "will be stopped"
and leave the container running for an hour.

The net goes where every unhandled failure already converges rather than at the
one throw site we know about: the sites that can throw are the ones nobody
thought to guard, so a per-site catch would miss the next one the same way.
Retrying is safe because a pass is level-based - it re-derives desired against
actual rather than resuming half-finished work - and the deliberate no-retry
decisions all return rather than throw, so the net cannot override them.

Bounded, because scheduleRetry is a flat five seconds with no escalation: an
unhandled throw may be a permanent fault, and retrying one forever is a log
loop. Three attempts, then the sweep owns it; the count clears on the first
pass that completes and on forgetDesiredState, so a reinstall under the same
name does not inherit it.

Docker being unreachable is NOT this case - it is anticipated and defers, which
is why a dockerd restart cannot exercise this path (suite 45 covers that one
end to end). Three mutation drills, each killing only what it should: removing
the retry fails all three tests, unbounding it fails the bound and clear tests,
and never clearing fails the clear test alone.

fix: an apt failure resumes into the same failed task, forever

updateAptCache pushes with retainErrors: false so a failed apt-get update is
dropped rather than left at the head of the queue. queueAptGetCommand builds
workerOptions from retries alone, so that request never arrives and the queue
keeps the task it was told to bin.

The apt cache monitor then resumes on every failure. It is async - it awaits
several runCommands first - so its resume() lands after work() has already
exited and working is back to false. The queue restarts, finds the same task,
and it fails instantly, because retries: 0 means there is no delay between
attempts. Measured against the real modules: 55,812 worker attempts in two
seconds, one core flat out.

That monitor also cannot see what failed. runWorker emits the whole payload as
`options`, and for the {commandOptions, workerOptions} shape the command sits a
level down, so options.command is always undefined. Its opening shortcut - an
apt-get update failure is not worth panicking over, just resume - has therefore
never once fired. Every apt failure instead takes the recovery path: up to
thirty minutes waiting on the dpkg lock, then fuser -KILL on it, then
--fix-broken. For a node that simply could not reach a mirror.

Both are one-line faults and neither is reachable today by luck alone: apt
usually works. Making the fleet hermetic removes that luck - a legacy node with
no route to a mirror is the normal case afterwards, not the exception.

The queue is also built complete now, with its worker and its listener, instead
of being half-constructed at module load and finished off inside monitorSystem
650 lines later. addWorker refuses a second worker rather than silently keeping
the first, which is what let the tests reach in and leave each other a queue in
whatever state they finished with; the file no longer installs a worker of its
own.

Regression cover is on the two faults, not on the queue behaviour underneath
them: the forwarding test fails when workerOptions loses retainErrors, and the
event test fails when the payload is emitted in place of the command. A first
attempt asserted only that FifoQueue honours retainErrors when handed it, which
passed just as well before the fix.

were up.

The dependency closure is now resolved at image build, into a signed repository
the image carries. Nothing here names a package or a version: whatever apt puts
in the archive cache IS the closure it resolved, against this image's own
package state. Built against bare ubuntu instead it would come to 22 packages
rather than 21, naming one the image already has.

Recommends are deliberately not suppressed. aptRunner passes no
--no-install-recommends, so a node's own install pulls them - 21 packages rather
than 4, and shared-mime-info among them, which is what the capture caught in

packages the node goes on to ask for.

Pre-seeded, so a normal fleet boots into the steady state every node after its
first boot is in: monitorSystem() runs for real, finds its prerequisites
satisfied and installs nothing. aptSeeded: false purges them first, so a suite
that wants the install path gets a node that genuinely lacks them. Purge, not
remove - a removed package leaves config behind and reports as `deinstall ok
config-files`, which is neither installed nor absent.

writes that source and serving it over HTTP would cover nothing. The one source

the keyring fetch, the source write, apt's HTTP transport and the signature
check all run as they do on a node. The stub copies the repository out of the
node image rather than building its own, so what a node installs at runtime is
the file it was seeded with and not a second download that resolved differently.

Signed, and the signing is load-bearing: swapping the keyring for an impostor's
makes apt refuse both distributions and the packages become unlocatable.

Syncthing arrives as a Debian package now, which is what production runs, so
getPackageVersion finds it - against the release tarball that query came back
empty and the version check had nothing to compare. Its version is whatever the
repository serves at build time and cannot be pinned: syncthing publishes only
its two most recent releases, so the tarball's v2.0.15 is not available as a
package at all. The build records the version and the stub reads it, because a
restated one goes stale silently the next time the image is built. The package
is also built [noupgrade] where the tarball is not, so the upgrades.syncthing.net
traffic in the capture goes with it. The relay traffic is a separate mechanism
and stays.

the layer that needed them, so any later apt-get update refreshes them - egress
that appears in no product source file.

monitorSystem publishes system:packages-checked, on the same principle as
fileops:recovered: published whether or not anything was installed, because a
seeded node has its packages either way and presence cannot tell a check that
ran and found its work done from one that never started. Suite 94 asserts on

fix: one package apt cannot find stops a node installing any of the others

A retained task goes back to the FRONT of the queue, so the next resume hands it
straight to the worker again, ahead of everything already waiting. If it can
never succeed, nothing behind it ever runs. Seen on a node whose package index
was empty: netcat-openbsd failed with `Unable to locate package` every sixty
seconds from 07:22:55 onwards, and chrony and syncthing - queued behind it -
were never attempted at all.

It also has no ceiling. Each resume grants a fresh ladder of retries, so the
pair of retain-and-resume is unbounded: the ladder ends after six attempts, the
apt cache monitor resumes the queue, and it begins again, once a minute for the
life of the process.

Retained tasks now go to the back, and a task is handed back only so many times
before the queue gives up on it and says so. Abandoning is announced rather than
silent: the caller took its error when the ladder first ended, so nothing else
would ever learn the work had stopped being attempted.

This is the slow sibling of the spin fixed in the previous commit. That one
needed retries: 0 to run hot; this one runs at the retry delay, which is why it
reads as a node that is merely busy rather than one that is stuck.

The ordering was documented - a test asserted the failed task sits at the head
and a comment said so. That expectation is the defect, and it is updated rather
than worked around.

Both new tests fail cleanly when the behaviour is put back, and the failure
names the fault: `expected [ 'bad', 'bad', 'bad', 'bad', ...(34) ] to include
'good'`. They yield through a macrotask the way the real listener does, because
awaiting a microtask starves the event loop and makes the same regression hang
instead of fail.

fix(queue): the queue settles its own state before it tells anyone

A failed apt-get update killed the apt queue for the life of the process.

runWorker halted AFTER emitting 'failed'. An emit is a synchronous yield: the
listener runs right there, and monitorAptCache resumes for a failed update with
no await ahead of it, so its resume landed inside the emit and the next line
overwrote it. The loop broke out with work still queued, working went false, and
nothing restarted it - push() only calls work() when the queue is not already
working. Every apt task behind the update was stranded, every one pushed later
too, and monitorSystem's allSettled never settled, so system:packages-checked
was never published and chrony, syncthing and netcat never installed.

Latent until this branch: the emit carried the raw payload, so options.command
was undefined and that shortcut could never fire. Fixing the payload switched the
trapdoor on, which makes this ours.

The fix is not to make listeners behave. It is to stop depending on when they
run: halt first, then notify, and a listener may reply instantly, slowly or not
at all. Two consequences follow. A resumed final failure now reaches the retry
sleep with no retries left, so the ladder-over break stops it waiting out the
full delay - 60s by default - holding everything behind it. And resume() no
longer reassigns `finished` when called re-entrantly: work() returns at once
while the loop is running, and storing that resolved promise told clear() the
queue was idle mid-flight, on the apt-is-broken path systemService reaches from
these very failures.

Four unit regressions, each killed by its own mutation alone: halting after the
emit again fails the draining pair, removing the ladder-over break fails only the
retry-delay test, and removing the re-entrancy guard fails only the clear() test.
The first pass of the retry-delay and clear() tests proved nothing - both passed
under their mutations - and were rewritten until they bit.

Harness: an apt command completing becomes a published fact. A legacy boot runs a
handful of them, so this is an event rather than a cadence, and WHICH completed -
in what order - is the only direct evidence the queue carried on past one that
failed. Suite 94 gains the third regime a real node boots into, packages missing
AND apt-get update failing: createTestEnv({ aptBadSource: true }) adds a source
apt cannot reach alongside the good one, so update fails as it does behind a dead
mirror while the work behind it stays doable - swapping the good source out would
fail that too and prove only that a broken node stays broken. The suite then
asserts two facts off the bus in order, the failure and the command after it,
rather than waiting to conclude that packages never appeared.

comes back because the peer is on older code: nothing was learned, so ask

path is what lets this ship in one go rather than behind an activation height:
the first nodes to take it would otherwise refuse every install until the rest
of the network caught up, and it stops happening on its own as it does.

The peer's reading is capped at 256 bytes. It relays what it read from a
stranger's port, and an uncapped relay is a node that can be asked to shuttle
a payload.

fix(ports): the review's findings, and the two the fixes uncovered

Cabecinha84's review of #1795, worked through. It was written against the
mechanism this branch replaced nine minutes later, so one of its three main
points no longer applies; the rest did, and two more surfaced while fixing them.

A NODE AT OUR OWN ADDRESS IS NOT AN OUTSIDE OBSERVER

The peer draw excluded only this exact node, not a Flux node behind the same
router. On the topology this release is about, asking one gives an answer that
depends on the router sending traffic straight back in, which most do not - so
it reports a closed port and a good install is refused.

The picker now answers two questions rather than one with a flag, because they
are two questions: getRandomSocketAddress is "another node", unchanged for its
callers; getRandomExternalObserver is "a node that can see me from outside".
Both run on one walk that takes a rule and returns nothing when none matches.

FOUR callers ask the second question, not the three the review names.
checkMyFluxAvailability is the fourth and the worst: a neighbour's honest "I
cannot reach you" was two points of dosState and a step towards the address
change handler. The hand-written same-IP redraw at the UPnP caller is deleted,
being what the picker now guarantees.

That also fixes a crash nobody had hit: landing on itself, the old draw took
"the one before, or else the next" without checking either existed, so a
single-node fleet threw. The shared walk returns null instead, which every
caller already handles.

ONE PEER'S WORD NO LONGER ENDS AN INSTALL

Our own token coming back is proof - a secret cannot be manufactured - so one
peer settles an acceptance. Anything else is one observer's report about a third
party, and a report can be wrong. Refusing on the first of those left a node
that quietly installed nothing until somebody went looking.

Two distinct peers must now agree before refusing, spending a retry budget that
already existed and was only ever used on peers too old to answer. Keyed on the
peer, because the draw can return the same one twice and one peer asked twice is
one witness. Uncorroborated, it proceeds on reachability alone - the path an
older peer already produces. A real collision corroborates itself for free.

THE SIBLING ASK IS SIGNED

It answered anyone. What it discloses is small, but answering means reading and
decrypting this node's own specifications, and an anonymous caller could ask as
often as it liked. It is now a signed POST verified against the deterministic
list - the check /flux/checkappavailability already makes, on the endpoint this
feature's own port test already posts to.

That check is extracted rather than copied. Two copies of a signature check is
the one duplication that must not drift.

The route cache goes with it: apicache stores what the handler produced, so a
transient failure answered 200-with-an-error-body was pinned for the window,
which routes.js says at the top must never happen. The thirty seconds moved to
the VALUE, as portsInUseCache beside every other TTL cache in cacheManager. A
throw produces no value, so an error can no longer be remembered.

Signing surfaced a fail-open of its own: signMessage catches its own failures
and answers with nothing, so a node whose key was briefly unavailable would have
sent an unsigned ask, had every sibling refuse it, and read that back as "no
sibling holds the port". It now says so and asks nobody.

missing field and produced [NaN] for a version 1 spec with no port. getAppPorts
keeps its name and its home beside specificationFormatter, and takes the
defensive body. specifiedPorts is deleted.

siblingHoldingPort takes the ports rather than the spec, so portManager no
longer parses specifications at all and the spawner stops deriving the same
fact twice, seventy lines apart. Its neighbour already worked that way.

DEAD BOOKKEEPING

portsNotWorking, originalPortFailed and nextTestingPort are written and never
read, one of them carrying an eslint-disable that told the linter to stop
pointing at it. The pre-existing branch does it and the branch this PR added
copied it, comment included. Both gone - and with them the parse that fed them,
whose one useful product, the port the peer could not reach, now reaches the log
instead of being discarded.

TESTS

Every behaviour above is asserted, and each was proven red first by reversing
the rule it tests: the corroboration count, the unsigned guard, the hardened
extraction, the single-node draw, and the spawner standing down rather than
faulting the app - which no unit test covered at all, so a refactor turning it
into a throw would have passed the whole tree.

Suite 98 gains the case the rule exists for: exactly one drawable peer, which
dissents on every attempt, and the install proceeds anyway. Deterministic on
purpose - with three peers and one dissenting, the draw decides, and a test that

Sixteen stubs pointed at method names the code no longer calls. Three failed;

fix(sync): asked-ness belongs to the peer, so it goes when the peer does

A node that lost one sync request never asked again, stayed SYNCING and never
reached READY. Permanently, from a five millisecond window.

The orchestrator recorded a peer as asked and then sent. A send into a socket
that is closing does not throw - it is accepted and discarded - so the catch
around it never fired and nothing noticed. The peer stayed in #askedPeers, every
later pass filtered it out, and the node logged "No new eligible sync peers to
ask" and asked nobody. Cleared only by #resetSyncState, which runs on degraded,
so in ordinary operation never.

Found on a real fleet by the residential-dos session: one direction of a 3-node
fleet answered in 74ms while the other timed out at 30s with zero completions,
and node 0's outbound socket closed with code 4019 five milliseconds after the
four requests went into it. That same log line appears 15 times in another
suite's node, which had been read as noise.

The fix is a deletion. FluxPeerManager already tracks this - markSyncRequested,
isSyncRequested, completeSyncRequest - and remove() already drops a peer's mark
when the peer goes. The orchestrator was keeping a SECOND set of the same fact,
and only the peer manager's copy followed reality. It now reads the owner's copy
instead of keeping one, so a peer whose connection went away becomes askable
again by construction rather than by a listener kept in step.

No new event, no un-ask handler, nothing to keep in sync: the duplicate was the
bug, so removing the duplicate is the fix.

The test harness now models that ownership the way production has it, which is
what makes the regression expressible: a peer asked, then removed, must be asked
again. Restoring the private set fails that test and the same-cycle one.

single lost request is fatal there and merely wasteful in the field.

fix(ci): a tag carrying the release version is not proof of a re-run

The idempotency check matched the tag by name alone, so a tag holding the
release version but pointing at another commit -- one cut by hand, or one master
was later rolled back behind -- was read as "this workflow already ran". Every
remaining step was skipped, including the merged-tree verification that is the

with no tag cut and nothing verified.

reliably. ls-remote answers empty when nothing matches, so pipefail is what
separates "no such tag" from a transport failure.

rather than retyped, across both tag forms and a dead remote; it also asserts the
rest of the job still reads the output this step writes, since an output that is

feat(dos): a residential node holds, then evacuates, and only then goes to DOS

DOS >= 100 is not a mark. nodeStatusMonitor calls removeAllAppsLocally on it,
and appStartupManager does the same on every boot, so putting a node there
`rm -rf`s every app directory and volume on the box. Doing that to a
residential node deletes its customers' data outright: on the fleet as this
was written it would have taken 329 node slots and left 84 apps with no copy
anywhere, 11 of them stateful.

The enforcement is staged so that the destructive step is only ever reached on
an empty node.

  HOLD      the node stops accepting NEW apps. Immediate, deletes nothing.
  EVACUATE  it gives up one app at a time, and only ones another host
            demonstrably holds.
  DOS       once it runs nothing, and removeAllAppsLocally finds nothing.

The hold is a separate flag from DOS because DOS conflates two things: it
stops the spawner AND deletes what the node already runs. A node that must
stop growing but keep its customer volumes needs only the first, so
placementHold has exactly one consumer, appSpawner.

Evacuation terminates because the departure creates the deficit that drives
it. Only 2 apps in the whole fleet carry any surplus - the trim path removes
above N and the spawner fills below N, so the network sits at exactly-N and a
drain conditioned on staying above the requirement never starts. So the node
leaves first: the app is one short, the spawner is already asking every 120s
who is short, a node that is not held volunteers, and the count returning to N
is what releases the next holder. Serialisation is free, because a node acts
only while it sees the app at full strength - the first departure makes every
other evacuating holder wait. No wire change, no coordination.

Position in the shared instance order sets a wait of 30 min + position * 15
min, and never a veto. "Only the most junior may leave" deadlocks: the
replacement is itself the most junior, holds the only permission, and does not
want to leave.

The settling window is persisted in wall-clock, in the nodeStartupTracker
collection the node already keeps. A counter of consecutive agreeing ticks
held in memory is reset by restarting FluxOS, which would make restarting on a
cron a way to postpone the drain indefinitely - and one an operator could fall
into without meaning to. It is keyed on the verdict rather than the address,
because residential lines get dynamic addresses and keying on the IP would
just move the evasion to power-cycling the router.

Two interlocks guard the empty-node path, which is the one that sets DOS:

- Readiness is the orchestrator's own SPAWNER_READY signal, the same one
  appSpawner waits on, so the DOS decision and the install decision agree
  about whether this node knows what it is running.
- "Could not read the app list" arrives as null, never as an empty list. A
  node that sets DOS-100 while wrongly believing it is empty has
  nodeStatusMonitor delete everything it holds - the exact catastrophe this
  staging exists to prevent, re-entered through a startup race.

The timings are config-tunable and default to the production values.
config.residentialDos.enabled is removed: with enforcement that no longer
deletes, an off switch protects nothing, and a config default is a poor safety
on a loaded mechanism.

fix(geolocation): no location table means no verdict, and the verdict is not stored

The classification was decided once, at boot, and kept for three days. Both
halves of that were wrong, and together they had a node enforcing against
itself on a verdict the published table would have overruled.

WHAT WENT WRONG

publishedClassification() returned the same null for three different things:
no table has been ingested, the table holds no covering row, and the table
deliberately carries no verdict for this organisation. Only the last two mean
"decide for yourself". The first means "I have not asked yet" - and collapsing
it into the others is precisely the mistake this classifier exists to avoid,
one level up: absence of evidence read as evidence.

It is not a rare state either. A node boots, fetches a 4.6 MB artifact and
ingests two million rows, while a single ip-api call answers in milliseconds.
serviceManager starts both unawaited, fifteen lines apart. The table is
reliably absent at the moment a booting node decides - which is every node on
the first rollout, every restart that beats the sync, and every fresh install.

Then the verdict was frozen and nothing recomputed it. ipLocationSync refreshes
the view of PEERS when a baseline lands; the node's own classification is not
among them, and setNodeGeolocation is the only writer. So the wrong answer
stood for three days, while the settling window is one - long enough to hand
customer apps back on it.

WHAT IT DOES NOW

publishedClassification answers `{consulted, classification}`. Not consulted -
no table ingested, or the store unreadable - yields NO verdict at all, and
nothing enforces on nothing. Consulted-but-silent is the abstention that
legitimately hands the decision to the node's own evidence, which is the 210
fleet hosts whose organisation the table does not carry.

And the verdict is no longer stored. setNodeGeolocation gathers the EVIDENCE -
ip-api, reverse DNS, bench figures, all of it expensive and external, all of it
right to refresh every three days - and stops there.
getNetworkClassification() reaches the verdict when asked, from that evidence
and whatever table the node holds at that moment.

That is what every other consumer of this table already does:
placementFeasibility, hwRequirements and appSpawner each call lookup() at the
point of decision. geolocationService was the only one taking a copy and
keeping it, and that anomaly was the bug. Removing it means there is no stored
answer left to go stale, so the table landing needs no notification and no
retry - the next ask simply gets it right.

isDataCenter() is unchanged and still synchronous: it remains what this node
observed about itself, which is what its two callers have always meant by it.

fix(dos): a deferred tampering DOS claims the slot when it comes free

There is one sticky DOS slot and two enforcers that want it. Whichever gets
there first holds it; the other declines to overwrite, because taking it would
leave the holder unable to recognise or release its own state.

That is right, but the tampering enforcer then waited out its full 12-hour
cadence before looking again - and the residential enforcer RELEASES. A node on
the tampering blocklist that is also residential and empty is DOSed by the
residential enforcer at boot, which reaches applyDos first: serviceManager
starts it before nodeConfirmationService, and tampering awaits daemon sync. When
that node's address later moves into a hosting range, the residential verdict
flips and it clears its own sticky - and the node sits at DOS 0 accepting apps

The wanted DOS is remembered on deferral and the slot watched, so it is claimed
within a minute of coming free. The watch is local: it reads the sticky message
and nothing else, no blocklist fetch, no benchmark call, no RPC, which is why it
can run every 60 seconds against a 12-hourly enforcement cadence. Re-running
enforcement that often would be a fetch a minute.

The remembered message carries the score from when it was computed, so it can be
a few hours stale by the time the slot frees. That is the right trade: the next
full tick refreshes it, and the node is one this build has already determined
should be out of service.

The watch stops when the reason does - a blocklist entry withdrawn while another
owner holds the slot must not be claimed afterwards - and on stop().

fix(residential): the queue ticket is an uninterrupted observation, not elapsed time

The ticket is the only thing separating two evacuating holders of one
app, and it stopped being binding after the first departure. The
interval gate returned before the ticket was touched, so a node blocked
for its six hours kept maturing every ticket it held and came out of the
block instantly ready for all of them. The pass is fired from a block
height, so the fleet runs it together: two holders whose blocks expire
on the same pass both read the app at full strength - fluxappremoved is
broadcast after the volume is already gone - and both hand it back. The
same defect the step was widened to 40 minutes to close, through the
other door. For a g: app the election still separates them, because the
primary's stand-down consumes its pass; an r:-only synced app at two
instances has no such guard.

The observation now carries `since` and `lastSeenAt` on the monotonic
clock, and the accounting sits BELOW the interval gate, so a blocked
node records nothing and its own block reads afterwards as one long gap.
A gap longer than the ticket's tolerance restarts the turn. The
tolerance is MAX_TICKET_GAP_MS, derived from the queue step rather than
written down, because the step is already required to outlast the pass.

Strength is tested where the clock is stamped rather than left to the
safety gate. The wait was documented as "seen at full strength for base
+ position x step" while the clock started on the first ASK, so an app
short for its entire wait served the full wait and was only refused
afterwards.

lastEvacuationAt moves to the monotonic clock with it, and to `null` for
"no departure recorded": 0 on that clock is the start of this process,
so `now - 0` would have held the gate SHUT on a fresh node rather than
open. The marker stays wall-clock and is converted on restore - what
survives a restart is how long ago the departure was, floored so a clock
that moved backwards cannot restore an origin in the future.

The harness could not have seen any of this. Suite 55 set a 4s departure
interval against a ~30s step, so the block was shorter than the gap a
ticket tolerates and a departure would never have restarted anything.
That is a third coupled pair: the interval must outlive the ticket gap,
derived by derivedEvacuationIntervalMs and asserted on the effective
config of every fleet before boot. Bounded by what it must outlive
rather than by production's ratio, as the sigterm window is bounded by a
node boot. It costs the suite time - one departure per interval, and the
interval is now tens of seconds - which is the price of the property
being observable at all.

fix(apps): a surplus copy that is writing stays, and the next copy trims

"The newest copy stands aside" is a stand-in for "the least valuable
copy stands aside". When the newest copy is the one WRITING it is
backwards: that is the most valuable copy on the network. The election
is allowed to seat the writer anywhere in the instance order - it will
not start a node whose data has not finished syncing, so it works down
the list until it finds one that is ready, and the designated-leader
branch leaves the order outright - so the two rules can land on the same
node.

They did nothing about it. The safety gate answered STAND_DOWN_REQUIRED,
the stand-down was wired for evacuation only, and the surplus giver-up
fell through to a refusal it repeated every pass. Nothing else
volunteered, because every other node ranks the same order and concludes
it is not the newest. The app stayed over its instance count, visible as
one warning line every twelve passes. The comment beside it called that
a case that cannot arise.

The newest copy now stays when it is running the writer, and the
second-newest trims instead. It steps in ONLY on a positive confirmation
that the newest holds the writer: every node ranks the same shared
order, but "who is writing" is each node's own reading and FDM's
registration lags it by ~110s, so a second node acting on anything
weaker is how two copies leave at once. Silence, a timeout, a refusal
and "not running" all mean it does nothing - which is the behaviour that
was there before. The rule can only fail towards no trim, never towards
two.

What it does NOT do is stop the writer to make the ordering come true.
An app that is over-served is not down; an app whose writer was stopped
to tidy up a count is.

The peer probe is lifted out of masterSlaveApps rather than copied. Two
implementations of "is that peer running it" drift, and they drift
towards whatever answer each caller finds convenient - which for this
one is a removal.

The harness could not express this and now can. A stub peer could claim
an app and withdraw the claim, but not HOLD one, so the only surplus any
suite could build was a contested claim - a different moment in an app's
life, with no volume, no election and no writer. stub-peer-helper gains
runApp (announced through the ordinary signed broadcast path, so the
receiving node validates and stores it normally) and holdApp (the same
on a keep-alive: locationTtlS is 63s here, and a suite that announces
once watches its own fixture expire mid-test). Suite 96 gets its own
fleet so suite 55's eighteen tests are untouched, and builds the
divergent shape with placeGAppInOrder - holders placed one at a time so
their runningSince values are distinct and ordered, which is what lets
the test choose which copy is newest and then elect that one the writer.

Numbered 96, past every suite on every branch now in flight: 83 through

apps and is in every other respect indistinguishable from one that has
simply not been given work, and the drain that follows produces log

deletes nothing, and it is the only part of this where the operator can
still put the node right - re-attest it, or install ArcaneOS - and lose
nothing at all. By the time anything was visible, that window was gone.

dos it leads to. Always present, never omitted: a field that appears
only on affected nodes cannot be counted across the fleet, and counting
it is half the point. Every fleet figure in this PR's description came
from scraping this endpoint; without the field, rollout day is the one
window where none of them could be produced.

fix(placement): a placement hold is released by its owner, and only by its owner

The hold was one slot holding one reason, and clearing it took no argument - so
any caller released whatever was there. One caller each today, so nothing could
go wrong yet; the shape is what is wrong.

Checking ownership on a single slot does not fix it, it moves the failure. Two
owners cannot coexist in one slot at all: the second SET overwrote the first
reason outright, so an ownership check would then refuse the first owner's
release and the node would stay held forever for a condition that had lifted.
Silent unhold becomes silent deadlock.

So the slot becomes a map of owner to reason, and the node is held while any
owner holds it. Releasing removes only your own entry. An owner is an identity
from a frozen enum rather than the reason text, because the reason is a message
for an operator and identity by message is identity by typo; an owner the enum
does not carry is refused at the set, where it would otherwise create a hold no
release path could ever name.

getPlacementHold now reports every reason rather than an arbitrary one - the
spawner logs it to say why the node is not installing, and naming one of two
holds sends an operator to lift a condition that will not release the node.

The residentialNodeDosService double is owner-keyed too. Kept as a single slot
it would accept a release from any owner and so could never fail the way the
module now refuses to.

fix(peers): a node that is not accepting connections refuses the upgrade instead of the connection

The websocket handshake is answered with 503 while `acceptingConnections` is
false, so a dialling node never gets a socket. Scoped to the peer routes:
browsers reach /ws/id, /ws/sign and /ws/payment, and whether this node has
peers yet has nothing to do with signing a login phrase.

A completed handshake is already a connection. The HTTP server answers about
100ms before the application gate opens, and this node's capabilities ride in
the upgrade response headers - so the dialler completes the handshake, reads
them, constructs a peer, counts it toward its thresholds and writes to it, all
before a line of the receiver's own code has run. Closing afterwards with
NODE_UNCONFIRMED does not undo any of it: the peer object existed, the count
included it, and a boot's state-sync requests went into a socket that was
already being torn down. Acceptance was asserted by the dialler and decided by
the receiver, and they were not the same event. Refusing the upgrade makes the
invalid state unrepresentable rather than detected afterwards.

NODE_UNCONFIRMED is retryable. It says the remote is still booting, which is a
statement about when rather than about us, and it is the one refusal certain to
stop applying - on the fleet the same node dialled back 150ms later. It sat in
the same bucket as policy violations and auth failures, so a node that dialled
during someone else's boot dropped that peer for good. A build that refuses the
upgrade never produces the code, but the network is mixed and older nodes go on

fix(appsync): each outstanding sync request is a slot with its own deadline

The pool of requests is now MIN_SYNC_COMPLETIONS slots, each held by one peer.
A slot ends in one of four ways - the peer answered in full, the peer declined,
the peer's socket closed, or the peer's deadline passed - and any ending except
the first frees the slot to be refilled from the remaining candidates.

The request had no clock of its own. It was fired at three peers under one
deadline for the whole batch, so nothing was re-examined unless something
external happened to poke it, and each fix for that added another poke: a peer
joined, a peer declined. A peer that simply never replied was invisible until
the entire budget expired, and a peer that stopped half way through was
invisible for exactly as long.

Two deadlines, because being quiet means two different things. FIRST_RESPONSE
is "never spoke", and it is armed when the request is sent - not when some other
peer answers, which is a clock that never starts if none of them answer. STALL
is "spoke, then stopped", measured between arrivals, and a peer keeps its slot
for as long as it keeps delivering: abandoning a peer that is most of the way
through a large answer is the worst thing this could do, so total elapsed time
per peer is deliberately unbounded.

Both derive from syncTimeoutMs, so they follow the harness override and add no
absolute numbers. A slot must be able to fail with its replacement still
finishing inside the budget, so with S as a healthy peer's completion time both
satisfy deadline + S <= budget: at 120s that is 10 + 60 and 30 + 60. The lower
bound on FIRST_RESPONSE is the responder's work before its first batch - a
signature check, one indexed query, and serialising 2000 documents - and the
upper bound on STALL is that a stalled peer must not spend the budget. In
production STALL also lands inside the transport's own 45s liveness window, so
the sync replaces a stalled peer before the socket layer decides it is dead.

A closed socket does not wait for any of this. FluxPeerManager announces a
removal as it announces an addition, and the slot frees on the fact rather than
on a deadline that would spend the whole first-response window re-deriving what
was already known.

Every arrival is reported, not only the last: a completion arrives at the end,
so without it a peer part-way through a large answer cannot be told from one
that has said nothing.

fix(appsync): one record per outstanding sync request, and one thing that writes it

"there is a request outstanding to this peer" was written down three times - an
asked-mark on the peer manager, a slot on the orchestrator, a declined flag on
the socket - by different code, cleared by different rules. Every way they could
disagree was a defect, and a fleet booting together hit the worst of them: each
node declines the others while none is authoritative, the manager drops declined
peers from the candidate list, the flag never clears, and the node reaches zero
eligible sync peers while holding a full set of healthy connections. Two gate
suites show it - eleven nodes across suite 71 completed no state sync at all.

The record is now one object per request, holding the connection it was sent on
and how it ended. The pool counts it, the deadline hangs off it, the candidate
filter reads it, and the response path asks it whether an arriving answer is
still wanted, so the gate that admits a response and the deadline that gives up
on one cannot drift apart. A record whose connection is gone, or that ended in
anything but an answer more than one responder-throttle window ago, has stopped
describing anything and is swept - which is what makes a peer askable again once
the reason it was set aside has expired.

The request path is a reconciler over that table rather than five callers each
deciding for themselves. Every trigger says the state changed; none of them acts.
A call arriving while a pass runs marks the table dirty and returns, and the
re-run picks up whatever that pass left behind - so a peer lost during the key
fetch is replaced rather than waiting for the next unrelated event. The threshold
crossing emits two triggers from one call, so before this every boot ran the pass
twice and asked twice as many peers as the pool holds.

A round ending closes its outstanding requests instead of clearing a separate set
of marks, so a peer that was still delivering when the budget expired is recorded
as having run out of time rather than accused of stalling, and nothing arriving
afterwards is taken as an answer to a round that is over.

Asking fewer peers than the requirement is better than asking none: the road that
returned without sending anything when candidates were short is gone, and the
answers it declined to collect are the ones a later joiner completes.

Suite 100 gains a fleet at appSyncMinCompletions 3. At the harness default of 1
the pool is a single slot, so "three peers" and "three answers" cannot be told
apart and the deficit arithmetic is never exercised.

once a chunk reaches the head of the per-peer queue and its awaits have settled.

is asked for first and re-verifies every pending registration at roughly a
second each, and announced nothing at all on its way past. So a peer holding a

instantly, and went unheard for a dozen seconds - past the ten-second
first-response deadline. It was recorded as having said nothing, set aside for
the responder-throttle window, and the three answers already queued behind it
were discarded by the gate on the way out. Its replacement was sent the same
temp messages and met the same fate, so a node could walk its whole candidate
list without one of them having done anything wrong - the stall this branch
exists to remove, arriving by a different road.

stream counted including the temp one, and independent of what processing costs.

extending it.

fix(appsync): the sync budget bounds the attempt, and a peer already tried is not tried again

Two rules were in contradiction. A record of a peer set aside expired after the
responder's own throttle window, so the peer could be asked again once its
reason to decline had passed; and that window is 300 seconds while the attempt
it belonged to lasts 120. So inside the attempt - the only place the expiry was
added to help - a peer set aside never came back, and the only thing the expiry
actually produced was re-asking peers after the attempt they belonged to was
over, on whatever schedule peers happened to join.

The expiry is gone. A record lives as long as the attempt, a peer tried in it is
not tried again, and the budget running out ends the attempt rather than one
round of an open-ended series: the records are dropped, nothing further is
asked, and the block fallback carries the node to readiness as it always has -
bypassing the hash-sync and rebuild gates on the way, so it lands.

That gives "how long before this node stops asking" an answer, which it did not
have: a peer arriving an hour later would open another round with a fresh
budget of its own.

A spent budget is not permanent. Dropping below the peer threshold and
recovering is a restart of the sync, not a continuation, and clears it - which
is asserted, because a guard that stops the asking is indistinguishable from a
node that has wedged itself unless the resumption is shown too.

The sweep keeps its one remaining reason to forget a record: the connection it
was sent on is gone, so the peer at that address never saw the request.

latched, from an identity read that returns null until the node's pubkey
resolves - null selecting the 125-minute branch and latching it - so an

feat(apps): a log poll answers when docker does, and from where the reader got to

/apps/applogpolling is what a browser polls on a timer to show an app's logs,
and it had two defects that a unit test could not see because both are about
what docker does rather than what FluxOS passes it.

COST. It asked for `follow: true`, which never closes, so the only way out was
a 1500ms timer - every poll took 1500ms to answer whether one line was waiting
or none. Measured against a live container: 1526ms, 1507ms, 1507ms, each
returning a single line. `follow: false` lets docker close the connection
itself, and with it go the PassThrough, the window, the closing flag, the four
stream handlers and the finally that existed only to release a connection that
never closed on its own.

LOSS. It asked for the last N lines and the reader replaced its view with them,
so anything written between two polls beyond N was never shown to anyone. The
`since` parameter did not help: it was a box a user typed in, never advanced,
and docker applies `tail` AFTER `since` anyway - so a burst of 500 lines with
tail:100 answers a reader asking for everything since T with the last 100 and
no sign the rest existed.

A reader is now given a position and hands it back. Verified against a real
daemon: docker's `since` is inclusive and millisecond-resolved, so the line
asked from always comes back - which is the proof there is no gap, and why the
position must never advance past a line already held. A line at .9265 is lost
forever to a reader that asked from .927.

The position is therefore a pair - the millisecond reached and how many lines
were delivered from it - and the overlap is dropped by COUNT, not by comparing
text: two writes of the same string in one millisecond are indistinguishable by
content, and a reader de-duplicating by value would drop the new one. The
dropping happens here, next to the docker socket, so no client reimplements it.
Opaque on the wire because clients and nodes upgrade independently.

A cursor arrives as a QUERY parameter: the route takes three optional path
segments and a fourth would not match, so a reader sending its position to a
node that predates this would get a 404 instead of logs. A request without one
behaves exactly as before, which is what keeps every deployed client working.

fix(apps): a log position is answered from a bounded read, or the reader is moved and told
