index to seek with: it decodes forward from the oldest file, and this function
then walks every frame of it. Measured on a live node against a 5MB log, 97,510
lines: 1099ms to fetch and 349ms of blocking decode, against 104ms and 1ms for
the bounded read. The event loop is the whole node, so those 349ms answer no
peer and no other request, and the route is uncached, unrated and reachable by
an app owner for their own app on every node hosting it.

Every read now carries a `tail`. When the window comes back full there is more
waiting than one read can see, and the reader is moved to the end of the log
rather than walked to it: seeing past the window is the unbounded read again,
and a container writing faster than a page per poll would pay it forever without
arriving. A viewer that far behind wants the end anyway, which is what docker
logs, kubectl and journalctl all answer. What it must not do is stay silent, so
`skipped` says it outright - distinct from `rolledOver`, where the lines are
gone rather than declined.

`hasMore` goes with it. The window read and the page returned are the same size,
so a positioned reader is either answered completely or resynced, and there is
no state in which more is waiting to be asked for. It was added on this branch
and has never shipped.

feat(apps): an app's logs are pushed as the container writes them

A poll reconstructs the reader's place from a timestamp on every request, which
is the operation docker's log API cannot do cheaply and the one every gap and
duplicate on this branch has come out of. A stream never does it: docker is
followed once and each line is forwarded as it is written, so there is no
per-poll window for a burst to overflow.

`/applogs` carries one docker stream per container however many viewers are
watching, fanned out by a socket.io room and closed when the last one leaves. A
stream per subscriber would multiply the daemon's work and this process's
decoding by the number of people looking.

Lines are collected for 250ms and sent as one message. A line at a time is what
would make a stream cost more than the poll it replaces: a container writing
1,000 lines a second would be 1,000 messages a second per node, where a
three-second poll answered the same 3,000 in one bounded read. The queue behind
that window is bounded too, and overflow drops and reports rather than making a
loud container the node's memory problem.

The follow read carries a `tail` like every other read here: establishing it
costs 2 CPU ticks against a 1 tick idle baseline, where the same read without
one costs 15.

A follow stream is chunked wherever TCP put the boundary, not on docker's frame
edges, so the decoder holds a partial frame AND a partial line - docker splits a
message over 16KB across frames, and splitting on newline per frame would call
each piece a log line.

The polling endpoint is untouched and remains the only thing a node that
predates this can offer. The network runs several FluxOS versions at once and
always will, so a viewer falling back to it is permanent rather than a migration
step.

during it, it tears the feed down as the last subscriber and the second viewer

perf(apps): a log read releases the event loop while it decodes

The decode ran to completion in one synchronous pass - a frame walk, then
`join('')` over every body into a single string, then a split. The event loop is
the whole node, so for as long as it ran no peer was answered, no block
processed and no other request served.

Measured on a node (4 cores, ArcaneOS, an 8.47MB container log, 163,417 lines)
against a 0.3ms idle baseline:

  synchronous, clean heap    40ms blocked, peak RSS +20.4MB
  synchronous, warm heap    564ms blocked
  chunked                   0.4ms blocked, peak RSS +9.3MB

It now decodes in 64KB slices through LogFrameDecoder - the decoder the follow
stream already uses - releasing the loop between them. That class carries a
partial frame AND a partial line across a boundary, which is what makes an
arbitrary slice safe to hand it, so the answer is identical line for line.
Chunking the frame walk alone would not have been enough: `join` and `split`
were a third of the time and neither can be interrupted. Going through the
decoder splits each slice as it arrives, so the 8MB intermediate string is never
built at all - which is also why peak memory halves and wall time does not
regress.

What this does not fix: the read is still the whole log, and the full line array
is still retained to hand back. Both are the workstream at
fluxModels workstreams/telemetry/TELEMETRY_LOG_SERVING.md, which moves the read
behind an indexed range query in flux-telemetryd and out of this process
entirely.

The test counts loop turns from the moment docker hands the payload over, not
from the call. Counting the whole call passes just as happily with the decode
synchronous, because the container lookup ahead of it yields plenty on its own -
which is what the first version of this test did.

fix(apps): the announcement period stops absorbing the work it announces

A node writes its OWN location row when it announces, and that row expires

contract: announce later than the row lives and the node stops being a holder of
its own apps, on its own reading and on every peer's.

The timer was recreated in the finally, so the real period was `interval + the
cycle's duration` - the work sat inside the thing it was being timed against.
Nothing reported it and nothing measured it, so a node whose cycle took 40s
against a 30s interval announced every 70s while every config file said 30. It
is scheduled from the cycle's START now, monotonically, clamped at zero so a
cycle that outran its interval runs again immediately rather than being
scheduled into the past. The debounce the finally was written for survives: any
call still postpones the next scheduled announcement.

The interval is capped at half the row's expiry. Both configurations in use are
already inside it - production 3600000ms against a 3750000ms cap, the harness
30000ms against 31500ms - so nothing changes today. What it stops is the pairing
that deletes the property in silence, which is how this was found: the harness
compresses the interval and the expiry together by 120x and the ratio survived
that, because the term it could not compress was the cycle's own duration.

An overrun is said once on the transition and once when it clears. A node whose
cycle no longer fits its interval decays its presence on the network, and until
now nothing anywhere reported it.

The work stays inside the announcement deliberately. A node that cannot
determine what it is running announces nothing, peers expire its rows, and the
network draws the right conclusion. Separating the timer from the payload would
make the cadence exact and the content stale - a wedged read would announce a
stale snapshot punctually and forever, which is worse than being late.

announces, that row expires locationTtlS later, and peerNotifyIntervalMs

had already been set to the same ratio by hand: two announcements to a
lifetime, with a little slack.

node must be able to miss one announcement and still be refreshed before

gives 3600s and the harness's 63s gives 30s - the values both files were
carrying - so nothing changes on any node, and there is no longer a
pairing an edit can put wrong in silence.

arming the next one, so a stop taken while a cycle was running was undone
a moment later by the work it was trying to end; and the stop returned
before that cycle had finished. Whether the node announces is one flag
now, consulted by every path that ends a cycle, and the stop holds the
cycle's lock so it returns when the cycle has actually let go. An

fix(controller): a stopped loop stays stopped, and a stop waits for what it owns

An AbortSignal fires once and has to be replaced to run again, so it
cannot also carry whether a loop is wanted: abort() reissued it as soon as
the lock freed, and loop() read it after the runner had had a chance to
yield. Whether a stop held came down to which of the two resumed first,
and for a runner that took no lock it did not hold at all - measured: the
loop ran twice more after the abort, and the timer it armed kept the
process alive.

The controller now has a state of its own, taken at the first line of the
stop, and that is what decides whether an iteration schedules another. A
generation goes with it, so an iteration already in flight when the
controller was stopped cannot arm a timer beside the loop a later start
has begun. The signal goes back to being what it is - a cancellation for
the work in flight - and is reissued when the abort finishes, because it
is also handed to clients that have no loop and are rebuilt on stop.

`abort` waits on the default lock and on any lock added with blocksAbort.
A named lock usually holds a caller's own coordination - the network
state manager's `fetcher` is how its readers wait for a fetch - and a stop
that waited on every lock deadlocks against the work it is stopping.

`running` covers stopping as well as running, since a caller guarding its
start on it must not read a stop in progress as stopped and reset its own
state for a loop that startLoop then refuses to begin. `active` is the new
question: is this run still wanted. It is the condition for a runner that
loops on its own rather than returning a delay, which the signal cannot
answer - and it is false outside a run, so a function called both as the
runner and directly must still ask the signal. The syncthing events
consumer is the one loop of that shape.

A runner that throws ends the loop with a log rather than a rejection
nobody handles, which in this process is an exit.

against its connection's limit for the life of the socket while naming a

filed to another viewer's feed. It is only replaced when the same id is
subscribed again, which a redeploy never is: the container comes back with
a new one.

can see a connection's map, so the record carries the way to forget it,
guarded by identity: a later pass may have taken that container over and

both in parallel and be refused afterwards - 60 verifications against a
limit of 10, measured. That is the cost the refusal exists to avoid, taken
as many times as the subscribes were sent.

'subscribed' says one thing: you are receiving this container. It is
answered now only for a record that is a member of its feed's subscribers,

pass to answer for both. Answering it early told a client it was
subscribed to a feed that had not opened yet, and nothing corrected it if

attribute 'Not authorized.', 'Container not found.', a refusal at the

fix(applogs): a line no reader can hold is cut, and a viewer is told what it lost

A line is held until its newline arrives, which nothing obliges a container to
send. Unbounded, a process writing a large blob to stdout decided how much of
the node's memory a viewer cost - measured, 10MB of newline-free output holds

throws and the feed is finished still holding it - and then how much crossed the
socket, because a line that completes is delivered whole.

because `skipped` counts lines that never arrived and this is a line the viewer
HAS, missing its tail. Counted per line rather than per batch, and sent after
the lines rather than before them.

Docker splits a message longer than 16KB into 16KB chunks and copies the
message's stamp onto every one - measured on a live daemon, three chunks of
len=16415 all carrying the first one's. Joined as they arrived, any line over
16KB came back with docker's timestamps spliced through its body, which is a
line the container never wrote and one a reader cannot tell from one it did.
A continuation's leading token is now dropped when it is byte-identical to the
stamp its line began with, so content that merely looks like a timestamp is
left alone and a daemon that stops repeating it falls back to passing the body
through.

Two more the review found. The limit refused the tenth container to a connection
holding nine: a pass is in `pending` until its setup ends and in `following`

outlives the feed it was opened for - the events after a destroy still reach its
handlers, by which time a later viewer's feed is filed under the same id, so a
dead subscription's lines went to the live one and a dead stream's error closed

fix(sync): the readiness fallback is time spent with peers, not uptime

A node with zero peers reaches spawning readiness today. #checkReadiness has
no peer condition, and every gate that peers would satisfy - #hashSyncComplete,
#dbRebuilt, #isStateSyncReady - is waived by the block fallback. The fourth,
#canSendMessages, is on-chain confirmation and says nothing about peers. So
~250 blocks after a confirmed node with a synced explorer starts, it spawns,
having never spoken to anybody.

Nothing catches it. peersBelowThreshold fires only `if (#aboveThreshold &&
size < degraded)` (FluxPeerManager.js:287) and #aboveThreshold is latched on
the way UP, so the demotion path covers the node that fell off the network and
misses the node that never joined it.

The fix is the counter rather than a new gate: #blocksSinceSyncStarted only
advances while the peer threshold is met, and is zeroed when it is lost. The
invariant then falls out instead of being enforced - a peerless node's counter
never advances, so the timer never expires, so it never reaches READY - and
every consumer of the timer inherits the correction with no second condition
for a later change to forget.

Three parts, the first two of which are prerequisites:

- #peersReady becomes a level. It was set at start and cleared nowhere, which
  was survivable while it only meant "has the sync ever been allowed to start".
  It now mirrors FluxPeerManager's latch, so it is the HYSTERETIC pair - up at
  appSyncPeerThreshold 12, down at appSyncDegradedThreshold 4 - and not a raw
  count. A node oscillating between 5 and 11 peers must not reset, which is
  what the hysteresis is for.
- #onPeersDegraded zeroes the counter, before its state check rather than
  inside it: the method only acts from READY and SYNCING, and a node that loses
  its peers a second time while RESYNCING moves no state at all yet holds the
  same false credit. That case is the road to READY with an empty peer set that
  survives every other guard.
- the increment in #onBlocksProcessed is conditional on the level.

A node past the fallback also stops answering peers' state-sync requests until
it has earned that again. That is a second correction, not a price: the claim
the fallback buys is that every holder of a running-app location has had time
to announce itself TO THIS NODE, and a node below four peers was not hearing
them, so answering served a view it no longer had. Everything else
#onPeersDegraded does already takes that view - it drops #hashSyncComplete,
#dbRebuilt, globalState.dbReady and #stateSyncComplete. The comment at
#reconcilePass claimed the opposite and is corrected.

Eleven existing tests drove the block timer with no peer set, which is the
defect written down as a premise; they now say the peer set is up and keep
their subjects. The eligible-sync-peer list stays empty in the ones that meant
"no sync peers available", because connected peers and peers eligible to answer
a state sync are different sets.

The hysteresis band was load-bearing and untested: fluxPeerManager now pins
that 12 -> 5 -> 11 -> 5 emits neither edge and only 5 -> 3 announces the fall.

Refs: fluxModels/workstreams/peer-gated-readiness/README.md

feat(network): a node whose peer set keeps collapsing is taken out of service

The readiness fix makes a node that keeps losing its peers silently never reach
READY. That is correct and it is invisible: the operator sees a node not taking
apps and nothing says why. This is the half that says why, and it is a DOS
rather than a note because a node whose network keeps going away is not serving
the apps it already holds either.

A dip is the fall edge of the hysteretic pair - the peer count crossing below
appSyncDegradedThreshold having been above appSyncPeerThreshold. Five of them
inside a rolling two hours sets the sticky DOS at 100, which is what
isNodeDos() reads, so the spawner stops and nodeStatusMonitor takes the apps
off. Both numbers are config.

MEASURED, not assumed. A deterministic random sample of 250 fleet nodes, 228
answering, median uptime 90.7h - about 20,700 node-hours and 890 connectivity
diagnoses from /flux/networkhealth on 2026-09-12:

- peers held per node: p10 26, median 36, p90 52, max 73, and those are counts
  taken DURING a disturbance, so steady state is at least that. Against
  appSyncDegradedThreshold 4, the floor is ~11% of a median peer set.
- the lowest peer count at any of the 890 diagnoses was 7. Not one observation
  at or below 4. A dip is therefore the loss of roughly ninety per cent of the
  set - an outage, not a bad minute - and the tally counts outages.
- two candidate signals were rejected by the same data. The health monitor's
  own DEGRADED is common (698 episodes; 21 of 228 nodes hit 5+ inside 2h, one
  hit 19) and a DOS on it would fire on ~9% of the fleet. NETWORK_LOSS sounds
  like collapse and is not: it fires with 33-70 peers still connected, and one
  node produced it at 05:31 on four consecutive days.

Five rather than the three "keeps dipping in and out" would justify, because a
regional outage can take the whole set and a node must not lose its customers'
apps over one of those. Deliberately loose: the rule is inert on the healthy
fleet at any of these values, and tightening a threshold that never fires is
easier than giving an operator their volumes back.

It is NOT the 5-in-2-hours of UNSTABLE_DISCONNECT_THRESHOLD, which it matches
by coincidence. That counts disconnects of individual peers, where there are
three dozen candidates and five events is cheap. This counts the node's own
set, which is one thing.

Two things do not count. A teardown this node performed on itself:
disconnectAll() drops every peer on confirmation loss, crossing the same edge
for a different reason, and nodeStatusMonitor already removes an unconfirmed
node's apps - counting it here punishes one fault twice. FluxPeerManager now
states which it is on the fall edge, because it cannot be inferred from
acceptingConnections, false before a node has ever been confirmed. And a
restart, which cannot fire the fall edge at all because the rise latch starts
false.

The release needs positive evidence, not quiet. A node out of service loses
confirmation, drops every peer and then cannot dip because it has none, so "no
dip in the window" would let it back in having shown nothing, take on apps and
collapse again. It comes back only after the peer set has been UP and dip-free
for the whole window - the same continuous stability the readiness fallback
asks for, which it would have had to meet to spawn anything anyway.

The single sticky slot keeps its one-owner rule: the slot is left alone when
another owner holds it, and released only while the message in it is still
ours.

fix(syncthing): make the health signal robust and stop peer traffic driving it

The node's syncthing health flag (syncthingStatusOk, read by isRunning) was set
as a side effect of getDeviceId, which getDeviceIdApi runs on every peer request
to /syncthing/deviceid. getDeviceId probes syncthing with three sequential calls
on a 5s timeout behind a lock, and a single failure flipped the flag false. So a
peer asking for this node's device id while syncthing was briefly busy could flip
the node's health, and on Arcane the sentinel never refreshed it at all (the only
refresh path was gated behind !isArcane). A transient blip then propagated:
isRunning false -> loginPhrase throws -> fluxbench CheckFlux fails -> the node's
benchmark fails. That is why nodes saw "Error on FluxOs response" benchmark
failures with no lasting fault.

Three changes decouple and harden the signal:

- probeSyncthing() is the raw, side-effect-free probe. getDeviceId() returns a
  cached device id (the id is SHA-256 of syncthing's cert - immutable for the
  life of the install, verified against lib/protocol/deviceid.go), so peers cost
  a lookup, not three requests, and getDeviceId no longer touches the flag.
- refreshSyncthingHealth() owns the flag with debounce: a success restores it at
  once; failures must reach SYNCTHING_HEALTH_FAILURE_THRESHOLD (3) consecutively
  before it drops. A blip can no longer fail the benchmark; a real outage still
  does. The sentinel calls it every loop, on Arcane and non-Arcane alike.
- The cached id is cleared in stopSyncthing - the only window a new cert (hence a
  new id) could appear.

ensureSyncthingRunning's liveness check now uses a fresh probeSyncthing rather
than the cached id. loginPhrase still gates on isRunning for now; the flag it
reads is simply trustworthy. Removing the one-strike grace hack in loginPhrase,
and moving node fitness off loginPhrase entirely, follow once a dedicated health
endpoint exists and fluxbench moves to it.

fix(peers): a ping in flight is not a missed pong

missedPongs was incremented when a ping was SENT, so it counted pings sent
since the last pong rather than pongs missed. A peer answering every ping
perfectly still read as having missed one for the whole round trip after each
ping, and everything that reads the counter believed it.

getEligibleSyncPeers believed it, and pingAll() pings every peer in one loop -
so for that window EVERY peer failed its `missedPongs !== 0` bar at once and the
pool of peers worth asking for app state was empty however healthy the fleet
was.

That window is not the rare RTT-sized race it looks like. A silent peer is
terminated from inside onPingSent, which runs inside that same pingAll loop, so
the disconnect fires while every surviving peer has just been pinged and none
has been credited with a pong yet. Measured on a node: 20ms from "missed pongs,
terminating" to "No peer left to ask, 1 state-sync answer is still needed". The
one moment the node must find a replacement peer is the moment it is structurally
blind to all of them - and nothing re-examines a pass that found nobody, so the
sync slot stays empty until an unrelated event happens by. Suite 83's ninth test
is exactly this and had been intermittent since at least 2026-09-06.

A ping going out now marks the peer as owing a pong; the NEXT ping is what
decides the previous one was missed, because by then it has had a full interval
to arrive. A peer answering normally sits at 0 always, and getEligibleSyncPeers'
existing bar becomes correct as written - it is not touched here.

A silent peer now takes maxMissedPongs whole intervals to drop rather than one
short: ~45s at the production interval, which is what peerResponsiveness already
documents ("keeps a full peer list for ~45s", "missedPongs moves on the first
missed round (~15s)"). Neither was true of the old counter, which dropped at 30s
and moved at 0s.

The five tests that encoded the old counting are updated, and the assertion that
a single ping leaves missedPongs at 1 - which was the defect written down - now
pins the opposite.

fix(apps): the reinstall pass takes its lock at the door, not where it announces itself

reinstallOldApplications guarded itself on
globalState.reinstallationOfOldAppsInProgress, which is a signal to other
subsystems rather than a lock. It is raised late and deliberately - deep inside
the loop, only for destructive work - because forceAppRemovals and the spawner
stand aside on it, and raising it at the door would hold them off for every
scan including the ones that find nothing.

So the guard covered everything except the setup: a daemon sync call, a
database read and one spec lookup per installed app. A second pass starting in
that gap saw the flag down and ran. Nothing stopped it afterwards either - the
per-app guards ask operationHolding('reinstallation'), which excludes that very
flag so a pass can ignore its own, and therefore ignores the other pass's too.
Two passes on one app is the case that destroys it.

One flag cannot be raised at two different moments, so this is two mechanisms.
The signal keeps its timing; a module-scope AsyncLock is taken on the first
line, checked and registered with no await between them, and released in a
finally that also clears the signal - so no return or throw inside the body can
leak either.

The canary set the flag and called once, which proves a guard reads a flag and
would pass just as happily against the open window. It now parks the first pass
inside checkSynced and starts a second, and a third test drives two sequential
passes so a lock that is never released is loud rather than silent. Each of
dropping the check, dropping the register and dropping the release turns one of
them red on its own.

fix(syncthing): derive health from the last good probe, and gate on it only where the operator owns syncthing

syncthingStatusOk was a stored verdict that defaulted to healthy and was only
lowered by an explicit write. Every path that failed to reach that write
reported health with nothing behind it: a throw out of ensureSyncthingRunning -
the exact state the repair path exists for, and it stops syncthing first - a
sentinel that never starts because the binary is missing, a probe that threw
rather than returned, or the loop dying outright. Those are not four bugs to
patch; they are one default asserting something it has not measured.

Health is now derived from lastHealthyProbeAt, and only success is ever
recorded. Nothing has to write a failure, so nothing can fail to. Staleness is
the failure, whatever caused it - including the sentinel never running at all,
which no amount of patching the lowering line could have covered. The window
absorbs the consecutive-failure counter, which was approximating a freshness
bound and only counted the passes that actually ran. Stamped at startup, so the
node has one window of grace while the webserver is up before the first probe.

probeSyncthing now parses the meta body inside its own try. It promises
{ok, deviceId}; a body that answers but does not parse is a failed probe, not
an exception thrown at the caller.

The fitness gate is scoped to legacy. It answers "has the operator broken
syncthing" - which is why the whole repair path, the ownership dance and the

fix(syncthing): a node that has not looked at syncthing says so, rather than blaming it

A node whose fluxd was slow to warm up reported that its SYNCTHING was broken.
The two are unrelated. Health was stamped healthy when the module loaded, and the
sentinel - the only thing that probes syncthing - started behind an unbounded wait
for daemon RPC, so a daemon that took more than the window to come up outlived the
stamp. The node then answered /id/loginphrase with "Syncthing is not running
properly" while nothing had ever looked at syncthing at all, and fluxbench, which
polls that endpoint, reported the node as failing for a reason that was not true.

The stamp was the defect. Deriving health from the last good probe is right, and
it left the other direction invented: a healthy default asserts a probe that never
ran. So health has three states and not two, and the absence of a verdict is one
of them rather than a guess dressed as one. UNMEASURED refuses nobody, because a
node that refuses itself on a check it has not run is reporting its own startup as
somebody else's fault.

Unmeasured is not a place to hide either. The sentinel stamps itself before its
binary wait, not after, so a legacy node whose syncthing executable is missing -
which never leaves that loop - still reads UNHEALTHY once the window passes. And
the sentinel now starts above the daemon wait, which it never had any business
being below: it talks to syncthing's own API and reads userconfig, and nothing it
does needs fluxd. Below it, a node with a broken daemon never measures syncthing
at all.

Both stamps are on the monotonic clock. They are elapsed-time decisions and
nothing outside this process reads them, so wall time buys nothing and costs the
one case the window exists for - a node boots, ntp steps the clock, and a window
measured on Date.now() either expires on the spot or never.

The transition log was comparing two readings taken either side of one probe. A
derived state changes with the clock rather than with an event, so those two are
the same reading almost every time and the line essentially never fired. It
compares against what was last reported now, the same bookkeeping idService keeps
for the fitness verdict, and it catches UNMEASURED -> UNHEALTHY too: a syncthing
that never once answered is the more serious of the two.

The window and the sentinel's cadence are config, because a suite that shortens
one has to shorten the other - shorten the window alone and a healthy node goes
stale between two good probes.

Suite 1701 booted the default node type, which is Arcane, where the syncthing term
is carved out entirely: it covered the endpoint without ever reaching the branch
that decides anything. It runs against both node types now. Suite 1702 is the
defect itself, reproduced rather than imitated - rpcFailures makes the daemon stub
answer -28 "Loading block index...", which is what waitForDaemonRpc loops on.

github harder is not the answer to a node with no policy: the design is
peers first, github as backstop, and under that a node boots, asks its
neighbours, and has a signed map off the local network in milliseconds.
The backoff, the jitter, the attempt counter and the cap all exist to
make polling one remote dependency less destructive, and none of them are
needed once the same signed bytes are available from six thousand local
sources.

Keeping them would also entrench the topology the design inverts, by
treating github as the source and peers as an optimisation.

The gap they were covering is real - the first fetch failing leaves a
node unable to acquire apps until the next refresh - and is closed by the
resolve ladder instead, where it costs nothing extra.

feat(policy): verify a signed policy bundle

FluxOS has no way to tell what fluxos-network-policy published from what
something in between handed it. That is tolerable while github is the
only place a node fetches policy from, and stops being tolerable the
moment a node takes policy from a peer -- which is the point of this.

verifyBundle is pure: bytes and a key list in, payload or null out. It
knows nothing about where a bundle came from, because once the signature
holds the source stopped mattering, and that is the property the whole
peers-first design rests on.

Null is the only failure signal. A caller that cannot tell forged from
malformed from too old treats all three identically -- this is not a
policy I can use -- so the reason goes to the log rather than into a
return value nobody would branch on.

Checks that are not obvious: the signature is verified over the
transmitted payload bytes rather than a re-serialisation, so key order
and whitespace never matter; signature length is checked first because
crypto.verify THROWS on a wrong-sized ed25519 signature instead of
answering false; a size cap is applied before parsing, because a source
that will not stop talking is the cost it is trying to impose; and seq
and documents are validated AFTER the signature holds, because a
signature proves who wrote a payload and not that its contents are sane.

minSeq refuses a bundle below the floor. A source asked for something
newer that answers with something older has not answered, and accepting
it is indistinguishable from there being nothing newer, which is the
whole of a freeze attack. Same contract as fluxbench PR #67.

Config gains signedBaseUrl and the two pinned public keys. Any of them
verifying is enough, so the cold key can take over without a release --
removing a compromised key from the list is what needs one.

The twelve tests found two bugs before anything depended on this. The
reject path was `return onReject(reason) || null`, which returns the
logger's own value when it is truthy -- Array.push returns a length. And
a regex I used to fix that collapsed five guarded returns into
unconditional ones, so verifyBundle rejected everything. Both were
invisible to reading and immediate under test.

Verified against the live published bundle: seq 1 accepted with the
pinned keys, refused against a higher floor.

feat(policy): resolve policy from what is nearest, verify all of it

The store behind the signed bundle: what this node holds, then peers,
then the published source. The same ladder contentBlobService.resolveBlob
uses for app content, for the same reason -- every candidate is verified
by the receiver, so a source that answers wrongly is skipped rather than
believed, and the ladder can prefer whatever is nearest without that
being a trust decision.

The ORDER is the point. In steady state nothing is fetched at all: the
stored bundle is valid and that is the end of it. When a refresh is due,
sixteen peers on the local network are asked before one request leaves
for github. A node that boots while github is unreachable gets its policy
from a neighbour -- which is what closes the gap the reverted retry
commits were flailing at, and closes it by removing the single point of
failure rather than by polling it more carefully.

The stored bundle is re-verified at boot, not trusted. That row is only
as good as whatever can write to this node's database, and the pinned
keys may have moved on since it was written. It is stored as the bytes
that were verified rather than the parsed payload, because re-serialising
leaves a document whose signature no longer checks and the whole point of
keeping it is to check it again.

The backstop response is taken as text. Letting axios parse it and this
module re-serialise would verify something the signer never signed.

Every read answers null rather than an empty value when no bundle has
been obtained, and adopting one opens globalState.policyReady. A node
that has never read policy must not act on the absence of it.

peerFetch is injected rather than reached for, so this module does not
depend on the communication layer and the ladder is testable without one.
It is wired in the commit that adds the peer messages.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat(policy): a change spreads from peers, github only seeds it

Peers-first did not make peers primary, and could not have. Polling can
only ask the source "is there anything newer?" -- so however low github
sat in the ladder, every node reached it on every refresh, because when
policy has not changed no peer has anything newer to offer and the ask
returns nothing useful. Peers were insurance, not the path.

Being TOLD inverts it. A node that adopts a sequence announces it to its
direct peers; a peer that is behind asks that node, adopts, and announces
to its own. A change spreads outwards from whichever node reached the
backstop first, in seconds rather than a refresh interval on every node
independently.

This is the shape contentBlobService already has. resolveBlob never asks
whether anything is newer -- it cannot, because content is immutable and
content-addressed: the node learns what it needs from the app spec and
then fetches those exact bytes from the nearest source, with FluxDrive
reached only when no peer has them. Steady state is no network at all.
Policy is mutable, so the equivalent of "learning what it needs" has to
come from somewhere, and an announcement is that.

Announced on adoption, never on a timer. That is what keeps it
affordable: the traffic is bounded by how often policy changes, weekly at
most, rather than by how often nodes check. A periodic announcement is
the same volume forever, which is why it was rejected earlier and why
this is not that.

The announcement carries a sequence only. A peer cannot check a claim
about a number, so it is a prompt to ask rather than something to
believe, and what comes back is a signed bundle, which it can check. A
peer claiming a sequence it cannot produce costs one request; a claim at
or below what the node holds costs nothing, because that is checked
first.

The backstop poll drops from 6h to 24h. It is no longer how a change
reaches a node -- it is for one that missed the announcement, and for the
cold start where there was nothing to miss.

Also replaces the peer wait: it polled Date.now() in a loop, which with
an instant delay spins for the full window and blew mocha's timeout. It
is a promise resolved by the arriving bundle now.

fix(harness): restartNode re-attaches the log collector

withLogConsumer's stream is a following read of the container's log and a
restart ENDS it. The collector recorded [LOG_STREAM_ENDED] and then heard
nothing for the rest of the run, so every log assertion placed after a restart
could only time out -- and it timed out looking like the product had stopped
doing the thing, rather than like the harness had stopped listening. It cost
most of a session on suite 99, and the workaround since has been to write
restart suites that never assert on a log.

`since` rather than `tail: 0`, captured BEFORE the restart: restart() does not
return until the wait strategy passes, by which time FluxOS has printed its
whole boot, so asking for no history would lose exactly the lines a restart
suite wants. The cost is that docker's filter is whole-second and re-delivers
what was written in that second, which the collector already holds -- so it is
handed the list and drops each replayed line once, for a bounded window, and a
line that genuinely repeats later is still recorded.

Measured against the collector this file ships, over a container printing a
unique line per tick, restarted mid-run:

  without suppression   85 captured, 51 distinct, 34 DUPLICATED
  with suppression      51 captured, 51 distinct,  0 duplicated

and the restarted container's first banner - written while restart() was still
waiting - is present in both. countPattern after a restart was previously
either blind or double-counting; it is now neither.

fix(policy): the peer rung was never offered a peer at boot

policyStore.start() runs at serviceManager.js:505. Discovery starts at :560 --
initializeDiscovery() and startDiscovery() are both still ahead of it, with an
awaited nodeConfirmationService.start() in between. So the boot refresh's
requestPolicyFromPeers broadcast reached an empty set, the 3s PEER_WINDOW_MS was
waited out for nothing, and the ladder fell through to the published source.

Peers were therefore first asked at the 24-HOUR backstop tick. A node that
booted while the source was unreachable held no policy for a day, with
neighbours beside it that had it -- which is the gap peers-first was chosen to
close, and it was open. The module's own comment says a node booting while
github is unreachable gets its policy from a neighbour; it did not.

An inbound peer may have dialled in before :505 on a restart into a live fleet,
so it was not always zero. Nothing made it so, and on a cold start it was.

The fix is to ask when there is finally somebody to ask: serviceManager tells
the store on peerConnected, and the store decides. While it holds NOTHING every
new peer is a fresh chance and gets one ask, bounded by the peer count and
stopping the moment a bundle is obtained; once it holds something, one ask is
enough, because being slightly behind is not urgent and the tick covers it.

This is not the retry that was reverted in 886a2dd90. That one polled github
harder on a timer, which is the wrong layer and reproduced the content-delivery
review's N7. This asks PEERS, once, on an event that already exists.

refresh() is now single-flight, which that change makes necessary: sixteen peers
connecting in a second would otherwise start sixteen refreshes, each able to
reach the backstop -- the same stampede by the back door.

Both properties are mutation-tested. Making notePeerAvailable inert fails all
four new tests; removing the single-flight guard fails exactly the one that
names it.

fix(policy): phase the backstop tick by node identity, and gate on the peer threshold

Two corrections, both David's.

THE TICK PHASE. The period is per node, so the fleet's distribution of ticks
IS its distribution of restarts. In steady state that is spread and the first
node to look finds a change within seconds of it being published. After a
release wave it is not: thousands of nodes restart together, their ticks bunch,
and the fleet then both waits a whole period for the first look AND makes that
look simultaneously - a synchronised fetch against the published source, which
is the content-delivery review's N7 wearing a 24-hour period. The phase then
persists until the next wave re-scatters it.

I proposed +/-10-20% jitter. That is arbitrary, and worse, it is RE-DRAWN on
every boot - so a restart wave still has every node rolling inside the same
minute and the spread decays back toward the restart distribution. The phase is
now derived from the node's collateral, which is unique and outlives a reboot:
a node returns to the slot it already had, restarting moves nothing, and the
fleet is uniformly spread over the period by construction rather than by luck.
Ticks are aligned to absolute time, so the schedule is a property of the node
and not of when it started.

Tested on the property, not the implementation: 6300 identities bucketed by
hour fill all 24 within +/-20% of even, and 200 nodes land on 200 distinct
slots. A CONSTANT phase fails both of those; a RANDOM phase passes them and
fails the determinism test instead, which is the whole distinction.

THE PEER GATE. I had used a raw outbound+inbound tally and triggered on
peerConnected, which fires per connection - sixteen asks as the set fills.
peerManager already defines "enough peers to gossip with" hysteretically:
appSyncPeerThreshold 12 on the way up, appSyncDegradedThreshold 4 on the way
down, with peerThresholdReached as the edge and peerCountIfAboveThreshold as
the level for a subscriber that attaches after the crossing. Using those means
the policy rung opens and closes with the same peer set the spawner and the
sync orchestrator use, one ask per crossing, and no flapping on a reconnect.

feat(policy): a restored bundle is held until no reachable peer is ahead

A node must not spawn on stale policy. restore() used to read a bundle off
disk, verify the signature, and open the acquisition gate on the strength of
that - but disk proves a bundle is REAL, not that the network still agrees with
it. A node that was down while policy moved came back and started installing on
the old documents.

The window is small and the consequence is not: what happens inside it is an
INSTALL, and an install placed against superseded policy is the defect this
whole workstream exists for - an app put somewhere it should not be and taken
away from its owner by the ownership sweep minutes later.

So a restored bundle is HELD, and the gate opens when:

  - a peer reports a sequence no higher than ours, or
  - we adopt something, from anywhere

A peer reporting HIGHER is not agreement, it is the discovery that we are the
stale one; we ask for what it has and the adoption opens the gate.

WHAT THIS CLAIMS, EXACTLY: no peer I can reach is ahead of me. Not "my policy
is current" - no node can know that without an authority, which is the
dependency this design removes. The distinction matters because a peer may hold
its copy only because we just gave it one, and its report looks identical
either way. That echo is harmless: "nobody I can reach is ahead" is true
whoever the copy came from. What it cannot see is an isolated segment where
everyone is stale together, and no node can see that from the inside - the
backstop tick corrects it.

Excluding peers we had served was tried and is wrong: we only ever serve a peer
that asked with a LOWER sequence, so in the case the rule exists for - we hold
the freshest policy on our segment - we serve everybody, exclude everybody, and
never open the gate at all. Stuck is worse than echoed.

Peers now answer a request they cannot improve on with their sequence instead
of with silence, because silence cannot be told from absence, and that
difference is the whole question being asked.

No fallback for "nobody answered", deliberately: a node with no peer set is
below appSyncPeerThreshold and should not be acquiring apps anyway. See
workstreams/peer-gated-readiness - that invariant is not enforced today, and
this rule assumes it.

Mutation-tested: re-opening the gate in restore(), treating a peer that is
AHEAD as agreement, and removing the check from adopt() each turn a distinct
set red.

The peer rung serves a node holding NOTHING and a node holding something
STALE, and they are different questions. Holding nothing needs the whole
ladder, because the peer may hold nothing either and the published source is
the floor. Holding something needs one answer -- is THIS peer ahead -- which
is one signed message and one reply on the local network.

That second rung is now targeted and separate. requestPolicyFromPeer asks a
single socket; respondWithPolicy answers it exactly as it answers a
broadcast, so nothing changes on the far side. It settles on the peer's
reply rather than on a clock: every peer answers, with a bundle if it is
ahead, its sequence if it is not and null if it holds nothing, so silence
means only that the peer is gone and peerWindowMs bounds that case alone.

It cannot reach the published source. The source is rate-limited and shared
by the fleet, so anything able to reach it has to run on the backstop's
timer; a rung that runs on every arrival must not be able to. That
separation is what makes asking per join affordable, and askedPeersSinceBoot
is gone with it -- a node now asks each peer that arrives, for as long as it
holds policy.

Without it a node that was behind had no rung at all. It could only be TOLD,
and being told is a broadcast it has to be connected to hear: a peer that
adopts in the seconds before it connects announces to nobody, and nothing
afterwards revisits it. On a fleet, node 1 adopted seq 7 at 14:18:09.9 and
connected at 14:18:14.0; node 2 stayed on seq 2 with its next backstop tick
nine hours away. Suite 1502's fourth test is that node, and it fails on the
code this replaces.

1502 also gains the assertion that keeps the rung away from the source under
churn: arrivals made by healing a partition rather than by restarting, since
a restarted node fetches during its boot refresh and would move the counter
for a reason the assertion could not tell apart.

NOT covered, and known: a node that is stale with a stable peer set and no
arrivals still has nothing to trigger it, and waits for the backstop. Closing
that needs a periodic peer reconciliation, which this makes affordable but
does not add.

fix(comms): a question is not news, so two nodes may ask the same one

messageCache is a flood filter keyed on the payload alone, and for news that
is exactly right: two copies of "I have seq 2" are the same fact whoever
relayed them, and acting once is the point.

A request is not news. `{fluxapprequest, version, hash}` is what EVERY node
missing that hash sends, and `{fluxpolicyrequest, version, seq}` is what
every node at that sequence sends -- so the sender is the only thing telling
two askers apart, and it is the one part the key throws away. The second
asker looks like a repeat of the first and is dropped with no answer, no NAK
and no log. On a five-node fleet, one node's request was served and two got
silence.

Directed types now skip the cache in both directions. They are
point-to-point, so they cannot arrive twice by different routes and there is
nothing to suppress; and nothing ever fetches a question from the store by
hash, so there is nothing to keep. The cache holds less, not more.

Everything else is untouched: the content hash stays the message's name on
the wire, which the hash-gossip protocol depends on, and the cache check
stays ahead of signature verification so flood duplicates still never reach
it -- the ~2,400 messages a minute that collapse to ~135.

THE TEST FOR THE LIST IS NOT "IS IT RELAYED". fluxpolicyseq is relayed by
nobody and is still news, spread by each adopter announcing to its own
peers; classifying it as directed would remove its flood suppression, and
since notePeerSeq broadcasts a request whenever it sees a higher sequence,
26 peers announcing one sequence would become 26 broadcast requests. The
test is whether the sender's identity changes what the message means.

fluxapprequest has carried this defect independently of any policy work: two
nodes missing the same app message ask, one is answered, the other waits.

1502 gains the case a single asker cannot show - both the one-hop and the
two-hop node must be answered, with the source held down so neither can have
fetched it - and an afterEach that restores the source per test, because a
failure that left it down turned one red into three.

fix(policy): holding a bundle is not being up to date

The peer rung chose between the full ladder and the targeted ask on whether
the node held anything. Restored is the case that breaks: a node that read a
bundle off disk holds one and is still behind until something says
otherwise. restore() says so itself -- it adopts the bundle without opening
the gate, because disk proves a bundle was real, never that it is still the
network's.

Such a node took the targeted rung, which by design cannot fetch, so it
could not reach the published source at all. Its peers may be equally stale,
which leaves nothing able to move it until the backstop tick, up to a day
out. On a fleet: a node restarted while the source held a newer sequence
never picked it up.

The gate is `confirmed` instead. Unconfirmed covers the cold start and the
restart alike, and both want the same thing -- the whole ladder, on every
arriving peer, with the source as the floor under a network that may have
nothing newer to offer. Once something confirms the node is current, arrivals
cost one message and one reply.

The distinction was already in the module and already named; this uses it.

fix(policy): a fleet that restarted together cannot confirm itself

Peers-first needs one guarantee to stand up: that the ladder runs at all.

A node that restores a bundle holds something stale and cannot tell. Its
peers answer "not ahead", which is true and useless, and that answer marks it
confirmed in milliseconds -- so gating the ladder on confirmation meant a
restarted node asked nobody anything beyond "are you ahead", and the answer
was always no.

A whole fleet restarted together is the case that breaks: every node restores
the same stale bundle, every node reassures every other, and no node ever
reaches the point where peers come up empty and the published source decides
it. A document published while they were down would wait for a backstop tick
up to a day out. Suite 1601 is exactly this -- it restarts every node,
publishes a ban, and the ban never arrived.

The ladder now runs once per boot regardless of what any peer says. Peers are
still asked first and still answer first; the source is still only the floor
they fall through to. What changed is that agreement between nodes that all
just restarted no longer counts as evidence.

This is what askedPeersSinceBoot guaranteed before it was removed, restored
without the half that stopped a node which is merely BEHIND from ever asking
again: arrivals after the first still take the targeted rung.

fix(policy): confirmation is not a token, and an unverified 200 is not the publisher

globalState.policyReady is the conjunction of two independent facts - this node
HOLDS a bundle, and NO REACHABLE PEER IS AHEAD of it. markConfirmed recorded that
conjunction in a one-way latch that only tracked one of them:

    if (confirmed) return;
    confirmed = true;      // spent here
    if (!current) return;  // guard runs after

Reached with an empty store, the latch was gone and the gate could never open
again for the life of the process. adopt() calls markConfirmed, so a node that
subsequently obtained perfectly valid policy held exactly the right bundle and
returned installDelay from trySpawningGlobalApplication forever. Only a restart
cleared it, and nothing in the database looked wrong.

Two ways in, both reachable. A backstop 200 whose body does not verify, on a node
with nothing stored - which on the release that ships this is the entire fleet.
And one peer sending seq 0: {type:'fluxpolicyseq', version:1, seq:0} is a single
signed broadcast from any node in the deterministic list, not relayed, so it
wedges its direct peers and survives them obtaining good policy afterwards.

The gate is now DERIVED from the pair rather than written by whichever fact
arrives second, so no ordering of the two can strand it. Every write to either
one re-derives, restore() included: start() awaits restore(), a peer can answer
inside that await, and a restore that set `current` without re-deriving would
strand the gate exactly as the latch did.

THE SECOND DEFECT IS THE ONE THAT FAILS OPEN, and moving the guard does not fix
it. refresh() confirmed on any body the source returned, because consider()
collapsed "did not verify" and "verified, nothing new" into the same false. A
node holding restored seq 2 while the network is at seq 50 therefore opened its
acquisition gate because a captive portal answered 200 - acting on policy the
network has moved past, which is the one thing this module exists to refuse.
consider() now says which kind of no it means, and only a signature distinguishes
the publisher from whatever answered for it.

Five of the six unit tests fail against the previous module. The sixth is the
control - the publisher serving the sequence already held must STILL confirm, so
that "never confirms" cannot pass as a fix. One of the five fails against the
smaller version of this change (guard moved, gate still written by hand), which
is what makes the derived gate load-bearing rather than tidier.

1502 gains the fleet case. A node that met the bad answer and is STILL RUNNING is
the only one that can show this: a restart builds a fresh process and clears it,
so node 1 is restarted as the courier and node 0, never restarted, is the
subject. It must not merely end up holding the bundle - holding it is what the
defect already did - it must get past the policy gate and consider apps again.

fix(comms): a peer that lies low is acted on, and says why that is safe

The comment claimed the opposite - "a peer that lies low is ignored (we only act
on a HIGHER claim)". policyStore.notePeerSeq takes a sequence at or below its own
as confirmation and opens the acquisition gate, so a low claim is acted on.

What the comment was reaching for is true, but for a different reason than it
gave. The protocol does not depend on the claim: a peer that is genuinely ahead
does not send a sequence at all, it sends the bundle, which is signed and
verified by the receiver. Being ahead is PROVEN; only being level is asserted.

A peer lying low therefore buys the time between its lie and the real bundle
arriving from any honest peer, because the ask goes to all of them. For the lie
to stand, every peer would have to be at or below this node - which is the
network being level, and confirmation being right.

fix(comms): say where the bound on a directed message actually lives

Taking fluxapprequest and fluxpolicyrequest out of messageCache reads like
removing the only thing limiting them, and it is the first conclusion a reader
reaches. It is wrong twice over, and the comment now says so rather than leaving
each reader to re-derive it.

messageCache keys on the payload, which the sender of a QUESTION controls - vary
the hash on a fluxapprequest and it is defeated in one line. It suppressed
accidental duplicates, which is what it is for, and was never a bound against a
peer that did not want to be bounded.

The per-peer bound is FluxPeerSocket's inbound token bucket, lruRateLimit at 120
messages per second, applied to every frame before dispatch. It counts messages
rather than bytes, and a ~60-byte request does draw the whole bundle back - 127 KB
as published today. That is worth knowing and it is still not a reflection vector:
these arrive on an established websocket, so the sender cannot be spoofed and
receives every byte it asked for. A peer can make this node serve it quickly; it
cannot make this node serve anyone else.

Also records where a byte budget would go if one is ever wanted - lruRateLimit,
covering every type - rather than a second counter beside the first, because two
places to look is how a rate limiter stops being one.

fetched the table from config.policy.baseUrl - the UNSIGNED branch, under the
mutable name - and checked nothing but that it parsed.

So the release that moves policy inside a signature left its largest artifact
outside one. Four point eight megabytes that decide every node's geolocation, and
therefore which apps may be placed where, taken on the publisher's word while the
hash that would have settled it shipped in the bundle, unread.

bundle verifies under the fleet's pinned keys at seq 2; its artifact entry names

content-addressed file from signedBaseUrl, and refuses anything whose length or
digest disagrees. A node holding no bundle does not fetch at all: there is nothing
to verify against, and an unverified table is the thing this refuses.

the content does, so "do I already hold it" is a comparison against a signed value
rather than a question put to the server that would be serving the answer. The
repository stores the digest in place of the etag and computes it from the bytes it
actually wrote, so the record cannot claim a hash it does not hold. A record from

where every real bundle reads `file`, and carried no `bytes` at all. A consumer

test(policy): the stale fleet is corrected by a tick, not by a fetch at boot

1502's "a node behind its peers catches up from them when it regains one"
restarted a node and waited for it to fetch from the source. What made that

fix(policy): ask peers before github, and ask github only once they have answered

A node with no policy went to github at boot, every time, even when the neighbour
beside it held the bundle. The peer rung could not be taken: policyStore.start()
runs at serviceManager.js:554 and startDiscovery() at :609, so the peer set is
empty on every node at that point, and the rung below asking peers is the
published source. "No peers yet" and "peers have nothing" were the same answer.

Boot now reaches the source never. Each peer is asked as it arrives, which is
where the bundle actually comes from, and the source is reached only when all
three of these hold: no ask is outstanding, the peer set is above the threshold,
and this node still holds nothing. Together they mean nobody reachable has
policy, which is the first rollout and the only case github is for.

Derived as each ask settles rather than fired on peerThresholdReached, because
the edge can never satisfy it: the peer that crosses the threshold is asked
first, so its own ask is always outstanding at the moment the edge fires.
Reading the threshold as a level also leaves no latch of ours to re-arm - a node
that fell below the degraded level and peered back up asks its new peers, and
the last of those answers with the level true again. There is no retry timer,
deliberately; a source that does not answer is left to the phased tick.

peerCountIfAboveThreshold is gone. It returned the peer count above the
threshold and 0 below it, so 0 meant "no peers" and 0 also meant "eleven peers",
and every caller had to be told which it was reading. All three wanted the flag;
the one that read it as a tally is the defect above. isAboveThreshold answers the
question that was being asked, and getNumberOfPeers - which always means what it
says - covers the one log line that wanted a number.

peerConnected is now emitted before peerThresholdReached. A listener that starts
per-connection work and reads the result of it on the edge needs the connection
handled first; the reverse order declares the set complete while withholding the
peer that completed it.

THE LOCATION TABLE FOLLOWS THE BUNDLE, ON AN EVENT. The bundle names which file
is the iplocation table and what it must hash to, so ipLocationSync cannot act
until one is held - and it starts on dbReady, which is a fact about the app
database and says nothing about policy. Both chains hang off the peer threshold
and nothing orders them, so which finished first was a race, won in practice and
guaranteed nowhere; and a bundle arriving later, naming a new baseline, was not
noticed until the next daily refresh. policyStore.onBundleChanged is fired
wherever `current` is written - adoption and restore, because a bundle off disk
is equally the one this node holds - and ipLocationSync subscribes. A bundle
cancels a pending backoff rather than letting the node sit out an interval
chosen for a condition that has since changed, and one arriving mid-fetch is
coalesced, because a pass reads the bundle it had when it started.

refresh() now answers whether a request left the node as well as whether a table
was installed, so the retry is armed only for a fetch that failed. A pass that
found no bundle asked nobody anything, and waiting ten minutes to ask nobody
again achieves nothing - what it waits for arrives on an event.

Unit: 6569 passing, 17 pending, 0 failing. Six mutations tried and each caught by
one test - the outstanding-asks term, the threshold term, the emit order, the
seed's placement in askPeer's finally, the restore notification, and the
mid-fetch coalescing. Two harness events added and allowlisted:
policy:bundleChanged and ipLocation:tableInstalled.

test(policy): cover the peer ramp, the fleet that never peers, and the table following the bundle

Three blocks, for the three properties the change to acquisition rests on and
that no suite could previously observe.

THE RAMP. appSyncPeerThreshold is 2 in the harness against 12 in production,
which makes "has peers and is below the threshold" one connection wide - and
that state is the whole subject, because it is where the count the store used to
read said zero while peers existed. Ten nodes give the derived ring an arc of 4,
so every node settles on eight peers and a threshold of six is crossed on the way
there. Only the threshold is pinned; the arc stays derived, as E2E_FLEET_SIZING
requires. A late-joining node must take policy from a peer with the source up and
counting - not a fixture that makes github impossible, but a node choosing not to
use it.

THE FLEET THAT CANNOT FINISH PEERING. Three dialers at arc 1 give every node two
peers against a threshold of six, so the edge cannot fire however long it waits,
and an available source must go untouched. This is the sharpest form of the rule:

fix(applogs): a node cannot say what was cut from a line it joined part-way through

Suite 84 has been red on development since the applogs work landed, and no open
PR touches the handler - 1801 and 1361 do not, 1767 and 1197 touch dockerService
only. The four commits that own this behaviour are ancestors of both development
and this branch, so it is inherited rather than ours, and it will sit in every
gate until someone takes it.

THE ARITHMETIC NAMES THE CAUSE. A truncation notice reported 306308 characters
where a whole cut line is 251458 - a 31-character stamp plus the 1300003-byte
blob less the 1048576 cap. The remainder is 54850, and 251458 - 54850 is 196608,
which is exactly twelve of docker's 16KB frames. The stream had opened twelve
frames into a line.

It opens with `tail`, and docker's tail counts ENTRIES, not lines. A container
whose lines fit inside one 16KB frame gives one line per entry and the stream
does begin on a line boundary; one writing 1.3MB lines does not, and the first
thing to arrive is the end of a line the node never saw the start of. It then
reported what it had cut from that line - a figure true of what arrived and false
of the line, which is what a reader takes it for.

The decoder now withholds that one claim until the first newline proves the next
line was seen from the start. The line itself is still handed over. Dropping it -
skipping to the first record boundary, which is the usual discipline for joining
a line-delimited stream at an unknown offset - costs every ordinary container a
real line of backfill to protect the rare one, and eleven handler tests said so.

The join ends inside #settle rather than beside either caller, because a line can
end in two places - the loop that hands lines over, and the branch draining the
tail of one past the cap - and a flag cleared in only one of them stays set
through the other, silencing every line after it. That was a real defect while
this was being written, caught by tests that already existed.

BACKFILL_LINES was two quantities sharing a number. It set docker's `tail`, which
is entries, and it capped feed.recent, which is lines - so a viewer arriving
second got 200 lines where the first got 200 frames, and on a container writing
long lines those are not the same amount of history. Split into BACKFILL_ENTRIES
and REPLAY_LINES, with the entries one saying what it costs: a fixed number of
LINES would mean over-fetching and counting newlines, and the bound exists
because a tail establishes at 2 CPU ticks against 15 without one.

Suite 84 needs no change, which is the test that this sits at the right level.
Three mutations, each caught: counting the joined line anyway, never clearing the
join, and defaulting it on - the last breaks four decoder tests, because the
polling read is handed one whole payload and starts at a boundary.

with the message. It rides inside `data`, where the signature already covers

messages are kept - the old write happened before verifyFluxBroadcast, so an

fix(policy): one ask, put to the peers that can answer it, settled by its answer

There were two ways of asking. The targeted one records the question, names it, and
ends on the reply that names it. The broadcast one recorded nothing: it sent to
everybody and then waited a fixed moment to see whether the sequence had moved, so
which peers had answered was never known and "nobody has policy" was a conclusion
drawn from a timer. A question that is not recorded cannot be answered, only outlived.

Asking the network is now the same ask put to each peer, and it returns when every one
of them has answered or gone. The broadcast, the latch it woke, and the window it raced
are gone; the window is the deadline on a single ask again, which is what its comment
already claimed. A peer that says it is ahead is asked directly rather than prompting a
question to everybody, since it is the one that made the claim.

Peers are asked only if they advertise the policyBundle capability. One that does not
has no handler for the ask, so including it bought a deadline's wait for a reply that
could not come and put an unrecognised-type warning in its log once per adoption.

An answer settles the ask it names, and nothing else settles anything. An adoption
announcement carries no id, and that is deliberate: it is what keeps the content address
identical across the nodes that adopted the same sequence, which is what lets the flood
filter collapse them into one. So whether a given peer's announcement arrives at all
depends on whether an unrelated peer sent the same bytes first, and a fact about one
peer cannot ride on that.

fix(policy): seeding is a question about the peer set, not the tail of one ask

A node asked every peer that connected, including ones advertising no policyBundle
capability. Those have no handler for the question, so the ask bought a deadline here and an

next line, so the arrival that crosses the threshold evaluates the decision while the level

that stops exactly at the threshold has nothing left to re-trigger it.

A settled ask is kept until its peer disconnects, so the question belongs to the connection:
an arrival does not repeat what this peer already answered, a reconnect is a new question,
and the tick asks again regardless. peerDisconnected discards it, which also ends an ask

demand four different reactions: the app is already there, the node is busy

Merge pull request #1807 from RunOnFlux/fix/apprunning-is-a-claim

fluxapprunning is a placement claim, not a health report

fix(volumes): a disk an app can be put on is one the node may use and can write into

An app's hdd allocation is enforced by giving it a filesystem of exactly that
size: a file is allocated, an ext4 image made inside it, and that image mounted
at the app's directory. The image is a file, so where it goes is a question
about a directory - and the answer was being derived from device names.

Placement enumerated every mount on the box and took the first whose free space
cleared the reserve. Nothing asked whether the mount point was a directory, so
where docker binds its own files into a containerised FluxOS - /etc/hostname,
/etc/hosts, /etc/resolv.conf, each reporting the host disk's free space - the
first of them won and fallocate answered "Not a directory". Every install on
such a node failed, and testAppMount failed the same way at boot, which puts the
node in DOS with "Unavailability to mount applications volumes".

Those binds are also one filesystem reported four times, and their free space was
added up once per bind, so a node with 1.8 TiB free believed it had 7.3 TiB.

There is one notion of a disk here now. isHostFilesystem is a filesystem the node
may use: real, surviving a reboot, not the boot disk, and not an app volume it
has already placed - a loop mount IS such a volume, except at the root, where a
loop is the host disk itself. Three questions are asked of it: capacity counts
each filesystem once; placement adds that the mount point is a writable
directory, counts each disk once and takes the emptiest; and the search for an
existing image asks the same as placement minus the root, whose images live in
appvolumes, and does not deduplicate, because two directories on one disk are two
places an image can sit.

Ranking by free space replaces taking the first that fits. Taking the first put
every app on one disk: a node with three of them filled the one the mount table
happened to name first, reaching the others only for an app too big for what was
left, so the apps contended for a single disk's I/O while the rest of the
operator's hardware sat idle. Which disk that was is a docker and kernel detail -
the same two nodes, one on docker 29.3.1 and one on 29.8.1, order those mounts
differently. Emptiest first spreads volumes across the disks an operator
provided.

The block-device test is gone. findmnt --real has already dropped the pseudo
filesystems and a container's overlay, so what it added was refusing a ZFS or
btrfs root, which findmnt names by dataset - on such a node the candidate list
came back empty and no app could be installed at all. What it has to say instead
is said directly: a filesystem whose contents do not survive a reboot is never a
host disk.

Placement and the search for an image now share that predicate, so the place an
image is put and the places it is looked for cannot drift apart.

What is excluded is a mount UNDER the apps folder, which is an app's own volume,
and not the folder itself: that is an ordinary directory, and an operator with a
small root disk may well have given it one of its own. An image there is named
<appId>FLUXFSVOL and collides with no mount point.

The fixtures are mount tables read off the fleet rather than composed: two Arcane
nodes, a legacy node, and a containerised FluxOS, plus a loop-mounted root and a
dataset-named root for the shapes the fleet may hold and these three did not.

fix(policy): the compliance sweep follows the policy, not a clock

The blocklist reaches a node in seconds now that it travels in the signed bundle, so
the hourly tick the sweep was armed on became the whole of the wait between the
network banning something and this node acting on it - up to an hour, and a full hour
after boot before anything looked at all.

It is driven by the bundle instead: a pass when the gate opens and a pass on every
change while it is open, which is what every other consumer of the bundle already
does. Both are staggered, because adopting a bundle fires both - adopt opens the gate
before it announces and the gate drains its waiters synchronously, so an unstaggered
gate trigger puts the whole fleet's removals into one instant.

A REFUSAL IS NOT A REMOVAL. removeAppLocally returned void: its guards return having
touched nothing when the node is already installing or removing, and its catch does
not rethrow. A caller could not tell "removed" from "refused", so a blocked
application could be marked done while still running, with nothing coming back for
it. It now answers a RemovalOutcome, the mirror of the InstallOutcome the install side
has carried since it had the same problem. Thirty-seven callers ignore the value and
are unaffected.

The list is asked again before each removal, and so is the record. A pass holds itself
open for minutes: an entry lifted while it ran was still acted on and the uninstall
broadcast, and an application redeployed onto a clean image was judged on the one it
no longer runs.

What has no event is owed by name, on a self-cancelling backoff: a specification that
did not decrypt, a removal the node was too busy to take, one that failed, and the
applications a stopped pass never reached. A node owing nothing runs no timer.

An owner transfer reaches reinstallOldApplications through the branch that writes the
record without redeploying - owner is not part of the comparison that chooses it - so
the new owner was never judged against the blocklist by any path. The names are
collected and swept after the pass, outside its lock: that function's own header
records what concurrent uninstalls cost the last time.

The sweeper is an object that owns its state and takes its dependencies, including the
clock and its knobs. As file-scope state it was reachable from two entry points that
disagreed about it, and a test could only get a clean one by deleting the module from
the require cache.

Suite 1601 no longer restarts every node to make them see a new document, and that is
the assertion: same processes, same mesh, same installed application, and the only
thing that changes is the document. Its bound is under any periodic pass, because at
the harness's compression of the old interval a generous bound measured nothing.

fix(volumes): a disk that went read-only is not a missing image

will not. A recorded path is where an image was put; a volume re-created

because the refusal returns before the line that would replace it.

Syncthing indexes the volume as root on every node. FluxOS is root on Arcane
and the operator's user elsewhere, and the volume holds what the app's
container wrote under the ownership and mode that container chose - postgres

folder is demoted and the app stopped.

of those exclusions is anchored. The reading the caller asked for travels
with the question, since a folder whose payload is empty directories holds
none of the regular files the other reading looks for.

The verdict is the exit status: find renders its errors in the node's locale.
The path is absolute or the probe refuses it - find reads a leading dash as
an option, and an app names the directories on its own volume, so a bare
`--version` would answer with find's own version and read as content.

fix(daemon): a fluxnode has no wallet, so FluxOS stops publishing one

FluxOS proxied fluxd's entire wallet surface: 63 routes covering key export and
import, spending, signing, wallet backup and the shielded pool. A fluxnode has
no wallet to drive - the only daemon-side secret it uses is the node identity,
and the single call that touches it creates the confirmation transaction - so
none of it was ever called, by FluxOS, by the frontend, or by any other repo.

Three of the 63 were reachable unauthenticated: gettransaction and both
fundrawtransaction variants sat in the public block while every sibling asked
for the node operator. gettransaction answers only for transactions in the
node's own wallet, verified against a live node by asking it for a confirmed
on-chain transaction and being refused; getrawtransaction already serves the
chain-wide lookup publicly, so nothing legitimate is lost.

The other 60 were behind the operator, which is why this is not a vulnerability
fix. It removes what the next authorization mistake could reach: with the
routes gone there is no supported way to put a spendable key on a node through
the API, and every remaining wallet route becomes an empty room.

Also gone: the Sprout-era raw joinsplit RPCs, which fluxd's own help marks
DEPRECATED and which take secret keys as URL parameters, where a GET puts them
in the access log.

sendrawtransaction stays public. It holds no wallet secret and broadcasting is
a service a node can reasonably offer.

The five getaddress lookups move to the public block they belong in. They read
the chain's address index, their POST twins were already public and return the
same data, and their handlers never checked a privilege - so the operator
banner over them described a protection that was not there.

The RPC client's method map loses the wallet names too, so a wallet RPC is now
unreachable rather than merely unrouted: fluxRpc refuses any method not in the
map, and nothing FluxOS invokes was among the 67 removed.

createconfirmationtransaction moves to the fluxnode RPCs, which is what it is,
and the wallet and shielded modules are deleted whole.

The surface is pinned as the complete list of daemon routes rather than as
absences, because "this route is gone" passes just as happily over a route
table that failed to build.

registered the app. A node must not treat that as an address it may dereference

21,357 links in the chain's history already names it and nothing else, so this
describes the feature rather than narrowing it, but the rule stands on what the

and a substring test admits any host carrying the name in a query, and both

than revalidated per hop: with one legitimate host there is no hop to allow,

choose the node's next request for it.

identity rule that is held there for the same reason. Replayed messages must
validate as they always did: 166 links on chain would fail this rule, and a

from the same chain.

F_S_CONTACTS is left alone. It has the same shape and nothing in FluxOS
dereferences it, so a URL there is not a request any node will make.

The host is configuration, so the unit and harness configs can point it at a

storage.

cache for an hour, and the amount, coin and addresses a wallet sends are
recorded nowhere.

whoever holds a live one can leave a transaction id for the browser waiting on

feat(apps): compressobject archives a list of entries

`source` may be a list of entries. The archiver runs in the deepest
folder holding all of them and is handed each entry's path from there,
so the archive holds exactly the listed entries: entries sharing a
folder arrive under their bare names, and an entry in a subfolder keeps
that subfolder. A directory in the list arrives as itself rather than
as its contents. A client compressing a selection no longer copies it
into a temporary folder first, which needed the selection's size again
in free space and left the folder behind when the client went away
partway.

Each entry is paired with the destination and so gets every guard a
single source does: it exists, it resolves inside the volume, it is not
a reserved name or inside staging however it is spelled, and the
archive is not written over it or inside it. An entry listed twice, an
entry inside another listed entry, an empty list and a list of more
than 1000 entries are refused before anything runs. Entries are
resolved and measured one at a time, so a long list does not queue its
filesystem work ahead of every other request, and the space check
covers all of them together. A single `source` string keeps its
meaning.

feat(volume): pin flux-volume-tools v1.5.1; compress and extract limit each file as it is written

v1.5.1 splits the result ceiling from the write-time limit. --max-bytes
checks a command's result once it has finished, by what it occupies;
--max-file-bytes limits each file's length as the command writes it.
Compress and extract pass both, since their output size is unknown until
it is written. Copy passes only --max-bytes: its source is measured
before it starts, so a sparse file that fits the volume is copied.

v1.5.1 also exits 1 for a command that fails, writing the command's own
status to stderr, so the statuses the executor maps to a refusal come
only from flux-op: a corrupt archive no longer reads as a full volume.

The ids are the config digests of each architecture's manifest under
the v1.5.1 manifest list, the method that reproduces v1.5.0's pins.

fix(volumes): an operation writing into staging is refused if it starts under the floor

The free-space floor applies from the start: an operation that writes
into staging is refused before its container is created when the volume
is already under minFreeBytes, whatever its length. One that writes
nothing into staging - a removal, a move - still runs, since that is
how an owner gives the space back.
